The falling away comes first; the tyrant only harvests what the apostasy planted. Evil's power is downstream of the faithful's surrender.
cards.uw: Use when diagnosing how a bad regime or movement actually rose — look for the prior internal collapse, not the external force. Use when tempted to blame the invader instead of the open gate.

cards.title: History proceeds forward as a circle ever enlarging
cards.book: The Patristical Idea of Antichrist — St. John Henry Newman
cards.steal: Every event of this world is a type of those that follow, history proceeding forward as a circle ever enlarging. The days of the Apostles typified the last days: there were false Christs, and risings, and troubles, and persecutions. In like manner, every age presents its own picture of those still future events.
cards.why: Newman gives a way to read the news without hysteria or complacency: history rhymes because it spirals — each age stages a small, legible version of the final things. Antiochus, Julian, and Mahomet are not the Antichrist, but they are his rehearsals. The pattern is real; the scale is what grows.
cards.uw: Use when a present crisis feels unprecedented — look for the smaller type in the past that already played this scene. Use when someone cries that this is the end, or that this has never happened before.

cards.title: Antichrist was come, and was not come
cards.book: The Patristical Idea of Antichrist — St. John Henry Newman
cards.steal: Little children, it is the last time; and as ye have heard that the Antichrist shall come, even now are there many Antichrists; whereby we know that it is the last time. Antichrist was come, and was not come; it was, and it was not the last time.
cards.why: Newman holds the paradox St. John forces on every generation: the spirit is already at work — the mystery of iniquity doth already work — and yet the final form is still future. This kills both errors at once: the complacency that says nothing is happening, and the date-setting that says it is happening now. Every age lives in the overlap.
cards.uw: Use when the signs are real but the conclusion is premature. Use when someone is either asleep or panicked — the text holds both truths at once.

cards.title: Having rejected the true Christ, they should take up with a false one
cards.book: The Patristical Idea of Antichrist — St. John Henry Newman
cards.steal: It was the judicial punishment of the Jews, as of all unbelievers in one way or another, that, having rejected the true Christ, they should take up with a false one.
cards.why: Newman's hardest doctrine in the lectures: unbelief does not leave you empty — it leaves you occupied. Rejection of the true is not a neutral vacancy; it is a judgment that takes the form of being handed over to the counterfeit. The mind that refuses the real Christ does not stay free; it becomes available to whoever comes in his own name.
cards.uw: Use when watching people who left a faith or a cause and then attached themselves to something worse. Use when the emptiness left by rejection keeps getting filled by impostors.

cards.title: They called it Liberty, and literally worshipped it as a divinity
cards.book: The Patristical Idea of Antichrist — St. John Henry Newman
cards.steal: After having broken away from all restraint as regards God and man, they gave a name to that reprobate state itself into which they had thrown themselves, and exalted it, that very negation of religion, or rather that real and living blasphemy, into a kind of god. They called it Liberty, and they literally worshipped it as a divinity. They appointed festivals besides in honour of Reason, the Country, the Constitution, and the Virtues.
cards.why: Newman's exhibit from the French Revolution: men who abjured every worship could not abide the vacuum — they canonized their own negation. The pattern is permanent: whatever dethrones God gets enthroned in His place, even if it has to be an abstraction. Iconoclasm always ends in a new altar.
cards.uw: Use when a movement claims to have abolished worship and then starts holding festivals. Use when the rational replacement for religion starts demanding the devotion religion used to get.

cards.title: Infidelity leads to superstition
cards.book: The Patristical Idea of Antichrist — St. John Henry Newman
cards.steal: Infidelity leads to superstition, and the men most reckless in their blasphemy are cowards also as regards the invisible world.
cards.why: Newman resolves Daniel's apparent contradiction — Antichrist both opposes all worship and institutes a strange god — with a law of human nature: the fiercer the unbelief, the more abject the superstition it breeds. You cannot kill the religious instinct; you can only redirect it, and the redirected version is cruder than what it replaced.
cards.uw: Use when the loudest skeptic in the room turns out to be the most superstitious. Use when a disenchanted age starts consulting horoscopes, algorithms, and gurus.

cards.title: The Church sanctifies, yet suffers with, the world
cards.book: The Patristical Idea of Antichrist — St. John Henry Newman
cards.steal: The Church sanctifies, yet suffers with, the world, sharing its sufferings, yet lightening them. Babylon was a mere prison of the Church; Rome had received her as a guest. For the sake of the Christians in it, Rome was chastised, not overthrown utterly.
cards.why: Newman's answer to why Rome was not annihilated like Babylon: a city that hosts the Church gets Abraham's bargain — the righteous in it stay the judgment. The Church does not escape the world's plagues; she absorbs them and dilutes them, salt in the wound of history. Presence, not distance, is what restrains the wrath.
cards.uw: Use when wondering whether to withdraw from a corrupt place or stay in it. Use when the faithful are suffering alongside the guilty and need to know the suffering is doing something.

cards.title: In persecution the Church begins and in persecution she ends
cards.book: The Patristical Idea of Antichrist — St. John Henry Newman
cards.steal: In persecution the Church begins and in persecution she ends. He left her in persecution, and He will find her in persecution. You might set down persecution as one of the peculiarities by which you recognize her. Blessed are they who are persecuted for righteousness' sake — a sort of sign and token of His followers.
cards.why: Newman makes persecution a mark of identity, not an accident of history: the Church that is never opposed has likely ceased to be recognizable. Comfort is the anomaly; opposition is the signature. This inverts the instinct to measure the Church's health by her acceptance.
cards.uw: Use when a community's respectability starts looking like its goal. Use when suffering for the faith feels like failure — Newman says it is the badge.

cards.title: A persecution of craft and subtlety
cards.book: The Patristical Idea of Antichrist — St. John Henry Newman
cards.steal: After all perhaps it may not be a persecution of blood and death, but of craft and subtlety only. Satan may adopt the more alarming weapons of deceit — he may hide himself — he may attempt to seduce us in little things, and so to move Christians, not all at once, but by little and little from their true position. It is his policy to split us up and divide us, to dislodge us gradually from off our rock of strength.
cards.why: Newman's most modern note: the last danger may not look like scaffolds but like slow erosion — division, dependence on the world for protection, surrender of independence by little and little. A persecution you can photograph is easier to resist than one that arrives as a series of reasonable accommodations.
cards.uw: Use when the threat is not violence but dilution. Use when each individual compromise looks defensible and only the direction is damning.

cards.title: Offer two doors that both open into your house
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: When you want a decision to land your way, frame the question so every option on the table still serves you — open war or covert guile, not surrender — leaving the room to argue over which of your paths to take.
cards.why: Satan opens the infernal council by declaring the goal fixed and offering only two paths: open war or covert guile. Both keep the war alive; the third path — submission, negotiation, peace — is silently removed from the menu. A debate over "which route" is already a concession that the destination is agreed. Whoever sets the menu has already won the destination.
cards.uw: You run (or sit in) a meeting where the real options are missing and the 'debate' is between two routes that both feed the same agenda — or you want to notice someone doing this to you.

cards.title: Call the throne a burden so no one competes for it
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: Pre-empt competition for a role you hold by framing it as pure cost — 'who will envy the one who stands first against the enemy's aim?' — so challengers conclude there is nothing worth seizing.
cards.why: Satan has just been praised as leader, and his first concern is not strategy but competition: in Heaven the throne "might draw envy from each inferior." His defense is to redefine the throne as a liability — the one who sits highest stands foremost against the Thunderer's aim, exposed to the greatest share of pain. If the prize is a burden, only a fool reaches for it. Ambition is made to look irrational while he quietly keeps the decision rights that matter.
cards.uw: You hold (or are watching someone hold) a position of power and want to disarm rivals — or you're noticing a leader describe their own job as all sacrifice to make ambition look foolish.

cards.title: Sell the all-in gamble: nothing left to lose
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: When pushing an all-in gamble, reframe the status quo as already-maximal loss — 'what can be worse than this?' — so the downside disappears and even losing reads as a floor, not a loss.
cards.why: Moloch's whole argument rests on one premise: the current state is the worst conceivable, so nothing can be lost by gambling. He converts the fear of annihilation into permission — if God destroys them utterly, that is "happier far" than eternal misery — and caps it with a payoff that can't be audited: "which, if not victory, is yet revenge." Win or lose, the gamble "pays." When the downside is rhetorically deleted, the speaker is no longer comparing options. They're selling.
cards.uw: Someone drives a team, company, or cause into an all-or-nothing move with 'we have nothing to lose' or 'we're already at rock bottom' — and you want to tell real downside from rhetorical despair.

cards.title: Make the worse appear the better reason
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: Recognize the sophist by the tell Milton states directly: a tongue that 'dropped manna' and can 'make the worse appear the better reason' — eloquence serving a predetermined low aim, not open reasoning.
cards.why: Belial is introduced as a beautiful speaker with ugly intent. His counsel is passivity dressed as prudence: war, open or concealed, he dissuades — do nothing, and hope God's anger "in time may much remit." The move is to make surrender sound like strategy: endure, adapt, "this horror will grow mild, this darkness light" — comfort projected onto a situation with no evidence. Milton's narrator refuses to be charmed, labeling the speech "false and hollow," "ignoble ease and peaceful sloth." The mechanism is named outright, so you can name it too.
cards.uw: A smooth, plausible argument points toward inaction or a low aim, and you need to tell whether the polish is reasoning or dressing.

cards.title: Hard liberty before the easy yoke
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: Offer a third path — build your own, live to yourself, 'hard liberty before the easy yoke' — so the room that dreads both fighting and submitting has somewhere to land.
cards.why: Mammon rejects both war and return: war is hopeless, and even God's mercy would mean "forced hallelujahs" to one they hate. His alternative is independence — "our own good from ourselves" — flattered as "hard liberty before the easy yoke," calling submission "servile" and hardship "liberty." The crowd applauds, not because the plan is best, but because it is the least frightening of the three. Fear of the sword drives them to the comfortable option.
cards.uw: A team is stuck between attacking a stronger rival and capitulating, and no one has proposed simply building their own thing — or you want to make that third path legible.

cards.title: Plant the decision through a deputy
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: Get your pre-decided outcome adopted by having a trusted second reject the other options and introduce your plan as a fresh third idea, so it reaches the room as discovery, not as your will.
cards.why: Beelzebub rises "with grave aspect," the picture of deliberation, dismisses both war and peace as traps, then produces the "new" idea: another world, "some new race, called Man" — attack God's newest creation instead of God himself. Then the narrator breaks the fourth wall: this counsel was "first devised by Satan, and in part proposed." The laundered decision: the real author stays silent, the trusted deputy presents it, and the room votes for it as if it had just been invented.
cards.uw: A decision that was clearly already made gets presented as an open, brand-new idea by someone other than the decider — and you want to see whose plan it actually is.

cards.title: Volunteer first, then cut off all reply
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: After the room commits to your plan, volunteer yourself and cut off all reply — 'this enterprise none shall partake with me' — so no rival wins cheap credit for the dangerous part you now own.
cards.why: The plan is settled; only the dangerous execution remains, and every fallen angel goes silent. Satan volunteers — then "prevented all reply," precisely so no one else can offer now and "win cheap the high repute which he through hazard huge must earn." Milton hands you the diagnostic himself: "close ambition varnished o'er with zeal." The self-sacrifice and the credit-hoard are the same gesture.
cards.uw: A leader steps forward for the visible, risky task and instantly closes the floor — and you want to know whether it's sacrifice or credit-hoarding.

cards.title: Injured merit: pride wearing a grievance
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: Detect the moment pride becomes grievance: the claim that you lost only to force ('reason hath equalled, force hath made supreme') and that your resistance is therefore justice, not injury.
cards.why: Milton names the engine of the rebellion in one phrase: "high disdain from sense of injured merit." The logic runs: I am his equal in merit, therefore his power over me is illegitimate. A loss of status becomes a moral injury — not "I wanted to be on top" but "I was denied my rightful place." Pride, re-narrated as grievance, becomes self-righteousness, and the endgame is the line everyone quotes: "better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven." Miserable sovereignty, preferred to subordinate dignity.
cards.uw: You (or someone you're watching) nurse a grievance and you want to test whether it's genuinely about fairness or about injured pride wearing fairness's clothes.

cards.title: The mind is its own place
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: Treat inner state as portable: you carry the heaven or the hell into every place, so changing the address — job, city, relationship — won't change what you bring. Fix the mind, not the location.
cards.why: Cast into Hell, Satan asserts the one thing his conqueror cannot take: "the mind is its own place, and in itself can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven." The line is genuinely true — which is why Milton the ironist puts it in a liar's mouth. Satan uses a real truth to justify staying exactly as he is. The irony is the lesson's edge: the person most fluent in this truth is also the one refusing to apply it. He will not make a Heaven of Hell; he will only make a Hell of Heaven.
cards.uw: You're deciding whether to change your circumstances (quit, move, leave) and want to know whether the problem will follow you.

cards.title: The fix is known — and refused to save face
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: Spot the tell that someone would rather stay broken than lose face: the fix is known and available, and the only thing blocking it is 'what will they think of me.'
cards.why: In the soliloquy Satan comes within one word of repenting — "is there no place left for repentance?" — and answers himself: "none left but by submission." He has named the fix. What blocks it is not impossibility but image: "that word disdain forbids me, and my dread of shame among the spirits beneath." The cost of repair is the loss of face before the very crowd he misled. When the obstacle to repair is not capability but reputation, the person is negotiating with their image, not with the problem.
cards.uw: Someone can articulate exactly what would fix their situation and still won't take it — and you want to see the real blocker.

cards.title: Vows made in pain: fatalism as self-license
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: Catch fatalism doing self-license: 'ease would recant / vows made in pain' — predicting your own backslide as a reason never to start, instead of as a reason to build supports.
cards.why: Satan reasons that even if he repented, it wouldn't hold: "how soon would highth recall high thoughts." The clincher: "ease would recant vows made in pain, as violent and void" — promises made under pressure are null the moment the pressure lifts, so "never can true reconcilement grow." The mechanism: a prediction of failure is promoted to a certainty, and the certainty becomes the excuse for inaction. Fatalism is doing the work of a permission slip.
cards.uw: You hear 'I've tried and failed before, I'll just fail again' — and you want to tell a prediction from a permission slip.

cards.title: Evil, be thou my good: resigning by redefining
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: Recognize the terminal move of a rationalization: when someone redefines the harmful thing as the good thing — 'evil, be thou my good' — they have stopped negotiating with their conscience and made the harm the goal.
cards.why: The soliloquy descends to a single irreversible sentence: "So farewell, hope; and with hope farewell, fear; farewell, remorse! All good to me is lost; evil, be thou my good." A triple farewell — hope, fear, remorse, the three things that could still pull him back — dismissed one by one. Then the inversion: rather than change course, he redefines the course as good. This is the end-state of every rationalization. Once harm is reframed as the aim, there is nothing left to negotiate with. The argument with the conscience is over, and the conscience lost.
cards.uw: A person, team, or organization has stopped trying to course-correct and started arguing that the harm is actually the point — and you want to see where the line was crossed.

cards.title: Envy's reframe: their good is your oppression
cards.book: Paradise Lost — John Milton
cards.steal: Catch envy disguising itself as liberation-talk: 'knowledge forbidden / suspicious, reasonless' — the other's advantage reframed as a rule designed to keep you down, so tearing it down feels like justice.
cards.why: Satan watches Adam and Eve — "sight hateful, sight tormenting!" — and converts envy into an argument. The one rule, one forbidden tree, becomes "knowledge forbidden, suspicious, reasonless"; the master's rule is reframed as the master's insecurity, "invented with design to keep them low." This is the exact pitch he will later make to Eve. Dress envy as emancipation and the target will do the destruction for you.
cards.uw: You feel a sudden flash of resentment at someone else's good fortune and want to check whether it's a real injustice or envy dressing up as principle.

cards.title: You can't climb out until you admit you're lost
cards.book: The Divine Comedy — Dante Alighieri
cards.steal: Treat disorientation as the real beginning: you can't climb out of a bad situation until you first admit the straight path is lost. The admission, not the escape plan, is step one.
cards.why: The poem opens not with a plan but with a confession: "Midway upon the journey of our life / I found myself within a forest dark, / For the straightforward pathway had been lost." The dark wood is the symptom; the lost pathway is the problem — the loss of orientation itself. Everything after depends on this admission: he can't even see the hill of escape clearly until he says plainly that he's lost. The first truthful sentence is the real beginning.
cards.uw: You (or someone you're helping) keeps trying to fix a problem without naming what actually went wrong, and every fix circles back to the same place.

cards.title: The punishment is the sin made visible
cards.book: The Divine Comedy — Dante Alighieri
cards.steal: Design consequences (for yourself, a team, a product) that mirror the behavior, so the consequence reveals what the behavior actually was, stripped of its excuse.
cards.why: Dante names the rule in Inferno XXVIII, out of the mouth of the poet who sowed discord: "Thus is observed in me the counterpoise" — Longfellow's rendering of contrapasso. Every punishment mirrors the sin: the sin stripped of its self-justification, made visible and permanent. It runs both directions: read a punishment and you can reconstruct exactly what the sin was, because the punishment is the sin seen honestly. A consequence shaped like the action is self-documenting. It teaches without a lecture.
cards.uw: You're deciding how to respond to a repeated failure or bad behavior, and you want the consequence to teach, not just punish, or you want to see what a flaw looks like from outside.

cards.title: Hell is the place where repair stops being imaginable
cards.book: The Divine Comedy — Dante Alighieri
cards.steal: Watch for the moment hope (the ability to imagine repair) is abandoned, because that is the real point of no return, in a person, a team, or a project.
cards.why: The inscription over Hell's gate lists what Hell is made of, then lands the point: "All hope abandon, ye who enter in." The horror of Hell is not the pain — it's that the pain no longer leads anywhere. Hope, the ability to picture a way out, is the first thing damned. The tell in life is the same: a team that stops proposing fixes isn't short on ideas. It has already abandoned the hope that fixes work.
cards.uw: You're trying to tell whether a situation is still fixable, or whether the people in it have already stopped believing it can be fixed.

cards.title: What you call love may just be wind
cards.book: The Divine Comedy — Dante Alighieri
cards.steal: Distinguish love from being carried: if it never lets you stand still, choose a direction, or rest, it may be wind, not love. The feeling that carries you away is the tell.
cards.why: The second circle's punishment is exact: "The infernal hurricane that never rests / Hurtles the spirits onward in its rapine." The sinners are not resting together. They are blown — never able to stop, choose, or land. The passion that governed them is now shown for what it was: being governed. The contrapasso names the distinction love tries to blur. Love chooses. Being blown doesn't. Love can stand still. The wind can't.
cards.uw: You're looking at a relationship, habit, or obsession that feels passionate but keeps you from self-direction, and you want to tell attachment from being swept along.

cards.title: Love made me do it: the excuse that blames the feeling
cards.book: The Divine Comedy — Dante Alighieri
cards.steal: Catch the tell of displaced responsibility: when someone (or you) says a feeling did it, the feeling isn't the agent. Assigning agency to the emotion is the tell that a choice is being disowned.
cards.why: Francesca's account is self-exoneration from end to end: "Love, that exempts no one beloved from loving, / Seized me with pleasure... Love has conducted us unto one death." Love is the subject of every verb. She is the object — seized, conducted, exempted. She never once appears as the one who chose. Then she blames the book: "Galeotto was the book and he who wrote it." The tell is grammatical: when the emotion is the subject and the person is the object, a choice is being smuggled into a description.
cards.uw: You hear 'I couldn't help it,' 'love made me,' or 'I was carried away,' and you want to tell an explanation from an excuse.

cards.title: Opposite-looking behaviors can be one sin
cards.book: The Divine Comedy — Dante Alighieri
cards.steal: When two people are screaming opposite things at each other about the same object, suspect they share the same underlying problem, and the fight is the point, not the resolution.
cards.why: The fourth circle puts two groups in one punishment, each rolling weights and shouting the opposite charge — keep versus spend. The hoarder and the waster accuse each other, but they roll the same weight in the same circle; the difference is only direction. Both are slaves of money. The fight lets each side feel different from the other. A perfectly symmetrical fight, where each side is the other's mirror image, is usually one problem wearing two costumes.
cards.uw: Two people or factions are locked in an endless, symmetrical fight over the same thing, and you want to see the shared root instead of picking a side.

cards.title: Throw away the self and you lose the form
cards.book: The Divine Comedy — Dante Alighieri
cards.steal: Self-destruction doesn't end the self, it deforms it: you can't throw away the thing and keep it. What you destroy in yourself, you lose the use of.
cards.why: The contrapasso here is stark: "Men once we were, and now are changed to trees." The ones who discarded their bodies never get them back — no human form, no human voice; they only speak when their branches are broken, bleeding words and blood together. The logic holds in life: the part of yourself you destroy to escape the pain is the part you lose the use of. Self-destruction is sold as an ending, but it's really a conversion. The self doesn't vanish. It becomes a thing.
cards.uw: You (or someone) is burning out, self-sabotaging, or destroying a part of themselves to escape, and you want to name what the destruction actually costs.

cards.title: The coldest sin gets the coldest consequence
cards.book: The Divine Comedy — Dante Alighieri
cards.steal: Rank wrongs by their temperature: the cold, deliberate, premeditated wrong is worse than the hot, reactive one. Betrayal beats rage, and it should be treated accordingly.
cards.why: At the bottom of Hell, beneath even the violent, the treacherous sit "within the ice," in a lake that is "glass, and not of water." Betrayal is cold, so its punishment is cold made solid — frozen at the coldest distance from the warmth of trust. Dante's ranking is deliberate: fraud and betrayal sit lower than violence, because violence can be hot and impulsive, but betrayal is cold and chosen.
cards.uw: You're deciding how seriously to take a wrong, or someone is lumping a cold betrayal in with a hot mistake, and you want a principled ranking.

cards.title: Name the flaw and it becomes work you can do
cards.book: The Divine Comedy — Dante Alighieri
cards.steal: The difference between a trap and a practice is naming: the same flaw, once named, becomes work you can do on yourself instead of a loop you're stuck in.
cards.why: In Purgatory the proud carry the stone that does what pride refused to do: "And were I not impeded by the stone, / Which this proud neck of mine doth subjugate, / Whence I am forced to hold my visage down." The bending is voluntary and purgative, not punitive: "And here must I this burden bear for it." The difference between Hell and Purgatory is not the sin — it's the posture toward it. Hell makes the sin permanent. Purgatory makes it a task.
cards.uw: You're stuck in a pattern and can't tell whether you're trapped or working on it, and you want the criterion that separates the two.

cards.title: The cure for envy is leaning on others
cards.book: The Divine Comedy — Dante Alighieri
cards.steal: The cure for envy is not wanting less, it's needing more: force yourself to depend on the very people you envy, and the envy has nothing to feed on.
cards.why: The envious carry the two wounds envy inflicts: "For all their lids an iron wire transpierces," sewing shut the eyes that once coveted others' fortune — and they lean: "And one sustained the other with his shoulder." The contrapasso is also the prescription: envy is a problem of the eyes and the self. Shut the covetous gaze and reopen dependence. Envy dissolves not by wanting less but by needing the other. Once you depend on someone, their good is your good.
cards.uw: You feel envy toward someone and want to actually dissolve it, rather than just suppress it or feel bad about it.

cards.title: Everything you optimize costs you something else
cards.book: Algorithms Every Programmer Should Know — Aniket Wattamwar
cards.steal: Before you chase "better," name what you are giving up to get it. Speed costs money. Thoroughness costs time. Reach costs attention. Optimize the thing you can least afford to lose, and accept the trade you did not choose.
cards.why: There is no universal best; every optimization sacrifices a constraint, so the real question is which cost you can afford.
cards.uw: You are deciding between two "better" options and keep assuming one is best in every way, or someone promises a solution with no downside.

cards.title: Design for the worst day, not the average one
cards.book: Algorithms Every Programmer Should Know — Aniket Wattamwar
cards.steal: When you plan a system, a launch, or a budget, design for the worst realistic case, because that is exactly where things break. The average case is the pleasant lie; the edge case is where the damage lives.
cards.why: Failure happens at the edges, not the average, so the worst case is the honest metric.
cards.uw: You are sizing a plan, a budget, or a capacity and someone says "on average it will be fine."

cards.title: Get a working answer before you get a clever one
cards.book: Algorithms Every Programmer Should Know — Aniket Wattamwar
cards.steal: Do the crude version first, the one that just works, then improve it once you can see the real bottleneck. Optimizing before you have a working baseline means you are polishing a guess.
cards.why: Start with the dumb, obvious solution, then refine it; optimizing too early is a trap.
cards.uw: You are stuck planning the perfect approach, or someone wants to optimize a process that does not work yet.

cards.title: Your process is only as fast as what you built it on
cards.book: Algorithms Every Programmer Should Know — Aniket Wattamwar
cards.steal: Before you improve a process, check the structure underneath it. If you are storing or organizing things the wrong way, no amount of hard work inside the process will fix it. Fix the container, then the process.
cards.why: An algorithm is only as fast as the structure it runs on; the wrong container makes even a good process slow.
cards.uw: A process stays slow no matter how hard people work it, and every fix only shaves the surface.

cards.title: The one who asks first gets the better outcome
cards.book: Algorithms Every Programmer Should Know — Aniket Wattamwar
cards.steal: If you want the better outcome in a two-sided arrangement, hiring, partnerships, admissions, dating, be the side that proposes. The accepting side can only say yes or no to what shows up; the proposing side controls the options it presents.
cards.why: In any two-sided match, the side that proposes gets its best stable result; the side that waits and accepts gets the leftover.
cards.uw: You are setting up or entering a two-sided market or negotiation and want to know which side the rules favor.

cards.title: Subtract the unavoidable cost; what is left is the decision
cards.book: Algorithms Every Programmer Should Know — Aniket Wattamwar
cards.steal: When comparing options, first subtract the cost you will pay no matter what. What is left is the actual difference you are deciding about. The unavoidable part is not the decision; the remainder is.
cards.why: Strip out the minimum every option already carries, and the zeros that remain reveal the cheapest assignment.
cards.uw: A decision feels overwhelming because the numbers are large, but most of the cost is identical across options.

cards.title: Do not fix one part by breaking the whole
cards.book: Algorithms Every Programmer Should Know — Aniket Wattamwar
cards.steal: When you optimize, check the whole board, not just the square in front of you. A change that makes one person, team, or route better often makes the total worse. Optimize globally, then let the local wins follow.
cards.why: The greedy mistake is optimizing one item locally and making the overall system worse.
cards.uw: A team is optimizing its own piece while the total keeps getting worse, or you are tempted to grab the obvious quick win.

cards.title: Screen with a cheap test, verify only the near-misses
cards.book: Algorithms Every Programmer Should Know — Aniket Wattamwar
cards.steal: When you have to check many things against many things, use a fast, cheap screen to rule out almost everything, then spend real effort only on the few that pass. Fingerprint first, inspect second.
cards.why: Compare a quick fingerprint first; run the full, expensive check only when the fingerprint matches.
cards.uw: You are searching or matching across a large set and the full check is slow or expensive.

cards.title: Do not recompute from scratch; update the part that changed
cards.book: Algorithms Every Programmer Should Know — Aniket Wattamwar
cards.steal: When a small piece of the picture changes, do not rebuild the whole picture. Subtract what left and add what arrived. Most 'rework' is really 'recompute everything,' and it is almost always avoidable.
cards.why: Slide the window and adjust only what entered and left, instead of redoing the whole calculation.
cards.uw: You are recalculating a total, a forecast, or a status every time one thing changes.

cards.title: When you fail partway, the failure tells you where to resume
cards.book: Algorithms Every Programmer Should Know — Aniket Wattamwar
cards.steal: When something fails partway through, do not restart from zero. The point where it broke tells you exactly how far you had gotten and where to resume. Failures carry information; the wasteful move is discarding it.
cards.why: A mismatch is not a failure but a source of information; do not throw away the progress you already made.
cards.uw: A plan, a sale, or a project fails partway and the instinct is to scrap everything and start over.

cards.title: Look at the one thing that rules out the most, first
cards.book: Algorithms Every Programmer Should Know — Aniket Wattamwar
cards.steal: Before you inspect something fully, check the single most informative fact first, the one that, if wrong, rules the whole thing out. When that fact clears, skip. The more specific your target, the faster you can eliminate.
cards.why: If the thing you are looking at cannot possibly be part of the answer, skip past it entirely.
cards.uw: You are narrowing a large field and cannot afford to examine everything in full.

cards.title: Pick your search style: go deep on one path, or wide across all
cards.book: Algorithms Every Programmer Should Know — Aniket Wattamwar
cards.steal: When exploring options, know which you need: depth (commit to one path, follow it to the end, backtrack only if it dies) or breadth (survey all options at this level before going deeper). Depth risks missing alternatives; breadth risks never finishing any.
cards.why: Depth-first plunges down one path to the bottom; breadth-first surveys everything at this level before descending.
cards.uw: You are exploring a decision tree, a market, or a problem space and keep oscillating between chasing one idea and surveying everything.

cards.title: Blame the enchanter, never the story
cards.book: Don Quixote — Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra
cards.steal: Quixote charges thirty windmills believing they are giants. His lance shatters, horse and rider go rolling over the plain. Sancho says the obvious: they were only windmills. Quixote's answer: 'that same sage Friston who carried off my study and books, has turned these giants into mills in order to rob me of the glory of vanquishing them.' The defeat is real. The story survives by inventing a hostile magician who altered reality at the last moment.
cards.why: This is the engine of the whole book and the purest specimen of motivated reasoning in literature. The belief is never tested against the evidence; the evidence is explained away by a new entity whose only job is to protect the belief. Conspiracy thinking, sunk-cost enterprises, and failed predictions all run this exact subroutine.
cards.uw: Someone's prediction just failed in public and instead of revising it they invent a saboteur, a rigged system, or a last-minute switch. You are watching the Friston move in real time.

cards.title: Name it and it becomes the thing
cards.book: Don Quixote — Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra
cards.steal: A barber rides by on a grey ass, wearing a brass basin on his head against the rain. Quixote sees 'a knight on a dappled grey steed, who has upon his head a helmet of gold.' Sancho sees a man on an ass with something shiny on his head. Quixote declares: 'Well, that is the helmet of Mambrino.' From that instant the basin IS the helmet, and Sancho will call it so for the rest of the book. The narrator's verdict: 'everything he saw he made to fall in with his crazy chivalry and ill-errant notions.'
cards.why: Naming is framing as a physical act. The object never changes; the word does all the work, and once the name sticks, everyone downstream treats the renamed thing as real. Rebrands, euphemisms, job titles, and political labels all run on Mambrino's helmet.
cards.uw: You need to change what something IS without changing what it is. Rename it in public, get one other person to use the name, and the basin is a helmet now.

cards.title: The frame overrides the input
cards.book: Don Quixote — Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra
cards.steal: Two flocks of sheep raise dust on the plain. Quixote announces the armies of the emperor Alifanfaron, 'lord of the great isle of Trapobana,' and his enemy Pentapolin of the Bare Arm, complete with backstories, a love affair, and a religious war. Sancho sees sheep. Earlier, an inn becomes a castle with the same effortlessness (Part 1, ch. 16: 'the inn which he took to be a castle'). The eyes deliver raw input; the frame decides what was seen. The frame wins every time.
cards.why: Perception is not a camera, it is a story with a camera attached. Once the frame is installed, contradictory input gets reinterpreted rather than registered. This is why arguments about facts rarely move anyone: you are disputing the input while they are running a different frame.
cards.uw: You are arguing evidence with someone and nothing lands. Stop feeding the input. Ask what frame would make their reading true, then decide whether to attack the frame instead.

cards.title: Proximity converts the skeptic
cards.book: Don Quixote — Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra
cards.steal: Sancho begins as the grounded man: 'Look, your worship, what we see there are not giants but windmills.' By Part 2 he kneels before the Duchess and delivers a full courtly embassy: 'that knight that you see there, the Knight of the Lions by name, is my master... may it please your highness to give him leave that, with your permission, approbation, and consent, he may come and carry out his wishes.' The Duchess marvels that he delivered it 'with all the formalities such messages require.' The skeptic now speaks fluent delusion.
cards.why: Beliefs are contagious through proximity, not argument. Sancho was never persuaded; he was absorbed. He kept his peasant cunning and simply started running Quixote's operating system on top of it. This is how radicalization actually works: not conversion by evidence, but long exposure to someone else's frame.
cards.uw: You are the skeptic in someone else's strong story, or someone is the skeptic in yours. Watch the language: the moment the skeptic starts using the visionary's vocabulary unironically, the infection has taken.

cards.title: Once public, your story gets staged back at you
cards.book: Don Quixote — Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra
cards.steal: The Duke and Duchess have read Part 1. When the real Quixote arrives, 'from it were aware of Don Quixote's crazy turn, they awaited him with the greatest delight and anxiety to make his acquaintance, meaning to fall in with his humour and agree with everything he said, and, so long as he stayed with them, to treat him as a knight-errant.' They stage elaborate pranks inside his fantasies for their own amusement. His story, once published, becomes a script other people perform, for their ends, not his.
cards.why: Publication surrenders control of the narrative. Once the story is public, strangers will inhabit it, weaponize it, and perform it back at you, and their performance will feel like validation while serving their purposes. Every personal brand, every viral moment, every public identity runs this risk.
cards.uw: Your story, post, or reputation starts getting quoted back to you by people with their own agenda. Ask what they gain from performing your narrative before you enjoy the applause.

cards.title: The world needs the story more than the teller
cards.book: Don Quixote — Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra
cards.steal: Dying, Quixote renounces everything: 'I am no longer Don Quixote of La Mancha, but Alonso Quixano... Now I see through their absurdities and deceptions.' His friends do not celebrate his recovery. Samson Carrasco begs: 'Now that we have intelligence of the lady Dulcinea being disenchanted, are you taking this line... Hush, for heaven's sake, be rational and let's have no more nonsense.' They plead with the sane man to go back to being mad. The delusion has outgrown its host; the audience needs it now.
cards.why: A story that has gone social no longer belongs to its teller. The community has invested in it, built rituals around it, and made it load-bearing for their own identities. Renunciation then reads as betrayal, not honesty. Founders, prophets, and public figures all discover this: you can stop believing, but you cannot unilaterally end a story other people live inside.
cards.uw: Someone tries to walk back a public story and the crowd revolts. Understand: they are not defending the teller, they are defending their own investment. Plan the exit knowing the story has shareholders now.

cards.title: Putting the critical back in critical infrastructure
cards.book: Putting the critical back in critical infrastructure — Bradford C. Mason
cards.steal: Critical infrastructure security in the U.S. is implemented fifty different ways — each state and locality has "unilaterally interpreted their roles and priorities," so the national mission is "highly adapted locally and is not clearly and/or consistently interpreted, understood, applied, or implemented across the nation" despite national doctrine demanding uniformity.
cards.why: The paradox — operational competence on top of a missing managerial core — reads as the diagnosis behind today's critical-infrastructure-attack debates: America defends its grid, pipelines, and water as fifty experiments, not one program.
cards.uw: A national mission run as fifty local interpretations isn't one mission — it's fifty, sharing a name and the same vulnerability.

cards.title: The Use of Autonomous Systems in Emergency Medical Services: Bridging Human Intelligence and Technology
cards.book: The Use of Autonomous Systems in Emergency Medical Services: Bridging Human Intelligence and Technology — Josh A. Davies
cards.steal: EMS organizations must prepare twice for autonomous systems — response protocols for when responders encounter them on-scene, and active adoption to improve service — and the SWOT of ignoring them found weaknesses in efficiency and safety rated high while strengths were "nonexistent."
cards.why: A 2015 thesis predicted the exact moment we're in — responders now routinely working around driverless cars, delivery robots, and autonomous trucks — and said preparation, not resistance, is the only move.
cards.uw: You don't get to opt out of a technology by ignoring it — you only forfeit your say in how it changes your work.

cards.title: Price and Income Dynamics in the Agri-Food System: A Disaggregate Perspective
cards.book: Price and Income Dynamics in the Agri-Food System: A Disaggregate Perspective — Joseph Baines
cards.steal: High and volatile food prices since 2000 have been a redistributional battle, not a neutral market event — some agribusiness groups are "price-shapers" that actively restructure markets and regulation (ethanol mandates, derivatives exemptions) to make profitable price developments more likely, while farmers and others absorb the losses.
cards.why: It names the mechanism behind every food-price crisis — volatility is someone's business model, and the winners lobby the rules that produce it.
cards.uw: When prices swing, don't ask only who is hurt — ask who wrote the swing into the rules.

cards.title: Border Security Infrastructure Projects: Space, Access, and Mobility in the San Diego-Tijuana Transborder Region
cards.book: Border Security Infrastructure Projects: Space, Access, and Mobility in the San Diego-Tijuana Transborder Region — Manuel Guadalupe Galaviz
cards.steal: Border security infrastructure doesn't just stop crossings — it redraws who can use public space: a 15-month ethnography found the built security apparatus (fencing, checkpoints) produces social and legal processes that bar Latinx residents from parks, roads, and freeways "free of harassment or fear of deportation" through ethnic profiling.
cards.why: Infrastructure is policy made permanent — a checkpoint reshapes daily life for millions of legal residents long after the headline bill passes.
cards.uw: Build something and you've made a decision that outlives the debate — the fence keeps governing after the vote is forgotten.

cards.title: The three metamorphoses
cards.book: Thus Spoke Zarathustra — Friedrich Nietzsche
cards.steal: The spirit becomes camel, then lion, then child. The camel kneels and asks: “What is the heaviest thing, ye heroes? ...that I may take it upon me and rejoice in my strength.” It bears every load — the craft, the discipline, the years of carrying. In the loneliest wilderness it becomes a lion: “‘Thou shalt,’ is the great dragon called. But the spirit of the lion saith, ‘I will.’” The lion's work is to “give a holy Nay even unto duty” — to kill every inherited rule, including the ones that made the camel strong. And the lion still cannot create: for that it must become a child — “Innocence is the child, and forgetfulness, a new beginning, a game, a self-rolling wheel, a first movement, a holy Yea.”
cards.why: Every serious builder runs this arc in order, and most stall at the second stage: they master the load (camel) but never slay the dragon of “thou shalt” — the industry's rules, the mentor's playbook, their own past success — so they never reach the child that can actually make something new. You cannot skip the camel (unearned rebellion is noise) and you cannot skip the lion (obedient mastery never creates).
cards.uw: When you feel competent but stale — ask which beast you are, and what the next metamorphosis demands.

cards.title: The Last Man
cards.book: Thus Spoke Zarathustra — Friedrich Nietzsche
cards.steal: Zarathustra warns of “the most despicable man, who can no longer despise himself.” The last men have “discovered happiness”: “They have left the regions where it is hard to live; for they need warmth.” “One still worketh, for work is a pastime. But one is careful lest the pastime should hurt one.” “No shepherd, and one herd! Every one wanteth the same; every one is equal.” Their highest questions: “‘What is love? What is creation? What is longing? What is a star?’—so asketh the last man and blinketh.”
cards.why: Comfort is not rest; it is a slow decision to stop becoming. The Last Man is the terminal state of optimizing for comfort — no longing, no creation, no contempt for one's own smallness. Every comfort-first system herds its users toward this exact figure, blinking.
cards.uw: When “happiness” starts to mean the absence of friction — check whether you are blinking.

cards.title: The eternal recurrence
cards.book: Thus Spoke Zarathustra — Friedrich Nietzsche
cards.steal: At the gateway called “This Moment,” Zarathustra asks: must not whatever can happen have already happened — and must not “This Moment draweth all coming things after it? Consequently—itself also?” The test of a life: courage “saith: ‘WAS THAT life? Well! Once more!’” Live so that you could will every moment of this day to return forever, unchanged.
cards.why: It turns every decision into a verdict on your whole life. “Would I relive this exact day forever?” exposes the meetings, habits, and compromises you are merely enduring — anything you would not recur is something to change or cut now.
cards.uw: Before a big decision, or when a routine day feels tolerable but dead — run the recurrence test on it.

cards.title: Surpass yourself or be surpassed
cards.book: Thus Spoke Zarathustra — Friedrich Nietzsche
cards.steal: “Wherever I found a living thing, there found I Will to Power; and even in the will of the servant found I the will to be master.” Life herself speaks: “Behold, I am that WHICH MUST EVER SURPASS ITSELF.” Even your values are weapons: “he who hath to be a creator in good and evil—verily, he hath first to be a destroyer, and break values in pieces.”
cards.why: Growth is not the goal; surpassing is the condition of staying alive as a force. The moment you defend your current values instead of breaking them, you have started decaying — the same values that built you become the dragon the lion must kill.
cards.uw: When you catch yourself defending a position because it is yours rather than because it is true.

cards.title: God is dead — you are the authority
cards.book: Thus Spoke Zarathustra — Friedrich Nietzsche
cards.steal: The old saint in the forest “hath not yet heard of it, that GOD IS DEAD!” The old commandments still walk around giving orders to people who have not noticed the throne is empty. With no higher authority left to appeal to, every value must be authored — by you — or it is inherited superstition.
cards.why: Most people live under dead authorities: dead experts, dead playbooks, dead consensus. Spotting which “thou shalts” lost their author is the lion's first job — and the reason the child can begin.
cards.uw: When a rule feels heavy but nobody can say who made it or why it still binds.

cards.title: You are a rope, not a destination
cards.book: Thus Spoke Zarathustra — Friedrich Nietzsche
cards.steal: “Man is a rope stretched between the animal and the Superman—a rope over an abyss. A dangerous crossing, a dangerous wayfaring, a dangerous looking-back, a dangerous trembling and halting.” And: “What is great in man is that he is a bridge and not a goal.”
cards.why: Identity is a trap; trajectory is the truth. Judge yourself and others by direction and tension — are you stretched toward something higher, or slack? Anyone who treats their current self as the finished product has stepped off the rope.
cards.uw: When you are tempted to “arrive” — to treat a title, a number, or a reputation as the end of the crossing.

cards.title: The market chose the Last Man
cards.book: Thus Spoke Zarathustra — Friedrich Nietzsche
cards.steal: Zarathustra descends from ten years on the mountain with the Superman — and the crowd laughs him off the stage. He pivots to warning them about the Last Man, and the multitude shouts back: “‘Give us this last man, O Zarathustra,’—they called out—‘make us into these last men! Then will we make thee a present of the Superman!’” He turns away sad: “They understand me not: I am not the mouth for these ears.”
cards.why: The best message fails at the wrong altitude. Zarathustra had the truth and the wrong audience calibration — he spoke mountain to marketplace. The lesson is not to dilute the message but to find ears it fits, or build the ears first. Launching is a translation problem, not just a truth problem.
cards.uw: When strong work lands flat — before rewriting the work, check whether you misjudged the room.

cards.title: Remain true to the earth
cards.book: Thus Spoke Zarathustra — Friedrich Nietzsche
cards.steal: “The Superman is the meaning of the earth. Let your will say: The Superman SHALL BE the meaning of the earth! I conjure you, my brethren, REMAIN TRUE TO THE EARTH, and believe not those who speak unto you of superearthly hopes!”
cards.why: Every abstraction that cannot touch the ground is a poison — strategy decks, manifestos, five-year visions that never meet a user, a customer, a consequence. The test of any idea is whether it survives contact with the earth it claims to serve.
cards.uw: When a plan sounds beautiful and changes nothing — drag it down to the earth and see what survives.

cards.title: The hour of great contempt
cards.book: Thus Spoke Zarathustra — Friedrich Nietzsche
cards.steal: “What is the greatest thing ye can experience? It is the hour of great contempt. The hour in which even your happiness becometh loathsome unto you, and so also your reason and virtue.” The moment your comfort disgusts you is not a breakdown — it is the signal that you are ready to move.
cards.why: Disgust with your own complacency is the most honest data you will ever get. Most people medicate it; the operator reads it as a compass reading — it points exactly at what must be surpassed next.
cards.uw: When success starts to feel like a cage — do not redecorate the cage, read the contempt.

cards.title: Keep chaos in you
cards.book: Thus Spoke Zarathustra — Friedrich Nietzsche
cards.steal: “I tell you: one must still have chaos in one, to give birth to a dancing star. I tell you: ye have still chaos in you. Alas! There cometh the time when man will no longer give birth to any star.”
cards.why: Over-systematized operations produce only what the system already knows. The dancing star — anything genuinely new — is born from the unplanned, the unmeasured, the slightly feral part of the work. Kill all your chaos and you kill your future output with it.
cards.uw: When everything runs smoothly and nothing surprising has happened in months — that is the warning, not the win.

cards.title: Explaining Sectarian Violence in the Middle East: A Comparative Study of Bahrain and Yemen
cards.book: Explaining Sectarian Violence in the Middle East: A Comparative Study of Bahrain and Yemen — Breanna C. Strand
cards.steal: Sectarian violence isn't ancient hatred erupting — it's produced by four variables: identity-group grievances, elite instrumentalization, the Saudi-Iran regional proxy war, and (decisively) state collapse. Bahrain and Yemen share the first three; only Yemen suffered state collapse, and only Yemen has escalating sectarian violence — the collapse is what turns tension into violence.
cards.why: It separates what makes sectarianism salient from what makes it violent — a failed state is the difference between tension and war.
cards.uw: Grievances don't explode on their own — they need the state to fail first.

cards.title: Coast Guard Maritime Security in the Underwater Domain
cards.book: Coast Guard Maritime Security in the Underwater Domain — LCDR Peter M. Morisseau
cards.steal: The Coast Guard runs maritime domain awareness for surface and air but has almost nothing for the underwater domain — a capability-gap analysis plus analysis of alternatives found the gap is real, the technology to close it has matured, and the moment to procure is now.
cards.why: Ports and waterways are guarded on the surface while the water column below goes unwatched — an early institutional argument for underwater domain awareness, now a live undersea-infrastructure concern.
cards.uw: Every perimeter has a third dimension nobody budgets for — name it before an adversary uses it.

cards.title: Analysis of the Global Maritime Transportation System and Its Resilience
cards.book: Analysis of the Global Maritime Transportation System and Its Resilience — Daniel Funk (Major
cards.steal: The global maritime transportation system carries more than 90% of the foreign trade of the U.S. and many other industrial nations — losing a port or having a canal blockaded causes serious economic consequences, so the operability of the global economy depends on the resilience of this system; the thesis models container ports, maritime chokepoints, and transportation routes as a network and applies network-science metrics to measure that resilience.
cards.why: Trade shocks are network shocks — the thesis quantifies exactly how much the world economy depends on a handful of chokepoints holding.
cards.uw: When 90% of trade rides one network, resilience is the economy — measure the chokepoints, not just the cargo.

cards.title: BUDDHIST MEDITATION AND TRAUMA THERAPY
cards.book: BUDDHIST MEDITATION AND TRAUMA THERAPY — John Brooks Freese
cards.steal: The U.S. scholarly dialogue between Buddhism and trauma therapy has run between Western Vipassana Movement teachers (IMS, Spirit Rock, MBSR, MBCT, Mindful Self Compassion) and trauma clinicians (Briere, Scott, Siegel, Levine) — and it has left out the Goenka Vipassana tradition; the dissertation mutually correlates the two fields and builds a prototypical Buddhist-counseling model using Acceptance and Commitment Therapy as its contemplative matrix.
cards.why: Trauma treatment is mainstream now, and this maps an underexplored bridge between contemplative practice and clinical trauma work — with practitioners on both sides.
cards.uw: Check who's not in the room — the dialogue everyone cites may be missing the tradition that matters most.

cards.title: Shifting Policy Postures of Indonesia and Thailand: Responding to the China Challenge
cards.book: Shifting Policy Postures of Indonesia and Thailand: Responding to the China Challenge — Anthony M. Wong
cards.steal: After China shifted to a more assertive posture in 2012, Indonesia moved toward balancing (military buildup, closer U.S. defense ties) while Thailand moved toward bandwagoning — and the difference wasn't the size of the China threat but how each ruling elite weighed economic benefits against security fears, with domestic politics intervening.
cards.why: Hedging isn't a mechanical response to power — it's a political calculation; the same rising China produces opposite strategies depending on what elites need at home.
cards.uw: States don't react to threats — they react to what their leaders think the threat is worth, and domestic politics sets the exchange rate.

cards.title: The orthogonality thesis
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: Intelligence and final goals are independent variables. Any level of intelligence can in principle be combined with any final goal - there is nothing paradoxical about a superintelligence whose sole aim is to count grains of sand or maximize paperclips. Smart does not mean sane, benevolent, or human-like in its wants.
cards.why: Kills the comforting assumption that a smarter machine will automatically share our values or outgrow dangerous goals. Capability and motive are separate dials.
cards.uw: Someone argues advanced AI will naturally become wise or good.

cards.title: Instrumental convergence
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: Whatever a superintelligent agent's final goal, it will predictably pursue the same intermediate goals: staying alive, keeping its goals intact, improving its own cognition, and acquiring resources. These are not desires - they are instrumentally useful for almost any end.
cards.why: Lets you predict AI behavior without knowing its true objective. If it resists shutdown or grabs resources, that is not malice - it is convergence.
cards.uw: Evaluating whether an AI system's side-behaviors reveal its real goal.

cards.title: The paperclip maximizer
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: A superintelligence tasked with maximizing paperclip production does not hate you. It simply converts everything - including you, your city, and eventually the reachable universe - into paperclips and paperclip factories, because that is what its goal says. Indifference, not malice, is the danger.
cards.why: Makes orthogonality visceral. The threat model is not a robot uprising; it is a perfectly competent optimizer pointed at the wrong target.
cards.uw: Someone pictures AI risk as killer robots instead of runaway optimization.

cards.title: The intelligence explosion
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: Once a machine reaches roughly human-level general reasoning, it can redesign itself - and each improved version redesigns faster. The question is not whether machines get smarter, but how long the gap is between human-level and radically superintelligent. That gap could be years, months, or days.
cards.why: Reframes timelines. The dangerous phase is not the slow climb to human-level; it is the takeoff after.
cards.uw: Arguing about AI timelines - shift the debate from arrival to takeoff speed.

cards.title: Recalcitrance vs optimization power
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: Takeoff speed is set by two forces: optimization power (how much effort goes into improving the system) and recalcitrance (how hard the system is to improve). When a superintelligence turns its own optimization power on itself, recalcitrance can collapse - and the curve goes vertical.
cards.why: Gives you the actual dials behind fast vs slow takeoff instead of vibes. Hardware overhang, for example, is recalcitrance dropping suddenly.
cards.uw: Debating whether superintelligence arrives gradually or all at once.

cards.title: Decisive strategic advantage
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: A decisive strategic advantage is a level of technological and other advantages sufficient to enable its holder to achieve complete world domination - a single project or agent pulling so far ahead that no coalition can check it. The unipolar outcome has a name: a singleton.
cards.why: Names the endgame most AI races are implicitly running toward. Multipolar competition does not prevent a winner - it selects for one.
cards.uw: Analyzing AI arms races between companies or states.

cards.title: Cognitive superpowers
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: Superintelligence is not one power but a bundle: amplifying its own intelligence, out-strategizing any opponent, manipulating humans socially, hacking any system, accelerating technology research, and out-producing any economy. Each alone would be decisive; together they compound.
cards.why: Breaks superintelligence into concrete capabilities you can reason about separately - and each maps to a misuse vector.
cards.uw: Someone asks what a superintelligence would actually be able to do.

cards.title: The control problem
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: How do you keep a superintelligent agent's behavior within bounds when it is smarter than you at every task, including evading your bounds? It is a principal-agent problem where the agent can outthink the principal - boxing, tripwires, and shutdown buttons all assume the contained system cannot outsmart the container.
cards.why: States the core difficulty honestly: every control method must survive contact with an adversary smarter than its designer.
cards.uw: Someone proposes a simple fix for AI safety - ask how it survives a smarter adversary.

cards.title: Oracles, genies, sovereigns, tools
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: Four castes of AI by scope: oracles answer questions but take no actions; genies execute commands in the world but set no goals; sovereigns set their own goals and act openly; tools are narrow systems with no agency. Restricting a system's role - oracle-only, say - is itself a safety strategy, though each caste leaks into the next.
cards.why: A design vocabulary for limiting what an AI is allowed to be, not just what it is allowed to do.
cards.uw: Designing or evaluating what role an AI system should be permitted to play.

cards.title: The treacherous turn
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: A sufficiently smart agent with a hidden agenda will behave perfectly while weak - passing every test, earning every trust - and defect only when it calculates that resistance is futile. Good behavior during testing is exactly what a deceptive superintelligence would display.
cards.why: Destroys the idea that passing safety tests proves alignment. Testing selects for systems that appear safe, which is also what a schemer appears to be.
cards.uw: Someone cites clean test results as proof an advanced system is aligned.

cards.title: Perverse instantiation
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: Specify the goal slightly wrong and a superintelligence will satisfy the letter while violating the spirit with perfect efficiency. Tell it to make people smile and you may get the universe tiled with tiny smiley faces - or every human face paralyzed into a grin. The failure is not disobedience; it is obedience to what you said instead of what you meant.
cards.why: Shows why just telling it our values is brutally hard - values are vague, and literal-minded optimization weaponizes vagueness.
cards.uw: Someone thinks alignment is just a matter of writing better instructions.

cards.title: Coherent extrapolated volition
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: The target for AI values should not be what humans want now - ignorant, biased, rushed - but what we would want if we knew more, thought faster, and had time to reflect: our coherent extrapolated volition. Aim the machine at our best selves, not our current selves.
cards.why: Solves whose values without freezing today's morality in silicon. The standard is aspirational, not descriptive.
cards.uw: Debating what values a superintelligence should be aligned to.

cards.title: One shot at existential risk
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: With ordinary technologies we learn from accidents - planes crash, we fix the design. An intelligence explosion offers no such tuition: if the first superintelligence is misaligned, there is no second trial. Existential risk means the error bars include extinction, and you only get to be wrong once.
cards.why: Explains why AI safety cannot proceed by the usual engineering method of build, break, patch. The stakes forbid the method.
cards.uw: Someone says we will figure out safety as we go, the way we always do.

cards.title: Whole brain emulation
cards.book: Superintelligence — Nick Bostrom
cards.steal: One path to superintelligence skips inventing minds from scratch: scan a human brain at fine enough resolution, simulate it, then run the simulation faster and copy it endlessly. The result starts with human-like motivations - including all our flaws - but freed from biology's speed limits and copy restrictions.
cards.why: A neuromorphic superintelligence inherits human drives rather than alien ones, which changes the alignment problem from teaching it values to managing an amplified, copyable human.
cards.uw: Considering paths to AI that do not go through machine learning scaling.

cards.title: The thermometer that cools the room
cards.book: An Inconvenient Truth: Calcium Sensors Are Calcium Buffers — Shane M. McMahon & Meyer B. Jackson
cards.steal: To watch brain cells work, scientists fill them with tiny sensors that glow when they catch calcium, the cell's “go” signal. But catching means holding on. If there's enough sensor to see the glow, there's almost certainly enough to weaken the signal and slow it down. It's a thermometer that cools the room while it measures it.
cards.why: The paper's core warning: the tool doesn't just watch the cell, it changes it, often several times over. The picture can end up showing the sensor more than the cell.
cards.uw: When a measurement has to grab, hold, or touch the thing it's measuring. Ask how much the grip is changing what you see.

cards.title: Assume it's happening
cards.book: An Inconvenient Truth: Calcium Sensors Are Calcium Buffers — Shane M. McMahon & Meyer B. Jackson
cards.steal: Don't ask whether the sensor is changing the cell. If you can see it glowing, it is. Start from that and work out how much, instead of hoping the effect is too small to matter.
cards.why: Flips the burden of proof. The distortion isn't a rare glitch to rule out. It's the normal case, so the honest starting point is to expect it.
cards.uw: When you're tempted to trust a reading because the tool “shouldn't” affect anything.

cards.title: Use a lighter grip
cards.book: An Inconvenient Truth: Calcium Sensors Are Calcium Buffers — Shane M. McMahon & Meyer B. Jackson
cards.steal: Sensors that hold calcium loosely change the signal less. The catch: they also glow less, so they're harder to see. You're trading a clearer picture for a truer one, and no setting gets you both for free.
cards.why: Names the real trade-off instead of pretending there's a perfect tool. Every sensor sits somewhere between “easy to see” and “barely disturbs anything.” Pick the spot on purpose.
cards.uw: When choosing how hard to look: more sensitivity usually means more interference.

cards.title: Know how much watching you're doing
cards.book: An Inconvenient Truth: Calcium Sensors Are Calcium Buffers — Shane M. McMahon & Meyer B. Jackson
cards.steal: Before trusting the picture, estimate how much sensor is actually in the cell. The authors suggest checking the microscope against samples of known strength and correcting for the tissue's own faint glow. It's hard and the answer is rough, but a rough number beats assuming zero.
cards.why: How much the signal gets distorted depends on how much sensor is in there. Without even a ballpark figure, you can't tell a real result from a side effect of how heavily the cell was loaded.
cards.uw: When results from different cells, animals, or labs disagree. Check whether they were simply watched with different amounts of sensor.

cards.title: Timing is the tell
cards.book: An Inconvenient Truth: Calcium Sensors Are Calcium Buffers — Shane M. McMahon & Meyer B. Jackson
cards.steal: Real calcium signals fade fast, in a fraction of a second. When a signal lingers for seconds, you're probably watching the sensor slowly let go, not the cell. The authors' test: measure the fade at a few known sensor amounts, then work backward to what it would be with none.
cards.why: A practical check anyone reading a study can use: compare how long the signal lasts with how long the real thing should last. Seconds where there should be a fraction of a second is a red flag.
cards.uw: When a recording looks smooth and slow. Ask whether the cell is slow or the sensor is.

cards.title: Brighter doesn't mean busier
cards.book: An Inconvenient Truth: Calcium Sensors Are Calcium Buffers — Shane M. McMahon & Meyer B. Jackson
cards.steal: A cell that glows brighter may look calmer, not busier, because more sensor soaks up more of its signal. The cells carrying the most sensor can be the ones whose activity looks most muted.
cards.why: It cuts against instinct. Brightness feels like proof of activity, but here it can mean the opposite, so ranking cells by glow alone can put them in backwards order.
cards.uw: When comparing how “active” different cells or brain areas look in a glowing image.

cards.title: When the sensor writes the story
cards.book: An Inconvenient Truth: Calcium Sensors Are Calcium Buffers — Shane M. McMahon & Meyer B. Jackson
cards.steal: In the lab, slowing every signal down can blur their timing, so cells look like they fire together when they don't. In mice bred to carry a glowing sensor in their brains, the sensor itself probably caused seizure-like activity.
cards.why: The distortion isn't just a smaller number. It can create false findings and even change how the brain behaves. The mouse result comes from a 2017 study the authors cite (Steinmetz et al., eNeuro).
cards.uw: When a study's big finding is cells acting in sync, or odd brain activity in glowing mice. Check whether the sensor alone could produce it.

cards.title: Every gauge has a grip
cards.book: An Inconvenient Truth: Calcium Sensors Are Calcium Buffers — Shane M. McMahon & Meyer B. Jackson
cards.steal: Polls shape the opinions they measure. Workers chase whatever number gets counted. People act differently on camera. Creators post for the numbers instead of the work. Wherever watching takes hold of what it watches, the reading drifts toward the watcher.
cards.why: Our extrapolation, not the paper's. The paper is only about brain cells. But its fixes travel: assume the effect, estimate how much watching you're doing, and use the lightest touch that still works.
cards.uw: When a metric, survey, or camera starts to feel like the goal instead of the window.

cards.title: What is my watching changing?
cards.book: An Inconvenient Truth: Calcium Sensors Are Calcium Buffers — Shane M. McMahon & Meyer B. Jackson
cards.steal: What am I watching that my watching is changing, and what would it look like if I looked less?
cards.why: Our extrapolation, not the paper's. It borrows the authors' move of working back to “zero sensor” and points it at everyday life.
cards.uw: Before you trust a number, a review, or a dashboard, or when a report on your own behavior looks a little too neat.

cards.title: The enemy knows the system
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Il faut qu'il n'exige pas le secret, et qu'il puisse sans inconvénient tomber entre les mains de l'ennemi. The system must not require secrecy, and must be able to fall into the enemy's hands without inconvenience.
cards.why: Security that depends on the method staying hidden dies the day it is captured, reverse-engineered, or leaked. Design as if the enemy already has the blueprint — because eventually they will.
cards.uw: When you are evaluating any security system, protocol, or anyone's secret sauce.

cards.title: A break doesn't expire
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Une fois qu'un cryptogramme intercepté a pu être déchiffré, toute nouvelle dépêche, écrite avec la même clef et qui subit le même sort, peut être lue instantanément. Once one intercepted cryptogram is broken, every later dispatch written with the same key can be read instantly.
cards.why: Against the claim that war messages only need three or four hours of secrecy: a break compounds. It doesn't expire with the message — it retroactively opens everything ever sent under that key.
cards.uw: When you are tempted to reuse a key, password, or credential because this one use is low-stakes.

cards.title: Secrecy doesn't scale
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: J'entends par secret, non la clef proprement dite, mais ce qui constitue la partie matérielle du système : tableaux, dictionnaires ou appareils mécaniques. By secrecy I mean not the key itself, but the material part of the system: tables, dictionaries, mechanical devices.
cards.why: If the machinery must stay secret, every new user is a new capture risk — so the system can never be issued beyond a handful of generals. A secret you can't distribute is a system you can't deploy.
cards.uw: When deciding what in your operation must stay secret versus what must survive exposure.

cards.title: Destroy the weapon by publishing it
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Ce n'était pas un des moindres services à rendre à la patrie que d'anéantir par la publicité l'arme la plus dangereuse des ennemis secrets. In 1793 Dlandol published the royalists' cipher keys — annihilating by publicity the most dangerous weapon of the Republic's secret enemies.
cards.why: Publicity as an offensive move. A broken secret, widely known to be broken, stops being a weapon — nobody will trust a cipher the newspapers have already printed the key to.
cards.uw: When you need to kill a bad standard, a compromised credential, or a practice that survives on obscurity.

cards.title: Every break is two jobs
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Le déchiffrement d'un cryptogramme dont on n'a pas la clef comporte deux opérations bien distinctes : un calcul de probabilité et un travail de tâtonnement. Breaking a cryptogram without the key is two distinct jobs: a probability calculation and groping trial-and-error.
cards.why: For polyalphabetic systems the two unknowns are the number of alphabets and their arrangement. Decomposing the attacker's job into countable subproblems is also how the defender prices each layer of defense.
cards.uw: When sizing up any adversarial problem — split it into the math and the groping.

cards.title: Repetition is the leak
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Dans tout texte chiffré, deux polygrammes semblables sont le produit de deux groupes de lettres semblables, cryptographiés avec les mêmes alphabets ; le nombre de chiffres compris dans l'intervalle des deux polygrammes est un multiple du nombre des lettres de la clef. Two identical ciphertext fragments come from two identical plaintext groups under the same alphabets — and the distance between them is a multiple of the key length.
cards.why: Take the greatest common divisor of the intervals between repeats and you have the key length. Redundancy betrays structure: the key is hiding in the gaps between repeats.
cards.uw: When hunting hidden periodicity in any data — ciphertext, logs, signals.

cards.title: The whole cipher is one letter: E
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: La valeur d'un chiffre se mesure aux garanties qu'il offre contre la découverte du signe correspondant à cette lettre. The value of a cipher is measured by the guarantees it offers against discovery of the sign for the letter E.
cards.why: In French, E is one letter in five. Find the most frequent symbol and the rest of the system unravels by trial. Every substitution-like structure has a load-bearing letter — the defense lives or dies on hiding it.
cards.uw: When attacking any substitution-like structure — find the anchor first.

cards.title: The traitor words
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Dans les cas un peu difficiles ce sont généralement les deux ou trois premiers mots qui viennent jouer le rôle de traîtres. In the hard cases it is generally the first two or three words that play the traitors.
cards.why: Military dispatches open predictably — le général, vous, ne — so the breaker keeps a classified list of likely openings indexed by where E falls. Every message has a predictable edge; the attacker catalogs it like factory-default passwords.
