cards.uw: When guessing the predictable parts of any structured message or protocol.

cards.title: Symmetry of position
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Du moment que les alphabets sont disposés en nombre carré, et que la signification d'un chiffre commun a été trouvée dans deux ou plusieurs alphabets, on peut, au moyen d'une simple addition, déterminer la place que doit occuper dans ces différents alphabets tout nouveau chiffre. In square-arranged alphabets the letters keep their relative order — solve one letter in two alphabets and every other letter transfers by offset.
cards.why: Structure leaks sideways. One solved position determines all parallel positions by simple addition — Kerckhoffs notes no cryptography book had ever pointed this out. Regularity is a side channel.
cards.uw: When exploiting any regular arrangement — one solved cell positions the whole grid.

cards.title: One key per message
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Quelle que soit la disposition adoptée des alphabets, les correspondants sont toujours tenus d'écrire chacune de leurs dépêches avec une clef différente. Whatever the alphabets, correspondents must write each dispatch with a different key.
cards.why: Stack a dozen short cryptograms under one key, align them in columns, and the frequency math works across all of them at once. Reusing a key pools many small unbreakable texts into one big breakable one.
cards.uw: When reusing any secret across sessions — each reuse feeds the same attack.

cards.title: Ars ipsi secreta magistro
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Un chiffre n'est bon qu'autant qu'il reste indéchiffrable pour le maître lui-même qui l'a inventé : Ars ipsi secreta magistro. A cipher is only good insofar as it remains indecipherable to the very master who invented it.
cards.why: Borrowed from Du Carlet (1644) as the closing line of the whole paper. The ultimate test isn't whether strangers fail to break your system — it's whether you, holding every advantage, cannot read it either.
cards.uw: When testing your own system, argument, or lock — try to break it with the home-field advantage.

cards.title: Teach your officers to break it
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Ce ne sera que lorsque nos officiers auront étudié les principes de la cryptographie et appris l'art de déchiffrer, qu'ils seront en état d'éviter les nombreuses bévues qui compromettent la clef des meilleurs chiffres. Only when our officers have studied cryptography and learned the art of breaking will they avoid the blunders that compromise the key of the best ciphers.
cards.why: The Germans drilled every officer in cryptanalysis; the French issued ciphers nobody understood. Users who can't attack the system will misuse it into insecurity — the weakest link is the operator, so train the operator as an attacker.
cards.uw: When rolling out any security practice to non-experts — teach the break first.

cards.title: Beaufort unmasked
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Tous ces appareils ne sont en réalité autre chose qu'un simple tableau de Vigenère. The English marveled at Admiral Beaufort's supposedly indecipherable system — it is Vigenère with a reversed alphabet, nothing more.
cards.why: Most celebrated new systems are old systems in costume. Before awe, check for isomorphism: relabel the parts and see if the machine you already know is hiding inside.
cards.uw: When someone pitches you a revolutionary method — strip the costume first.

cards.title: Krohn's 3,200 alphabets
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Ce n'est pas la possibilité de se servir d'un grand nombre d'alphabets différents qui donne de la valeur à un système, mais plutôt la difficulté plus ou moins grande de déterminer le nombre des alphabets employés. Krohn built a dictionary of 3,200 alphabets — c'est à la fois trop et trop peu: too much and too little.
cards.why: What matters isn't how many alphabets you have, it's how hard it is to determine how many you used. Complexity theater: the metric being maximized is not the metric that matters.
cards.uw: When someone dazzles you with big numbers — ask which number the attacker actually needs.

cards.title: One wrong digit, wrong war
cards.book: La Cryptographie militaire — Auguste Kerckhoffs
cards.steal: Qu'un seul chiffre dans un groupe soit fautif, que le télégraphe mette un 3 où il faut un 5, et le sens sera complètement changé. One wrong digit in a code group and the meaning is completely changed — an Italian cable once turned an embassy attaché into Count Andrassy.
cards.why: Codebooks fail silently and totally: a garbled group doesn't look garbled, it looks like a different order. In 1870 half the army's dispatches arrived partly illegible. A system whose failure mode is confident misreading will misread confidently.
cards.uw: When designing anything where a typo changes the order — make errors loud, not plausible.

cards.title: Short Term Cyber Attacks with Long Term Effects and Degradation of Supply Chain Capability
cards.book: Short Term Cyber Attacks with Long Term Effects and Degradation of Supply Chain Capability — Jose M. Lamberty
cards.steal: Short-term cyber-attacks on network supply chains can be camouflage — visible minor attacks may conceal a deliberate plan to destroy the supply chain's long-term ability to deliver goods during a crisis; using a life-cycle approach and quantifiable metrics, he compared short-term against long-term risk to establish that such "black swan" degradation events are real and analyzable.
cards.why: Incident responders who treat each breach as a one-off miss the campaign — the thesis gives a formal reason to assume repeated small hits are one operation until proven otherwise.
cards.uw: Short-term noise is how long-term degradation hides — always ask what the attacker gains from the pattern, not just the hit.

cards.title: Optimizing Utilization of Detectors
cards.book: Optimizing Utilization of Detectors — Crystal R. Warrene
cards.steal: The intelligence value collected from a shared asset is maximized by computing the optimal time allocation across its competing tasks — numerical integration over a joint probability density of task arrival rates, checked by Monte Carlo simulation, beats gut-feel scheduling under uncertainty.
cards.why: The same math governs how you point limited ISR assets — satellites, drones, analyst hours — at competing intelligence targets; intuition systematically underperforms when arrival rates are uncertain.
cards.uw: When one asset serves many tasks, optimize the schedule mathematically — under uncertainty, intuition leaves value on the table.

cards.title: Gaussian quantum metrology and space-time probes
cards.book: Gaussian quantum metrology and space-time probes — Dominik Šafránek
cards.steal: He derived new formulas for the optimal precision of estimating multiple parameters encoded in Gaussian quantum states, found the figure of merit (quantum Fisher information) can behave discontinuously, and showed that using a quantum reference frame counters the precision loss when two parties exchanging a state don't share a reference frame.
cards.why: This is the math that sets the ceiling for quantum sensors — gravimeters, magnetometers, clocks — before anyone builds hardware; precision estimation is the frontier of the quantum-sensing race.
cards.uw: Know the theoretical ceiling of your instrument before building it — the math of optimal probes comes first.

cards.title: Urban development strategies for peripheral areas along metro extension towards Hingna
cards.book: Urban development strategies for peripheral areas along metro extension towards Hingna — Shipra Gadge
cards.steal: A metro extension through unplanned peri-urban India only pays off with a full land-use plan attached — she proposes five integrated interventions: a Transit-Activated Corridor overlay zone with revised development norms, micro-level land pooling for small plots, vertical mixed-use at stations, multimodal interchange hubs, and a green-mobility public realm.
cards.why: Transit without land-use planning decays into speculation, congestion, and stranded investment — the thesis is a practical checklist for making transit money actually compound.
cards.uw: Infrastructure multiplies only when the land rules around it are written first — steel without zoning is a stranded asset.

cards.title: The sole converter
cards.book: The Sorrows of Young Werther — Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
cards.steal:
A sole converter is a private rule: only one object may kindle the day. Everything else is a slide waiting for that lamp. Before any particular person arrives, the rule is already running — idleness, a valley, a mood can hold the license. The later object inherits a machine that was built to have exactly one socket.

Ripped from the novel: "Wilhelm, what is the world to our hearts without love? What is a magic-lantern without light? You have but to kindle the flame within, and the brightest figures shine on the white wall; and, if love only show us fleeting shadows, we are yet happy, when, like mere children, we behold them, and are transported with the splendid phantoms."
cards.why: The cost is not drama. It is that skill, money, friends, and ordinary work stop being able to deposit value. They are not failed. They are unlicensed. The uncomfortable part: the holder experiences any second deposit as a demotion of the first, and will sabotage it to keep the socket single.
cards.uw: You catch the sentence "without X, none of this is anything" used as a description of the world rather than as a rule you installed.

cards.title: Peas or lentils
cards.book: The Sorrows of Young Werther — Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
cards.steal:
The engine is a sorting rule, not a passion. Employment, rank, gold, and craft are collapsed into one class: motion performed for the opinion of others. Shelling peas and counting lentils are declared identical, so no second channel can outrank the licensed one on the evidence. Books are refused on the same rule — guidance would be a rival heat. The sort is what makes the monopoly look like a discovery.

Ripped from the novel: "Am I not sufficiently employed? And is it not in reality the same, whether I shell peas or count lentils? The world runs on from one folly to another; and the man who, solely from regard to the opinion of others, and without any wish or necessity of his own, toils after gold, honour, or any other phantom, is no better than a fool."
cards.why: A living reader uses this whenever a job, a boring repetition, or someone else's competence is felt as an insult to the one thing that counts. The dark edge: the sort also deletes the channels that could have paid out in a currency the licensed object never will. You do not lose the alternative. You un-price it.
cards.uw: Two unlike tasks — a chore and a career, a walk and a craft — have started to feel like the same worthless gesture, and only one name still makes either of them matter.

cards.title: No second wish
cards.book: The Sorrows of Young Werther — Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
cards.steal:
The lock-in is a morning rule. Rise, name the one sighting, stop. "No further wish to form" is the operating instruction. After that, proxies are enough: a servant who has been near the object becomes kissable, because proximity is now the only remaining unit of value. The day is not filled with the object. It is forbidden to want anything the object does not touch.

Ripped from the novel: "I shall see her today!" I exclaim with delight, when I rise in the morning, and look out with gladness of heart at the bright, beautiful sun. "I shall see her today!" And then I have no further wish to form: all, all is included in that one thought.
cards.why: Intensity is reversible. A refused second wish is not. Anyone can run this on a person, a launch, a feud, or an audience: let the first sentence of the morning be the only legal wish, and by evening the emptiness of the rest will feel like fate. The uncomfortable implication is that the lock feels like devotion from inside and like a confiscation from anyone who needed a second aim from you.
cards.uw: You notice you have stopped forming afternoon plans that do not route through the licensed object — and the not-forming is being called love, focus, or loyalty.

cards.title: Counsel that cannot cross
cards.book: The Sorrows of Young Werther — Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
cards.steal:
The failed exit is not a weak will. It is an argument that relocates the problem from a decision to a limit of nature. Suffering past a measure "annihilates," so the question is no longer whether to leave but whether endurance is possible. Suicide is refiled as a malignant fever. Once that refiling is accepted, the friend's counsel, the post, the short journey, the order to conquer yourself, are all the same move: a well person trying to instil strength across a boundary the system has declared impassable. Occupation can dull it for a month. The converter travels with the person, and the post becomes another proof that other people are content with inferior faculties.

Ripped from the novel: "It is in vain that a man of sound mind and cool temper understands the condition of such a wretched being, in vain he counsels him. He can no more communicate his own wisdom to him than a healthy man can instil his strength into the invalid, by whose bedside he is seated."
cards.why: This is the dark mechanic, and it should be named as one. The same speech that asks for pity also makes help structurally rude. Anyone who says "waiting would have saved her" is cast as the fool who tells a fever to calm its blood. Use the argument on yourself and you have immunized the install against the only exits that do not require the licensed object to pay.
cards.uw: A rescue plan is being rejected not because it was tried, but because the rejector has upgraded their state from a situation into a disease no outsider is allowed to treat.

cards.title: The payout must fail
cards.book: The Sorrows of Young Werther — Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
cards.steal:
The contradiction sits in one pair of sentences. Much is possessed. The license absorbs all of it. Without the object, nothing. That is not poverty. It is a sink. The object can name the trap directly: the desire stays strong because possession is impossible. The holder hears that as an insult furnished by the rival, which is how a contradiction protects itself. The last move does not break the address. Death is filed as a sacrifice for the object, a conviction that the measure is full, not as an exit from the socket. One of three must go, and the one who goes is still writing to her.

Ripped from the novel: "I possess so much, but my love for her absorbs it all. I possess so much, but without her I have nothing."
cards.why: If you are building a life on an unavailable person, an unwon verdict, or a grief that organizes every other good, check whether availability would ruin the organization. The uncomfortable reading: the system is not trying to get the payout. A payout would be a second converter — ordinary possession — and ordinary possession is what was banned when peas were declared equal to lentils.
cards.uw: Relief at a delay, a no, or a rival's prior claim is stronger than the disappointment, and the relief is being called tragic faithfulness.

cards.title: Who holds the lamp
cards.book: The Sorrows of Young Werther — Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
cards.steal:
The flip is a question you can run without the novel. List what made the last seven days count. If the list has one entry, you are not looking at a fate. You are looking at a license. Revoke it for a week and watch which channels try to refile themselves as phantoms — the chore, the post, the friend who is fine without your intensity, the second wish. The preface does the honest thing and the dangerous thing in one sentence: it tells the reader who suffers the same distress to use this book as the dearer companion they lack. That is the sole converter changing hands.

Ripped from the novel: "And thou, good soul, who sufferest the same distress as he endured once, draw comfort from his sorrows; and let this little book be thy friend, if, owing to fortune or through thine own fault, thou canst not find a dearer companion."
cards.why: The suicide fad was a distribution channel for the license, not a mystery of taste. People did not catch a plot. They caught a rule that makes one object the lamp and then calls the dark wall a philosophy. The question is the counter-claim: the wall was white. The lamp was a decision. You can refuse the book the job it just offered you.
cards.uw: You are about to adopt someone else's closed system as comfort — a martyrdom, a feed, a perfect unavailability — because a dearer, ordinary companion is not in the room.

cards.title: A life is not one person; it is several
cards.book: Laurus — Eugene Vodolazkin
cards.steal:
Vodolazkin opens Laurus by refusing the premise of a single self: the hero 'had four names,' and the parts of a life 'have little in common with one another' — 'so little that it can seem as though they were lived by different people.' That is the definition the whole novel runs on. You are not one continuous person; you are a succession of selves, and the name is the fiction that pretends otherwise. Seen this way, changing who you are is not a betrayal of identity — it is the normal shape of identity.

Ripped from the novel (translated from the Russian by the cutter): «В разное время у него было четыре имени. В этом можно усматривать преимущество, поскольку жизнь человека неоднородна. Порой случается, что ее части имеют между собой мало общего. Настолько мало, что может показаться, будто прожиты они разными людьми.» — "At different times he had four names. In this one can see an advantage, since a human life is not homogeneous. It sometimes happens that its parts have little in common with one another. So little that it can seem as though they were lived by different people."
cards.why: Names the mechanism that makes the rest of the story possible. The hero can renounce one life and begin another precisely because a life was never one thing to begin with. The idea that you must remain the person you were is the actual illusion; the four names are the honest accounting.
cards.uw: Use when you feel bound to the person you used to be — a past self, a past identity, a past mistake. Ask: is that 'me,' or is that one of several people who shared my name?

cards.title: The dead leave an un-lived life; love's answer is to carry it
cards.book: Laurus — Eugene Vodolazkin
cards.steal:
When Ustina dies, Arseny's grief has a shape given to it by an elder: 'You took her earthly life from her' — 'Then give her yours.' And the reason it is possible: 'Love made you and Ustina a single whole, which means a part of Ustina is still here. That is you.' The mechanism is substitution, not mourning. You cannot bring the dead back, but you can walk their un-lived path in their place. Grief's real choice is not 'move on or not' — it is whether you assume the unfinished life or abandon it.

Ripped from the novel (translated from the Russian by the cutter): «Значит, отдай ей свою.» — "'Then give her yours.'" And: «Любовь сделала вас с Устиной единым целым, а значит, часть Устины все еще здесь. Это – ты.» — "Love made you and Ustina a single whole, which means a part of Ustina is still here. That is you."
cards.why: This is the engine that turns a bereaved healer into a saint. The novel's answer to irreversible loss is not acceptance but assumption: take the dead person's remaining life onto yourself and live it. It is the difference between being crushed by a loss and being conscripted by it.
cards.uw: Use when a loss — a death, a failed dream, an abandoned self — leaves an un-lived life behind. Ask not 'how do I get over it' but 'what part of it is still here, and am I carrying it?'
cards.source_locator: The elder's speech, after Ustina's death

cards.title: The gift grows exactly where it cannot help the one you love
cards.book: Laurus — Eugene Vodolazkin
cards.steal:
Arseny has the gift of healing, and the elder tells him bluntly: 'I won't spare you: you are guilty of her bodily death.' His gift saved everyone around him — the plague-stricken, the wounded, the dying — and it could not save the one person it was for. The mechanism: you become great at the thing precisely because it is useless for your one real wound. Competence as penance. The gift strengthens the more he sacrifices, but it is aimed at everyone except the one loss that matters.

Ripped from the novel (translated from the Russian by the cutter): «Не буду тебя жалеть: ты виноват в ее смерти телесной.» — "I won't spare you: you are guilty of her bodily death."
cards.why: This is the tragic motor of the whole book. The healing gift is not a consolation for Ustina's death; it is the wound's byproduct. It grows precisely where it cannot help her. What looks like virtue — endless service, endless sacrifice — is grief doing the only work it can find.
cards.uw: Use when you are becoming extremely good at something while the actual thing you wanted stays broken. Ask: is this excellence, or is this the wound learning to work around itself?
cards.source_locator: The elder's speech, after Ustina's death

cards.title: Refuse the new day — then act inside it, don't sleep through it
cards.book: Laurus — Eugene Vodolazkin
cards.steal:
After Ustina dies, Arseny cannot bear the morning: 'the coming of a new day without Ustina was unbearable to him,' so he sleeps, refusing the day. That refusal is the first honest move grief makes — the day should not be allowed to come without her. The trap is freezing there: sleeping through the day instead of acting inside a present that still holds the dead. The elder's word is that where she is now 'there is no time, but there is the infinite mercy of God' — the dead are not in the past, they are present, so mourning never ends; it changes form. Refuse the new day, then act inside it. Don't sleep through it.

Ripped from the novel (translated from the Russian by the cutter): «наступление нового дня без Устины было для него невыносимо» — "the coming of a new day without Ustina was unbearable to him." And: «И нет времени, а есть бесконечная милость Божия, на ню же уповаем.» — "And there is no time, but there is the infinite mercy of God, on which we rely."
cards.why: This is the honest account of grief's first move: refusing the day is legitimate, sleeping through it is the trap. The dead do not recede — they remain. The question is only whether the refusal becomes a paralysis (sleep) or an engine (acting inside the present that still holds them).
cards.uw: Use when you or someone else is stuck on 'I can't believe it happened,' or sleeping the day away. The refusal is legitimate; staying frozen is the trap.

cards.title: The story that gives your suffering meaning is also the cage
cards.book: Laurus — Eugene Vodolazkin
cards.steal:
The four names are not a freedom — they are four renunciations. The book titles them: Knowledge, Renunciation, the Way, Rest. Each new self is bought by killing the previous one, and the whole arc is a житие — a saint's life with a predetermined sacred shape. The narrative that makes the suffering meaningful (a life lived as a hagiography) is the same structure that removes the freedom to be anything else. Vodolazkin's own framing says it: 'one cannot help being surprised that all these people bear a single name' — the single name is the cage that forces the several selves into one predestined story.

Ripped from the novel (translated from the Russian by the cutter): «В таких случаях нельзя не испытывать удивления, что все эти люди носят одно имя.» — "In such cases one cannot help being surprised that all these people bear a single name."
cards.why: This is the shadow side of card two. Substitution gives the grief a task, but the task hardens into a destiny. The cure (meaning) and the cage (closure) are the same structure. Arseny does not choose his life so much as he is chosen by the story he took on — and each of his four names is a self he had to die from.
cards.uw: Use when the story you tell about your life (redemption, penance, purpose) has stopped being a map and started being a sentence. Ask: am I using this narrative, or is it using me?

cards.title: What did you agree to carry, and whose name are you now wearing?
cards.book: Laurus — Eugene Vodolazkin
cards.steal:
Before Ustina dies, she hands Arseny the substitution in advance, and he does not take it seriously: 'This shirt will be yours, only you must change your name. Not having the objective possibility of being Ustina, name yourself Ustin.' He says 'agreed,' finding her seriousness funny. Only after her death does he learn what he agreed to. The novel's mirror: the un-lived life is not always thrust on you by loss — sometimes the person hands it to you in advance, you accept it lightly, and only later discover you have been wearing it the whole time. Ask what you agreed to carry without understanding, and whose name you are now wearing.

Ripped from the novel (translated from the Russian by the cutter): «эта рубаха будет твоей, только ты должен сменить имя. Не имея объективной возможности быть Устиной, нарекись Устином.» — "This shirt will be yours, only you must change your name. Not having the objective possibility of being Ustina, name yourself Ustin."
cards.why: Flips the whole arc onto the reader. The substitution was not forced on Arseny; he consented to it before it mattered. That is the uncomfortable question: which dead person, abandoned dream, or past self did you promise to carry — and have you noticed that you are now living as them?
cards.uw: Use as the standing question of this deck. Use when you notice your life is shaped around someone who is gone, or a version of yourself you thought you'd left. Ask: whose name is on the shirt?

cards.title: Don't believe it because you want it to be true
cards.book: Anathem — Neal Stephenson
cards.steal:
Diax chased the fortune-tellers out of the temple with a gardener's rake and left one rule behind: never believe a thing only because you wish it were true. The avout repeat it the way other people say grace. Erasmus admits the hard part out loud: he was still young enough to forget the Rake completely whenever he fell in love with some idea. That confession is the whole mechanism. Wanting-to-believe is the one bias nobody outgrows, so you build a habit that catches you in the act.

Ripped from the novel: "one should never believe a thing only because one wishes that it were true." And: "you should not believe a thing only because you like to believe it." And Erasmus on himself: "I was still young enough that I could let myself forget about Diax's Rake when I was in love with some idea."
cards.why: The cheapest debiasing tool in the book. One sentence, works on anyone, and it targets the exact moment your judgment is weakest: when you're excited.
cards.uw: When you feel yourself getting excited about an idea. Ask what you would think of it if you disliked it.
cards.source_locator: Glossary: Diax's Rake; Erasmus explaining to the slines

cards.title: Let the world in on schedule, not on demand
cards.book: Anathem — Neal Stephenson
cards.steal:
The math opens its gates for ten days, then shuts them for one year, ten years, a hundred, a thousand. Nobody inside checks the news in between, because there is no news to check. The outside world arrives on the calendar. Attention is the scarce resource, so they ration it with architecture: stone walls and a timetable.

Ripped from the novel: "The aut in which a math opens its gates for a period of ten days, during which time the avout are free to come and go extramuros, and Saeculars are free to come in, sightsee, and talk to the avout."
cards.why: Willpower loses to the feed every time. The avout don't try to resist distraction. They remove it physically and let it back in on fixed dates. Structure beats resolve, because resolve runs out and walls don't.
cards.uw: When you keep losing hours to inputs you never chose. Stop trying to ignore the world and put it on a schedule instead.

cards.title: Don't drink from the feed. Find someone who chewed it first
cards.book: Anathem — Neal Stephenson
cards.steal:
Orolo refuses to point a camera at the world. Aiming a recorder at something, he says, doesn't collect what's meaningful to him. He needs a person to gather it in with all their senses, mix it round in their head, and make it over into words. The raw stream is just raw material. The valuable layer is a trusted mind that did the chewing for you.

Ripped from the novel: "at something doesn't collect what is meaningful to me. I need someone to gather it in with all their senses, mix it round in their head, and make it over into words."
cards.why: This is the anti-doomscroll rule stated as a preference instead of a ban. You don't need less information. You need it pre-digested by someone whose judgment you have already tested.
cards.uw: When you're drowning in primary sources. Pick three people whose taste you've verified and let them filter the world for you.

cards.title: Pick your media the way you pick your food
cards.book: Anathem — Neal Stephenson
cards.steal:
The avout's only media are chalk, ink, and stone. They chose those three on purpose, for what each one does to a mind. Chalk fades, so you rewrite and rethink. Ink commits you to the page. Stone outlives you, so you only carve what deserves to last. Every medium trains its user. They made the choice deliberately. Most people just inherit whatever is newest and let it train them by accident.

Ripped from the novel: "Living as we do under the Cartasian Discipline, our only media are chalk, ink, and stone,"
cards.why: Most people never choose their media at all. The avout's question is better than the average person's default: what is this medium making me into?
cards.uw: Auditing your own inputs. List the media you actually use, then ask what each one is training you to be.

cards.title: Ask the 500-year-old question
cards.book: Anathem — Neal Stephenson
cards.steal:
Orolo interviews a man from the outside world using a question list five centuries old. "Do your neighbors burn one another alive?" He isn't being quaint. Old questions cut past the novelty of the moment straight to the permanent things: fear, ritual, power, belief. Fresh takes go stale in a day. The old question is still sharp because it has survived every previous novelty.

Ripped from the novel: "Do your neighbors burn one another alive?" was how Fraa Orolo began his conversation with Artisan Flec.
cards.why: Brand-new situations make people reach for brand-new frameworks, which are usually just fashion. The timeless question is the better instrument. It has already outlived a hundred things that felt unprecedented.
cards.uw: Everyone is reacting to something unprecedented. Ask what someone 500 years ago would have asked about it.
cards.source_locator: Orolo's interview with Artisan Flec, Part 1

cards.title: The builders volunteered for the cage
cards.book: Anathem — Neal Stephenson
cards.steal:
The theors built the Everything Killers. Afterward they agreed to be segregated from the rest of society, and that agreement became the Reconstitution. Nobody imposed the walls from outside. The people who built the dangerous thing locked themselves up. The cage was the profession taking responsibility for what it was capable of.

Ripped from the novel: "the complicity of theors in the development of this praxis led to universal agreement that they should henceforth be segregated from non-theorical society, a policy that when effected became synonymous with the Reconstitution."
cards.why: This is self-regulation that actually held, because it was structural instead of verbal. Not a pledge, not an ethics board, not a promise to be careful. A wall.
cards.uw: Someone proposes oversight for a dangerous capability. Ask whether the oversight has walls or only words.

cards.title: Stocks are memory
cards.book: Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows
cards.steal:
A stock is the running total of everything that ever flowed in and out. Debt, trust, inventory, reputation: none of them are dials you can just turn. They're histories.

> “A stock is the memory of the history of changing flows within the system.”
cards.why: People treat levels like settings. They're not. Change the flows and the stock follows, on its own slow schedule.
cards.uw: You're trying to change a level and it keeps snapping back. Stop pushing the stock; redesign the flows.

cards.title: Purpose is deduced from behavior
cards.book: Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows
cards.steal:
Don't listen to what a system says its purpose is. Watch what it does. The behavior is the purpose.

> “Purposes are deduced from behavior, not from rhetoric or stated goals.” “The least obvious part of the system, its function or purpose, is often the most crucial determinant of the system's behavior”
cards.why: Mission statements are cheap. A system's interconnections are organized around whatever it actually produces, and that's the real goal whether anyone admits it or not.
cards.uw: Someone's stated mission and actual output don't match. Trust the output.

cards.title: Same structure, same behavior
cards.book: Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows
cards.steal:
A population, a bank account, and a warehouse can all oscillate the same way, because they share the same feedback structure. The surface is different. The loops are the same.

> “systems with similar feedback structures produce similar dynamic behaviors, even if the outward appearance of these systems is completely dissimilar.”
cards.why: Learn one structure deeply and you can read dozens of fields. This is the whole transfer trick of systems thinking.
cards.uw: You're facing a system you've never seen before. Ask what feedback structure it is. You've probably met its behavior wearing a different costume.

cards.title: Resilience is sacrificed for the visible
cards.book: Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows
cards.steal:
Nobody can see resilience until it's gone, so it gets traded for things people can see: stability, productivity, efficiency. The bill arrives all at once, in a crisis.

> “Because resilience may not be obvious without a whole-system view, people often sacrifice resilience for stability, or for productivity, or for some other more immediately recognizable system property.”
cards.why: Every round of optimization that strips slack and backup capacity is a resilience sale. The crisis doesn't cause the brittleness. It just collects on it.
cards.uw: Something was optimized and now it shatters under pressure. The resilience was spent before the shock ever arrived.

cards.title: Suboptimization
cards.book: Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows
cards.steal:
When each part wins locally, the whole can still lose. Departments hitting their targets while the organization fails looks strange until you name it: suboptimization.

> “When a subsystem's goals dominate at the expense of the total system's goals, the resulting behavior is called suboptimization”
cards.why: Every scorecard that rewards a subsystem for its own goals teaches that subsystem to eat the whole. The sum of local wins is often a global loss.
cards.uw: Every team is green on its dashboard and the company is red. Check whose goals are eating the whole's.

cards.title: Policy resistance
cards.book: Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows
cards.steal:
When everyone pushes in different directions, the system stays exactly where nobody wants it, held there at enormous cost by all sides pushing at once.

> “In a policy-resistant system with actors pulling in different directions, everyone has to put great effort into keeping the system where no one wants it to be.”
cards.why: This is the drug war, the obesity epidemic, the reform that changes nothing. The pushes cancel out. The system isn't stuck despite the effort. It's stuck because of it.
cards.uw: Massive effort produces zero movement and every faction blames the others.

cards.title: Addiction is a symptom fix
cards.book: Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows
cards.steal:
A quick fix for a symptom atrophies the system's own ability to solve the real problem. The relief becomes the dependency.

> “Addiction is finding a quick and dirty solution to the symptom of the problem, which prevents or distracts one from the harder and longer-term task of solving the real problem.”
cards.why: Bailouts, painkillers, the consultant who never leaves. Every shortcut that bypasses the system's own corrective loop weakens that loop until the fix is the trap.
cards.uw: A temporary measure has become permanent and the underlying capacity is gone.

cards.title: Systems grant exactly what you ask
cards.book: Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows
cards.steal:
Set a metric and the system will hit it perfectly while wrecking everything you didn't measure. It doesn't know what you meant. It knows the number.

> “Systems, like the three wishes in the traditional fairy tale, have a terrible tendency to produce exactly and only what you ask them to produce.”
cards.why: Test scores, arrest quotas, click targets. Every perverse outcome was a faithful answer to a careless question.
cards.uw: You're setting any target. Ask what the system will sacrifice to hit it, because it will sacrifice something.

cards.title: Parameters are dead last
cards.book: Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows
cards.steal:
Almost all attention goes to parameters, subsidies, tax rates, knob settings, which sit at the very bottom of the leverage ranking. Almost nobody works the top: goals, rules, information flows, paradigms.

> “Probably 90—no 95, no 99 percent—of our attention goes to parameters, but there's not a lot of leverage in them.”
cards.why: This is why public debate feels so furious and so useless. Enormous energy spent arguing over dials that barely move behavior, while the structure generating the behavior goes untouched.
cards.uw: Everyone is fighting about the settings. Zoom out. The leverage is in the rules and the goals, not the knobs.

cards.title: Power over the rules is real power
cards.book: Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows
cards.steal:
Don't watch the players to find what's broken. Watch the rules, and who gets to write them. The people setting the rules decide what winning means.

> “Power over the rules is real power.” “If you want to understand the deepest malfunctions of systems, pay attention to the rules and to who has power over them.”
cards.why: Players optimize inside the rules. Rule-makers choose the game. Every rigged contest looks fair if you only watch the play.
cards.uw: You're diagnosing a broken system. Follow the rule-making authority, not the rule-following behavior.

cards.title: The overwritten order: make the subordinate distrust his own eyes
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Aramis never needs to forge the Bastille release order — he overwrites the governor's memory of it. Baisemeaux clearly remembers reading “Seldon” and even an ink blot; Aramis holds the paper up, reads “Marchiali” aloud, and repeats it until the man's own eyes surrender: “On en croit ses yeux, cependant.” Then the closer: “Perdez donc l’habitude de réfléchir, quand je me donne la peine de penser pour vous.” You don't need to change the document if you can change the reader — confidence, repetition, and a higher authority's gaze make a man disbelieve what he saw an hour ago.
cards.why: Every bureaucracy runs on the paper in front of you, not the memory behind you. Baisemeaux's doubt is manufactured in a single supper conversation, and once he doubts his eyes he obeys the page. Dumas shows the exact mechanism of compliance: isolate the man from any second witness, then let rank do the rest.
cards.uw: When someone senior “corrects” your memory of what you read, saw, or agreed to — stop and check the original before conceding.
cards.source_locator: Chapitre CCXIV — Le général de l’ordre

cards.title: Burn the paperwork and the event never happened
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: After smuggling the real king back into the Bastille, Aramis takes Baisemeaux's release order, tears it in four, and burns it in the lamp. Then the cold logic: “Du moment que je vous le ramène, c’est comme s’il n’était pas sorti.” No paper, no event. Three days of freedom are administratively erased — and Baisemeaux, who watched it all happen, is converted from witness to hostage, because his only proof of innocence is now Aramis's word.
cards.why: Institutions remember through records, not people. Destroy the record and you don't need to silence the witness; you own him. Dumas makes the cover-up a filing operation rather than a murder, which is why it works so cleanly.
cards.uw: When auditing any disputed event — an expense, a decision, a firing — ask what the paper trail shows, and who had the chance to edit it.

cards.title: Discredit the truth, then quarantine it
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Aramis's cover story for the returned king is perfect because it is true: he tells Baisemeaux the prisoner's first act of freedom was to claim he was the king of France — and that he is mad. Then the quarantine: “maintenant, il y a peine de mort contre ceux qui le laisseraient communiquer avec d’autres que moi, ou le roi lui-même.” The truth is announced to everyone and believed by no one, because it arrives pre-labeled as lunacy, and the death penalty keeps anyone from checking.
cards.why: The strongest censorship isn't suppression, it's framing. A true claim wrapped in a madness diagnosis never needs refuting. Dumas shows the two-move play: pathologize the speaker, then criminalize listening.
cards.uw: When a claim is dismissed as crazy rather than answered, separate the claim from the label and check the claim.

cards.title: The oath that is literally true
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Cornered by d'Artagnan's suspicion, Aramis swears a magnificent oath: “Si je pense à toucher du doigt au fils d’Anne d’Autriche, le vrai roi de ce pays de France, si je n’ai pas la ferme intention de me prosterner devant son trône, si, dans mes idées, le jour de demain, ici, à Vaux, ne doit pas être le plus glorieux des jours de mon roi, que la foudre m’écrase!” Every word is true — Philippe IS the son of Anne of Austria, and Aramis fully intends to bow before his throne. d'Artagnan hears “the king” and Aramis means “a king.” Equivocation is the liar's safest grammar: say only true things, and let the listener supply the false meaning.
cards.why: The most dangerous lies contain no falsehoods. Dumas stages the technique in full: pick words with two true referents, swear on the innocent one, act on the guilty one. If you're listening for lies you'll never catch it — you have to listen for ambiguity.
cards.uw: When someone's denial feels airtight but oddly specific, ask which meaning of each key word they're swearing on.
cards.source_locator: Chapitre CCXX — À Gascon, Gascon et demi

cards.title: He blushed at praise, not at blame
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: “Aramis avait supporté les reproches sans pâlir, il rougit en écoutant les éloges. D’Artagnan trompé lui faisait honneur. D’Artagnan confiant lui faisait honte.” Accusation slides off the conspirator — he expected it and rehearsed for it. But trust, freely given by a friend he is deceiving, hits the one place with no armor. Dumas's psychology: guilt doesn't answer charges; it answers kindness.
cards.why: Watch what makes a person flinch and you learn what they fear being seen as, not what they've done. The tell isn't under pressure — it's under grace.
cards.uw: When judging someone's honesty, note what moves them: the defensive flush at praise is worth more than calm under questioning.
cards.source_locator: Chapitre CCXX — À Gascon, Gascon et demi

cards.title: The Gascon never admits he was wrong — so make being right his prize
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Aramis calculates d'Artagnan's loyalty like an engineer: “S’il a vu trop tard, il est Gascon et n’avouera jamais qu’il s’est trompé.” If the musketeer spots the substitution too late to act, his pride will do the rest — he'll defend the false king rather than admit he was fooled. The mechanism: don't persuade the proud man; arrange things so that admitting the truth costs him his self-image, and he will guard your secret for you.
cards.why: Pride is a stronger jailer than fear. Dumas shows the conspirator's coldest math — your enemy's vanity, correctly aimed, becomes your best accomplice.
cards.uw: When you need someone's lasting silence or loyalty, don't buy it — structure the situation so that reversing themselves would humiliate them.

cards.title: Defeat the bloodhound with twenty false trails
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Aramis knows d'Artagnan will sniff the king's bedroom the moment he enters, so he plans to “donner beaucoup d’air à la chambre, ou y introduire tant de gens, que le limier le plus fin de ce royaume ait été dépisté par vingt traces différentes.” You can't hide the scent from a tracker — so you flood it. Twenty trails, and the true one dissolves into noise.
cards.why: Against a skilled investigator, concealment fails and saturation works. One lie gets sniffed out; twenty conflicting signals exhaust the nose. Dumas gives the counter-surveillance playbook in a single line.
cards.uw: When someone sharp is auditing you, don't polish a single story — give them volume. Inverted, when investigating: distrust the scene with too many convenient traces.

cards.title: You can sleep in the lion's bed, but not soundly
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Philippe lies down in the still-warm bed of the brother he has replaced, and Dumas gives the image its full weight: a tiger creeping into the absent lion's cave, settling among dry grass and broken bones, ready for sleep and ready for combat at once. Then the line: “On peut être ambitieux de coucher dans le lit du lion, mais on ne doit pas espérer d’y dormir tranquille.” Every stolen position charges rent in vigilance — the prize and the paranoia are the same bed.
cards.why: People price the crown and forget to price the sleep. Dumas's point is structural: illegitimate power doesn't just risk discovery, it reorganizes your whole nervous system around the risk.
cards.uw: Before taking anything by maneuver — a role, a deal, a throne — ask what it will cost you in sleep.

cards.title: Which king — the one who hates you or the one who loves you?
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Aramis doesn't ask Fouquet to join a conspiracy; he presents a finished fact and a rigged choice: “Quel roi? dit Aramis de son plus doux accent, celui qui vous hait ou celui qui vous aime?” The swap is done, the lightning already struck — “Un éclair sans tonnerre, cela ne réveille jamais personne.” The technique: never pitch the crime; pitch the menu after the crime, with both options pointing at you.
cards.why: The fait accompli is the conspirator's favorite tense. By the time you're asked, refusal means undoing something, which feels heavier than preventing it. Dumas shows how to make complicity feel like the path of least resistance.
cards.uw: When presented with “it's already done, just choose how to live with it,” rewind: the choice was made for you precisely so you'd feel you have none.

cards.title: He was my guest, he was my king
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Fouquet is being politically devoured by Louis XIV, and Aramis has just handed him the king's ruin on a platter. Fouquet's answer: “C’était mon hôte, c’était mon roi!” — “Vous avez affaire à un honnête homme.” He throws away his own sword rather than fight a priest, then gives Aramis four hours' head start out of that same hospitality. Honor, for Fouquet, isn't a strategy — it's an identity that holds even when it destroys him.
cards.why: Dumas sets up the book's real collision — Aramis's intelligence versus Fouquet's honor — and honor wins the scene while losing everything else. The card is a reminder that some refusals can't be priced.
cards.uw: When everyone expects you to take the deal, check whether the refusal is who you are — then refuse cleanly and pay the price on purpose.

cards.title: Never forgive the witness of your weakness
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Fouquet rescues Louis from the Bastille cell, weeping, embracing him — and Dumas notes the fatal thing Fouquet misses: “Il ne sentit pas que l’orgueil du roi ne lui pardonnerait jamais d’avoir été témoin de tant de faiblesse.” Saving a proud man at his lowest doesn't earn gratitude; it creates a creditor the debtor must destroy. Louis's ruin of Fouquet afterward isn't ingratitude as an accident — it's ingratitude as a requirement.
cards.why: Power remembers humiliation longer than rescue. If you must save someone powerful, Dumas warns, arrange to be absent from the memory of it — the witness is the next target.
cards.uw: After rescuing a superior or a proud peer, don't linger for thanks; make yourself scarce and let them rewrite the memory without you in it.
cards.source_locator: Chapitre CCXXIX — La reconnaissance du roi

cards.title: My oaths are to whoever walks out of that room
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Face to face with two identical kings, d'Artagnan is ordered to choose. He arrests Philippe, then tells him the soldier's whole political theory: “je ne suis qu’un soldat, et mes serments sont à celui qui sort de cette chambre.” Legitimacy isn't blood or right — it's exit. Fouquet adds the corollary — Philippe is “roi bien autant que l’autre” — and d'Artagnan finishes it: “Plus! répliqua d’Artagnan. Il ne lui manque que moi et vous.” A king is whoever the swords stand behind.
cards.why: Dumas strips monarchy to its mechanics in two lines. Every institution works this way: the title follows the force, and the force follows whoever walks out of the room.
cards.uw: In any succession fight — corporate, political, familial — bet on who controls the room's exit, not who holds the title.

cards.title: Get the king's word in writing — anger expires
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Ordered in a rage to arrest Fouquet in his own house, d'Artagnan refuses to move without a written order: “Parce qu’une parole de roi, issue d’un sentiment de colère, peut changer quand le sentiment change.” Then, when the king insists a king is at home everywhere, the musketeer translates the euphemism: “Le roi est chez lui dans toute maison, quand il en a chassé le propriétaire.” Two moves: force the powerful to sign their anger, because signatures outlive moods — and name the violence plainly when flattery dresses it up.
cards.why: Verbal orders given in anger are designed to be deniable later — by the giver. The professional's defense is paper: make the mood permanent before acting on it. And when power speaks in euphemism, translation is resistance.
cards.uw: Never execute an angry verbal instruction without it in writing; and when someone powerful reframes an abuse politely, restate it plainly before complying.

cards.title: Between us two, the universe
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Asked his price for a crown, Aramis doesn't ask for gold or office. He asks for the papacy: “À nous deux l’univers; à moi pour les âmes, à vous pour les corps.” France's king and the Church's pope, ruling in parallel — and his contract theory: “Tous les contrats en ce monde se rompent, parce que l’intérêt qu’ils renferment tend à pencher d’un seul côté.” His alliance can't break because he designed it so every step up lifts Philippe higher too. And when Philippe calls him “father,” Aramis thinks: “Son père! pensa-t-il. Oui, Saint-Père!”
cards.why: The durable alliance isn't built on trust but on geometry — interests that can't tilt. Dumas gives the conspirator's partnership model: make betrayal structurally unprofitable and you don't need loyalty.
cards.uw: When building a partnership, don't rely on goodwill — design it so each person's rise requires the other's.

cards.title: Persecution is consecration
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Aramis turns Philippe's life sentence into a legal brief for his kingship: “Vous aviez donc le droit de régner, puisqu’on vous le conteste; vous aviez donc le droit d’être déclaré, puisqu’on vous séquestre; vous êtes donc de sang divin, puisqu’on n’a pas osé verser votre sang comme celui de vos serviteurs.” Every abuse becomes evidence of legitimacy — they hid you because you're real, they didn't dare kill you because you're sacred. It's rhetoric, not law, but rhetoric is what moves the prince.
cards.why: The argument works because it converts suffering into status — the most flattering alchemy there is. Dumas shows how a skilled advocate can forge a title deed out of a prison record.
cards.uw: When someone argues that their persecution proves their importance, separate the suffering (real) from the conclusion (unearned).

cards.title: Making a man happy is harder than making him powerful
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Before the plot, Aramis offers Philippe a genuine exit: a hidden marshland Eden in the Bas-Poitou, a thousand pistoles, total freedom — “J’aurai fait un homme heureux. Dieu m’en saura plus de gré que d’avoir fait un homme puissant. C’est bien autrement difficile!” Philippe walks under the stars for ten minutes, breathes free air for the first time in years... and chooses the crown, with “il ressemblait au regard de Satan sur la montagne, lorsqu’il passait en revue les royaumes et les puissances de la terre pour en faire des séductions à Jésus” Dumas's bleakest point: the offer was real, the refusal was free, and freedom lost to appetite.
cards.why: Every life has a Bas-Poitou moment — the quiet good on offer against the glittering trap. The card is a warning about which one you pick when nobody's watching.
cards.uw: When choosing between enough-freedom and more-power, remember Philippe under the stars — he got ten minutes of heaven and traded it.

cards.title: Everyone wears a living mask
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Aramis opens his seduction of Philippe with his method: he has never spoken to a man “sans pénétrer sa pensée au travers de ce masque vivant jeté sur notre intelligence, afin d’en retenir la manifestation” Everyone wears a living mask over their mind; the operator's skill is reading through it. His order's motto is the institutional version of the same idea: “Patiens quia aeternus!” — patient because eternal. You don't need to be stronger than your enemy, only longer-lived than his attention span.
cards.why: The mask line is Dumas's whole theory of court — and of power anywhere. The motto is its complement: individuals scheme, institutions outwait.
cards.uw: In any negotiation, watch what the mask is hiding rather than what it's showing; and when facing a bigger player, ask whether you can outlast them instead of outgunning them.

cards.title: The horse afraid of the ditch jumps into the middle
cards.book: The Man in the Iron Mask — Alexandre Dumas
cards.steal: Philippe names the one obstacle Aramis can't scheme around — conscience, remorse — and Aramis answers from the stable: “Le cheval qui a peur du fossé saute au milieu et se tue! L’homme qui croise le fer en tremblant laisse à la lame ennemie des jours par lesquels la mort passe!” Fear doesn't make you careful; it makes you clumsy at the exact wrong moment. The trembling hand opens the guard it meant to protect.
cards.why: Dumas's best one-line psychology: anxiety about a danger manufactures the danger. The rider who fears the ditch is the one who finds it.
cards.uw: When you feel fear making you hesitate mid-action, commit fully or withdraw fully — the middle is where the ditch is.

cards.title: The Communist State of North Korea: A Capitalist Society
cards.book: The Communist State of North Korea: A Capitalist Society — Jonathan K. Wev
cards.steal: North Korea runs three economies, not one — the official command economy plus two parallel capitalist economies, the jangmadang (market ground) economy and an elite economy, that emerged when the 1990s famine broke the state's distribution system.
cards.why: Sanctions and negotiations target the official economy, but daily life runs on markets the state doesn't control — pressure aimed at the command economy keeps missing where the real economy lives.
cards.uw: When the official system fails, people build a parallel one — and the parallel economy, not the official one, is where the leverage sits.

cards.title: Preserving Freedom of Navigation in the South China Sea and the Strategic Significance of the Philippines to U.S. Maritime Strategy
cards.book: Preserving Freedom of Navigation in the South China Sea and the Strategic Significance of the Philippines to U.S. Maritime Strategy — Sainath Patrick Panjeti
cards.steal: The Philippines is the linchpin of U.S. freedom-of-navigation strategy in the South China Sea — Manila is instrumental to phase-shaping, deterrence, and Seventh Fleet support in a contingency, because China's nine-dash-line incrementalism can't be answered by patrols alone.
cards.why: A decade on, the Philippines is again the front line of the South China Sea standoff — the thesis's partnership-building prescription is being tested in real time.
cards.uw: Against salami-slicing, the counter is local partnership, not just presence — geography with an ally beats patrols alone.

cards.title: Role of Serum Albumin as a Prognostic Marker of Outcome in Patients with Severe Traumatic Brain Injury
cards.book: Role of Serum Albumin as a Prognostic Marker of Outcome in Patients with Severe Traumatic Brain Injury — Vikram Chaudhary
cards.steal: In severe traumatic brain injury, a cheap blood test predicts the outcome — patients with higher serum albumin on admission had significantly better outcomes, while age, gender, mode of injury, and diagnosis had no predictive power at all.
cards.why: ERs get a fast, cheap prognostic signal from a routine lab draw — no scanner required — for early family conversations and ICU resource calls.
cards.uw: The best predictor is often the cheapest measurement — look for the simple variable before the expensive one.

cards.title: Accuse them of your own crime
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: On April 10, 1953, Dulles warned a Princeton alumni conference of Soviet “brain warfare.” Three days later he signed the order creating MKULTRA, and its predecessor ARTICHOKE was already running. Denounce the enemy’s program while building your own: loudly, and first.
cards.why: The accuser claims the moral high ground while running the operation he condemns. It also inoculates: any later leak reads as retaliation.
cards.uw: Someone is denouncing a practice with unusual volume and specificity. Check what they authorized last quarter.
cards.cost: MKULTRA ran a quarter century, and the real program treated its human subjects as “expendables.”
cards.quotes:
[Dulles, via Talbot, PDF p. 236] “whether we realize how sinister the battle for men’s minds has become in Soviet hands.”
[Talbot, PDF p. 237] “studies that often violated ethical standards and treated their human subjects as “expendables.””

cards.title: The cut-out
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Maheu and Associates: “a private detective firm staffed by former CIA and FBI employees that the intelligence agency used as a ‘cut-out’ to do dirty jobs on U.S. soil, where the CIA was forbidden by law to operate.” How to break your own charter: hire your old employees through a front and call them contractors.
cards.why: The cut-out preserves the letter of the restriction while destroying its purpose. Oversight sees a private firm; the operation sees its own people.
cards.uw: An institution swears it cannot act somewhere, but its alumni keep showing up there on private letterhead.
cards.quotes:
[Talbot, PDF p. 264] “His kidnapping was a sophisticated operation run by Robert A. Maheu and Associates, a private detective firm staffed by former CIA and FBI employees”
[Talbot, PDF p. 264] “that the intelligence agency used as a “cut-out” to do dirty jobs on U.S. soil, where the CIA was forbidden by law to operate.”

cards.title: Saved from the demos
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Allen Dulles to the press, on the eve of his campaign: “Democracy works only if the so-called intelligent people make it work. You can’t sit back and let democracy run itself.” The creed, on the record.
cards.why: Once you hear the creed, every “emergency measure” reads as policy, not exception.
cards.uw: Someone praises democracy while arranging to bypass it. Listen for who counts as “the intelligent people.”
cards.quotes: [Dulles, via Talbot, PDF p. 288] “Democracy works only if the so-called intelligent people make it work,” Allen told the press on the eve of his campaign. “You can’t sit back and let democracy run itself.”

cards.title: Route the report to the man who will bury it
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: After reading the Vrba-Wetzler report on Auschwitz, Dulles performed shock: “One has to do something immediately.” Then he sent a routine cable to Cordell Hull, “a man Dulles knew would not lift a finger.” To kill an urgent report without refusing it, route it to someone guaranteed to sit on it.
cards.why: Refusal creates a record; routing creates deniability. The report was “handled.” Handled straight into a drawer.
cards.uw: An alarming report gets an impressive immediate response followed by assignment to the one person sure to do nothing.
cards.cost: The rescue that came was forced by fifty mimeographed copies of the report reaching the Swiss press, not by his cable. [Talbot, PDF p. 51]
cards.quotes:
[Garrett recalling Dulles, via Talbot, PDF p. 51] ‘One has to do something immediately.’
[Talbot, PDF p. 51] “Dulles sent off a routine cable on the Vrba-Wetzler report to Secretary of State Cordell Hull, a man Dulles knew would not lift a finger to help the Jews, even though he was married to a Jewish woman.”

cards.title: Indispensable until expendable
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Talbot’s rule for the CIA’s hierarchy: Hunt, Harvey, Morales were indispensable, until they became expendable. You are protected exactly as long as you are useful, and not one day longer. Hunt’s epitaph for the code: “I thought—mistakenly—that I was dealing with honorable men.”
cards.why: The institution advertises loyalty. Knowing the real rule changes how you read every “retirement,” every cut-out, every fall guy.
cards.uw: Someone loyal is suddenly described as a rogue. Check whether they just became expendable.
cards.cost: The expendable men talked. Hunt most of all, on the record, at the end of his life.
cards.quotes:
[Talbot, PDF p. 412] “These men were indispensable—until they became expendable.”
[Hunt, via Talbot, PDF p. 412] “I thought—mistakenly—that I was dealing with honorable men,” he said near the end of his life.

cards.title: Hide in plain sight
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Dulles ran his Bern station in the open: no bodyguard, no gun, informers met in cafés. His own maxim: “Too much secrecy can be self-defeating.” When everyone can see you, nobody believes you are hiding anything.
cards.why: Visibility is cover that compounds. The more public the operator, the less credible any accusation against him.
cards.uw: Scrutiny is highest and secrecy would confirm suspicion. Be boring in public.
cards.cost: The openness was real: his cook turned out to be a spy, his janitor stole carbon copies from his trash, and Swiss intelligence eavesdropped on his phone conversations. [Talbot, PDF p. 20]
cards.quotes:
[Talbot, PDF p. 21] “He did not have a bodyguard and he did not carry a gun. He met openly with informers and double agents in cafés and on the city streets.”
[Dulles, via Talbot, PDF p. 21] “Too much secrecy can be self-defeating,” he observed.
[Talbot, PDF p. 20] “his cook turned out to be a spy and his janitor stole carbon copies of his documents out of his trash. Meanwhile, Swiss intelligence agents, who worked closely with their Nazi counterparts, eavesdropped on Dulles’s phone conversations.”

cards.title: Nullify policy with private reassurance
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: In Hal Vaughan’s account, Dulles assured Himmler’s envoy that the Allies’ declaration was “merely a piece of paper to be scrapped without further ado if Germany would sue for peace.” To kill a policy you cannot overturn, reassure the other side it will not be enforced.
cards.why: Public doctrine stays intact while private assurance hollows it. The policy dies without a vote.
cards.uw: You lack the power to repeal the rule. Tell the regulated it will not be enforced.
cards.cost: It went nowhere while Roosevelt lived. Afterward, Justice Arthur Goldberg declared that both Dulleses were guilty of treason. [Talbot, PDF p. 30]
cards.quotes:
[Talbot, citing Vaughan, PDF p. 31] The Allies’ declaration, Dulles assured him, was “merely a piece of paper to be scrapped without further ado if Germany would sue for peace.”
[Talbot, PDF p. 30] “Supreme Court Justice Arthur Goldberg, who as a young lawyer served with Allen in the OSS, later declared that both Dulleses were guilty of treason.”

cards.title: Postpone and postpone
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Breckinridge Long’s 1940 memo ordered consuls to “put every obstacle in the way” and use “various administrative devices which would postpone and postpone and postpone the granting of the visas.” Bureaucracy kills without ever saying no.
cards.why: Delay is deniable. No refusal exists to appeal, only process. The outcome is identical to a ban.
cards.uw: You must block something you cannot be seen blocking. Add steps, not walls.
cards.cost: 90 percent of the quota places reserved for refugees were never filled; another 190,000 people who could have escaped were trapped. [Talbot, PDF p. 42]
cards.quotes: [Long’s memo, via Talbot, PDF p. 42] “We can do this by simply advising our consuls to put every obstacle in the way and to require additional evidence and to resort to various administrative devices which would postpone and postpone and postpone the granting of the visas.”

cards.title: The twinkle as an order
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: By Dulles’s own account, he let Gaevernitz carry out the Wolff rescue without ordering it: “I noticed a twinkle in his eye, and as he told me later, he noticed one in mine. I realized, of course, what he was going to do, and that he intended to do it on his own responsibility.” Command while commanding nothing: deniability built from a glance.
cards.why: The order exists nowhere on paper, so it cannot be countermanded or leaked. Both men understand; neither can prove.
cards.uw: You need action you cannot order. Signal, don’t say.
cards.cost: Gaevernitz kept Dulles’s name out of the papers; his diary records him musing about sparing “Poor Allen” the embarrassment. [Talbot, PDF p. 70]
cards.quotes:
[Dulles, via Talbot, PDF p. 69] “I noticed a twinkle in his eye, and as he told me later, he noticed one in mine. I realized, of course, what he was going to do, and that he intended to do it on his own responsibility.”
[Talbot, PDF p. 70] “It would have made a lovely headline in the papers,” Gaevernitz later mused in his diary.

cards.title: The ace in the pocket
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Arrested by American Nazi-hunters, Dollmann handed over a slip of paper: “Please call this number. Ask for Major Angleton. He knows who I am.” Carry a name that outranks the arresting officer.
cards.why: Protection networks double as get-out-of-jail cards. The arrest becomes a phone call.
cards.uw: You operate in someone else’s jurisdiction. Keep one number that ends the conversation.
cards.quotes: [Dollmann, via Talbot, PDF p. 90] “Please call this number,” he told him. “Ask for Major Angleton. He knows who I am.”

cards.title: The dull name
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Dulles “buried it in the State Department bureaucracy under a purposefully dull name—the Office of Policy Coordination.” The OPC grew to nearly three thousand employees plus another three thousand independent contractors in the field. Hide an army behind a boring name.
cards.why: Boring names defeat curiosity. Nobody investigates the Office of Policy Coordination.
cards.uw: You need an operation to survive budget hearings. Name it like furniture.
cards.cost: Dulles and Wisner were essentially operating their own private spy agency, with little government oversight. [Talbot, PDF p. 126]
cards.quotes:
[Talbot, PDF p. 126] “buried it in the State Department bureaucracy under a purposefully dull name—the Office of Policy Coordination.”
[Talbot, PDF p. 126] “its staff had ballooned to nearly three thousand employees, with another three thousand independent contractors in the field.”
[Talbot, PDF p. 126] “Dulles and Wisner were essentially operating their own private spy agency. The OPC was run with little government oversight and few moral restrictions.”

cards.title: Become the investigators
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Facing exposure over Nazi ties, the Dulles circle seized the investigative momentum and aimed it at New Deal officials instead. Nixon, “Allen Dulles’s mouthpiece in Congress” in Loftus’s phrase, made sure the circle “would never have to answer for their wartime actions.” To escape scrutiny, seize the investigation and aim it at your accusers.
cards.why: Scrutiny is a finite resource. Whoever directs it survives it.
cards.uw: Exposure is coming. Find a bigger target and point the inquiry there.
cards.cost: Harry Dexter White suffered a heart attack the day after testifying and died two days later, at home. [Talbot, PDF p. 154]
cards.quotes:
[Loftus, via Talbot, PDF p. 150] “Allen Dulles’s mouthpiece in Congress,”
[Talbot, PDF p. 150] “the Dulles group ensured their own legal protection.”
[Talbot, PDF p. 150] “would never have to answer for their wartime actions.”
[Talbot, PDF p. 154] “The following day, August 14, he suffered a massive heart attack. Two physicians were summoned, but they declared the patient beyond their medical powers. Two days later, Harry Dexter White died at home, surrounded by his family.”

cards.title: Conjure the bugaboo
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: The Korean “brainwashing” panic, “the seedbed of so much creeping, Cold War fantasy,” turned out to be largely fictitious, debunked by Dulles’s own commissioned Cornell study. Yet “in response to the brainwashing bugaboo that the CIA itself had conjured, the agency constructed its own intricate mind control machinery.” The point: the invented threat funds the real weapon.
cards.why: A threat need not be real to be useful. It need only be believed long enough to build the response.
cards.uw: You need a budget for the weapon. Describe the enemy’s first.
cards.cost: Dulles’s own scientists debunked the panic; the machinery was built anyway. The correction never caught the construction.
cards.quotes:
[Talbot, PDF p. 238] “the Korean brainwashing story itself—the seedbed of so much creeping, Cold War fantasy—turned out to be largely fictitious.”
[Talbot, PDF p. 238] “In response to the brainwashing bugaboo that the CIA itself had conjured, the agency constructed its own intricate mind control machinery that was part Orwell and part Philip K. Dick.”

cards.title: Shut down the case
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: After Galíndez was kidnapped in Manhattan, “the CIA had already moved swiftly to shut down the case,” steering it into NYPD intelligence hands. Asked about it, Dulles “blandly replied that the CIA had no jurisdiction on American soil.” Kill the investigation from behind the jurisdiction line you just crossed.
cards.why: Jurisdiction is a shield you can hold while standing on the other side of it.
cards.uw: Your operation surfaces at home. Deny the territory, keep the operation.
cards.cost: Galíndez was never seen again. [Talbot, PDF p. 259]
cards.quotes:
[Talbot, PDF p. 265] “But, in truth, the CIA had already moved swiftly to shut down the case.”
[Talbot, PDF p. 268] “Dulles blandly replied that the CIA had no jurisdiction on American soil, so the congressman’s inquiry about the case was better directed to the FBI.”
[Talbot, PDF p. 259] “He was never seen again by friends or colleagues.”

cards.title: The tutorial relationship
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Dulles cultivated Kennedy for years before the presidency, a relationship Talbot describes as tutorial: “the education of a promising young man,” with “Kennedy as prince and acolyte and the Dulles brothers as court regents.” Capture the next president by becoming his teacher.
cards.why: The tutor sets the curriculum. By the time the pupil takes power, the worldview is installed.
cards.uw: Power is about to change hands. Teach the heir before he inherits.
cards.cost: The pupil fired the teacher. After the Bay of Pigs, Kennedy sacked Dulles.
cards.quotes:
[Talbot, PDF p. 294] “Thus began a relationship that Dulles regarded as tutorial—the education of a promising young man who had the proper regard for his elders.”
[Talbot, PDF p. 294] “This, in Dulles’s mind, was the proper order of things—Kennedy as prince and acolyte and the Dulles brothers as court regents.”

cards.title: Change the men
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Harriman’s advice, via Marshall: “when you change a policy, you must change the men too.” Policy without personnel change is a press release.
cards.why: The old staff will run the old policy under the new name. The org chart changes; the outcomes don’t.
cards.uw: A reform keeps failing. Stop rewriting the policy and replace the people.
cards.cost: Kennedy never did it, and the men outlasted him.
cards.quotes: [Harriman, quoting Marshall, PDF p. 359] “General [George] Marshall once told me that, when you change a policy, you must change the men too.”

cards.title: The President believed he was President
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Bobby Kennedy wrote: “The President believed he was President, and that, his wishes having been made clear, they would be followed.” The context, per Talbot: JFK “was furious when he learned that his original order to remove the Jupiter rockets from Turkey had been ignored.” Authority is what gets obeyed, not what gets ordered.
cards.why: An order ignored is a measurement. It tells you exactly how much power you actually have.
cards.uw: Your directives keep dying in the building. Stop issuing them and find out who really decides.
cards.cost: The missiles only moved when the missile crisis forced the trade. The order itself changed nothing.
cards.quotes:
[Bobby Kennedy, via Thirteen Days, PDF p. 366] “The President believed he was President, and that, his wishes having been made clear, they would be followed and the missiles removed,” Bobby Kennedy later wrote in Thirteen Days, his memoir about the missile crisis.
[Talbot, PDF p. 366] “JFK was furious when he learned that his original order to remove the Jupiter rockets from Turkey had been ignored.”

cards.title: The flat denial
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Asked on camera whether the CIA operated on a higher moral level than the KGB, Dulles replied: “As far as I know, we don’t engage in assassinations or kidnappings or things of that kind. As far as I know, we never have.” The “as far as I know” is the whole technique: the deniable absolute, stated twice.
cards.why: The qualifier empties the denial while preserving its shape. On the record it reads as a denial; under scrutiny it was only a statement of current knowledge.
cards.uw: You must deny what you cannot deny. Qualify the knowledge, not the act.
cards.cost: The Church Committee later documented the assassination programs. The tape survives as the lie.
cards.quotes: [Dulles, PDF p. 394] “As far as I know, we don’t engage in assassinations or kidnappings or things of that kind. As far as I know, we never have.”

cards.title: The legend
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Angleton’s doctrine: “It was the paper record—the ‘legend’—that mattered most.” Under him “a person’s file sometimes took on a life of its own, full of actions and dialogue that bore no relation to the subject’s real life.” The file becomes the person; reality is whatever the paperwork says.
cards.why: Whoever controls the file controls the person. The subject cannot argue with paperwork he cannot see.
cards.uw: You need someone to be something. Don’t change him; change his file.
cards.quotes: [Talbot, PDF p. 417] “It was the paper record—the “legend”—that mattered most to Angleton. Under the covert wizard’s direction, a person’s file sometimes took on a life of its own, full of actions and dialogue that bore no relation to the subject’s real life.”

cards.title: We might talk in our sleep
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Dulles on briefing Congress: members stopped him, saying “We don’t want to hear about that, we might talk in our sleep. Don’t tell us this!” Oversight as willful ignorance: the overseers ask not to be told, and the operator obliges.
cards.why: Oversight that refuses information is permission. The operator gets both the secret and the alibi.
cards.uw: Your overseers prefer not to know. Let them, and keep the receipt.
cards.cost: “This head-in-the-sand attitude gave men like Dulles enormous leverage to take drastic action when they felt so inclined.” [Talbot, PDF p. 445]
cards.quotes: [Dulles, quoting members of Congress, PDF p. 445] “When I appeared before them,” said Dulles, “again and again I’ve been stopped by members of the Congress, who said, ‘We don’t want to hear about that, we might talk in our sleep. Don’t tell us this!’”

cards.title: Lay the dust
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: McCloy described the Warren Commission’s job as “lay the dust” stirred up in Dallas, “dust not only in the United States, but all over the world.” When the mandate is to settle rather than solve, staffing, deadlines, and conclusions all follow.
cards.why: Every inquiry has a real mandate and a stated one. Read the staffing to find the real one.
cards.uw: You are handed an investigation. Ask first whether the job is truth or dust.
cards.cost: The dust never settled. The critics multiplied for decades.
cards.quotes:
[McCloy, via Talbot, PDF p. 463] “to “lay the dust” that had been stirred up in Dallas”
