[McCloy, via Talbot, PDF p. 463] “dust not only in the United States, but all over the world.”

cards.title: I can’t look and won’t look
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: Shown Frame 313 of the Zapruder film, Schlesinger “visibly paled. “I can’t look and won’t look,” Schlesinger said, turning his head and walking briskly away.” A circle protects itself by refusing to look at the evidence.
cards.why: Unexamined evidence cannot contradict the story. The refusal is the defense.
cards.uw: The facts threaten the group. Don’t argue them; decline to see them.
cards.quotes:
[Schlesinger, via Talbot, PDF p. 484] “I can’t look and won’t look,” Schlesinger said, turning his head and walking briskly away from Marcus.
[Talbot, PDF p. 484] “This was a perfect summation of the prevalent attitude among the Kennedy crowd.”

cards.title: Portray them as Soviet dupes
cards.book: The Devil's Chessboard — David Talbot
cards.steal: The CIA’s 1967 guidance for handling Warren Report critics: give friendly journalists “material for countering and discrediting the claims of the conspiracy theorists,” including portraying them as Soviet dupes. The agency’s own document adds: “Communists and other extremists always attempt to prove a political conspiracy behind violence.” The smear template, in the agency’s own words.
cards.why: Discredit the critic and the criticism dies unexamined. The template outlives any single case.
cards.uw: Critics are gaining traction. Don’t answer them; diagnose them.
cards.cost: The guidance was declassified. The template is now public and quotable.
cards.quotes:
[Talbot, PDF p. 480] “One way that its media assets could impugn conspiracy theorists, the CIA suggested, was to portray them as Soviet dupes.”
[CIA document, via Talbot, PDF p. 480] “Communists and other extremists always attempt to prove a political conspiracy behind violence,” declared another agency document.

cards.title: Quantifying risk for decentralized offensive cyber operations
cards.book: Quantifying risk for decentralized offensive cyber operations — Michael S. Klipstein
cards.steal: Organizations below the national level can't adequately assess the risks and consequences of offensive cyber operations because of inexperience — but a simulation framework that combines subject-matter expertise with explicit assessments of uncertainty lets inexperienced organizations assess cyber risk at a proficiency level equivalent to an experienced organization.
cards.why: As authority for offensive cyber operations decentralizes, the binding constraint isn't tools but judgment — and this suggests a structured process can close the experience gap instead of leaving risk calls to heuristics and biases.
cards.uw: Inexperience is a process problem, not a talent problem — a framework that accounts for uncertainty can substitute for years of exposure.

cards.title: From Dependence to Causation
cards.book: From Dependence to Causation — David Lopez-Paz
cards.steal: Machine learning is stuck at prediction (dependence) and can't reach machine reasoning without causal inference — uncovering cause-effect structure so systems can answer "what if" questions under interventions; the thesis advances causal inference three ways: a framework for statistical dependence from copulas and random features, causal inference reframed as distribution classification (yielding a family of novel algorithms), and causal discovery inside convolutional neural network features — with scalable algorithms, theoretical guarantees, and state-of-the-art real-world benchmarks.
cards.why: Dependence is the difference between seeing and doing — and any system that acts in the world (an agent, a policy, a treatment) needs causal structure, not just predictions.
cards.uw: Prediction tells you what will happen; causation tells you what happens if you act — only the second one is useful to a decision-maker.

cards.title: Three qubit system for kicked top model
cards.book: Three qubit system for kicked top model — Ayrisha Sanjay Sondawale
cards.steal: A three-qubit kicked-top model — a toy quantum system kicked repeatedly — can be tuned between order and chaos: symmetric vs. asymmetric qubit interactions drive the system from periodic, entanglement-free revivals to quasi-periodic dynamics where entanglement persists, demonstrating the quantum-classical correspondence between regular motion and chaos in a system small enough to fully analyze.
cards.why: Quantum chaos in tiny controllable systems is the testbed for quantum computing — the boundary between predictability and chaos is where you learn what a quantum device can actually compute before it escapes control.
cards.uw: Complexity doesn't need size — three qubits are enough to go from perfectly predictable to chaotic, depending only on how they interact.

cards.title: Ezekiel's Prophecies under the Influence of Mesopotamian Literature: Hidden Transcripts against Empire
cards.book: Ezekiel's Prophecies under the Influence of Mesopotamian Literature: Hidden Transcripts against Empire — Inchol Yang
cards.steal: The book of Ezekiel — long read as pro-Babylonian for never criticizing the Neo-Babylonian Empire — is actually resistance literature: it uses Mesopotamian divine-abandonment motifs and encodes criticism of Babylon through the Babylonian New Year (akitu) festival's own symbolism, announcing YHWH's temple as the world's center and YHWH's kingship over even Marduk.
cards.why: It's a case study in how the powerless talk back — encoding dissent in the empire's own symbols so the message passes censors while the intended audience gets it.
cards.uw: When you can't attack power directly, steal its symbols — subversion works best in the language of the thing being subverted.

cards.title: Three inspections or ten, and nobody defined an inspection
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "The Soviet Union finally agreed to three inspections. The United States insisted on no less than ten. And there the talks broke down — over positions — despite the fact that no one understood whether an 'inspection' would involve one person looking around for one day, or a hundred people prying indiscriminately for a month."
cards.why: The Kennedy-era test-ban talks broke down over a count, three inspections or ten, when neither side had defined what one inspection was.
cards.uw: Two sides are dug in on competing figures and nobody has defined what the figures mean.

cards.title: Do the thing their picture of you says you'd never do
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "Sadat flew to the capital of his enemies, a disputed capital which not even the United States, Israel's best friend, had recognized. Instead of acting as an enemy, Sadat acted as a partner."
cards.why: Israel saw Sadat as the man who had attacked it four years before. He changed that with an act, not an argument, and the authors say it is hard to imagine the peace treaty without it.
cards.uw: The negotiation is stuck because the other side's image of you makes agreement unthinkable.

cards.title: Withdraw the deal so they can announce it as their own
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "Terms negotiated between a major city and its Hispanic community on municipal jobs were unacceptable to the mayor — until the agreement was withdrawn and the mayor was allowed to announce the same terms as his own decision, carrying out a campaign promise."
cards.why: The terms didn't change. What changed was who announced them and which past promise they fulfilled. Face is about reconciling the stand with past words.
cards.uw: The other side agrees with the deal but cannot be seen agreeing with you.

cards.title: Only one person gets to be angry at a time
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "The members of the committee adopted the rule that only one person could get angry at a time. This made it legitimate for others not to respond stormily to an angry outburst… 'That's OK. It's his turn.'"
cards.why: A 1950s steel-industry committee turned "don't react" into a turn-taking rule. Others did not have to answer an outburst, and anyone who broke the rule showed they had lost self-control and lost some face.
cards.uw: A negotiation keeps derailing because anger is contagious and every outburst demands a reply.

cards.title: Mediator means meddler in Persian
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "Similarly, the word 'mediator' in Persian suggests 'meddler', someone who is barging in uninvited… His efforts were seriously set back when Iranian national radio and television broadcast in Persian a remark he reportedly made on his arrival in Tehran: 'I have come as a mediator to work out a compromise.' Within an hour of the broadcast his car was being stoned by angry Iranians."
cards.why: Waldheim's 1980 arrival line used two words that read as insults in Persian. Check what your key words mean in the other side's ears before you open your mouth on their airwaves.
cards.uw: You are negotiating across languages or cultures and your standard vocabulary may detonate.

cards.title: Open a window in the next room
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "She asks one why he wants the window open: 'To get some fresh air.' She asks the other why he wants it closed: 'To avoid the draft.' After thinking a minute, she opens wide a window in the next room, bringing in fresh air without a draft."
cards.why: Asking each side "why" turned open-versus-closed into air-versus-draft, and the answer was a third option nobody was arguing about. Borrowed by the authors from Mary Parker Follett.
cards.uw: Two positions look irreconcilable and everyone is haggling over how far to open the same window.

cards.title: The flag flies everywhere, the tanks stay home
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "At Camp David, President Sadat of Egypt and Prime Minister Begin of Israel agreed to a plan that would return the Sinai to complete Egyptian sovereignty and, by demilitarizing large areas, would still assure Israeli security. The Egyptian flag would fly everywhere, but Egyptian tanks would be nowhere near Israel."
cards.why: The maps dividing the Sinai failed every time. Splitting sovereignty from security gave Egypt the flag (its interest) and Israel demilitarization (its interest) instead of splitting the territory.
cards.uw: Both sides claim the same thing but actually want different things from it.

cards.title: Draw up their presently perceived choice
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "In constructing the other side's presently perceived choice the first question to ask is 'Whose decision do I want to affect?' The second question is what decision people on the other side now see you asking them to make."
cards.why: The authors map the Iranian students' yes/no ledger as the students saw it in 1980, and keeping the hostages looks rational from inside it. Your arguments bounce off because you are answering a question they are not asking.
cards.uw: The other side keeps refusing something you think is obviously in their interest.

cards.title: They burned the gas rather than be disrespected
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "The Mexicans had a strong interest not only in getting a good price for their gas but also in being treated with respect and a sense of equality… Rather than sell their gas, the Mexican government began to burn it off, and any chance of agreement on a lower price became politically impossible."
cards.why: The U.S. Secretary of Energy treated it as a fight over money and blocked a price already agreed. Mexico wanted respect and equality too. It burned the gas off, and a lower price became politically impossible.
cards.uw: You are tempted to use leverage to squeeze a better number and the relationship has to survive the deal.

cards.title: Risk can be traded for revenue
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "In this difference lies the potential for a bargain advantageous to both sides. Risk can be traded for revenue."
cards.why: Deals exist because of differences, not agreements: the Law of the Sea priced seabed mining low while companies' risk was high and higher once risk fell. Hunt for what each side values differently and trade across it.
cards.uw: The negotiation looks zero-sum because both sides seem to want the same thing.

cards.title: The model both sides accepted
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "India, representing the Third World bloc, proposed an initial fee for companies mining in the deep seabed of $60 million per site. The United States rejected the proposal, suggesting there be no initial fee… No one backed down; no one appeared weak — just reasonable."
cards.why: An outside MIT model of seabed-mining economics moved both dug-in sides, and each could say the model changed its mind, not the opponent. Bring in a neutral standard both sides can test proposals against.
cards.uw: Two sides are dug in on competing numbers and neither can yield without looking weak.

cards.title: One cuts, the other chooses, at the bottom of the ocean
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "The solution devised was to agree that a private company seeking to mine the seabed would present the Enterprise with two proposed mining sites. The Enterprise would pick one site for itself and grant the company a license to mine the other. Since the company would not know which site it would get, it would have an incentive to make both sites as promising as possible."
cards.why: The informed party proposes, the uninformed party picks first. The procedure turns the expert's knowledge advantage into the other side's protection.
cards.uw: One side knows far more than the other and you need a fair division that doesn't require trusting the expert.

cards.title: How did you reach that figure?
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "I see. How did you reach that figure?… I understand, but what standard did you use to determine that amount? Do you know where I can buy a comparable car for that much?"
cards.why: Tom Griffith never answered the adjuster's number with a counter-number. Two questions moved the discussion from the figure to the reasoning behind it, which is where you can actually argue. He walked out with a check for $8,024.
cards.uw: The other side opens with a take-it-or-leave-it number and no justification.

cards.title: The town that knew it could annex the factory
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "In one case, a small town negotiated a company with a factory just outside the town limits from a 'goodwill' payment of $300,000 a year to one of $2,300,000 a year… The town knew exactly what it would do if no agreement was reached: It would expand the town limits to include the factory and then tax the factory the full residential rate of some $2,500,000 a year."
cards.why: The authors say power here was set by each side's best alternative, not budget or clout. The town knew exactly what it would do with no deal: take in the factory and tax it at about $2.5 million a year.
cards.uw: You are the smaller party and the other side assumes you have nowhere to go.

cards.title: What would happen to Golda Meir tomorrow morning?
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "The American asked, 'What would happen to Golda Meir if tomorrow morning she appeared on Israeli radio and television and said, 'On behalf of the people of Israel I hereby promise to withdraw from every inch of territory occupied in '67…''"
cards.why: Nasser burst out laughing: "Oh, would she have trouble at home!" Walking him through the morning after his own demand exposed it as unworkable, from his side. The authors say this may have contributed to his stated willingness later that day to accept a cease-fire.
cards.uw: The other side's position sounds principled but collapses the moment you imagine it implemented.

cards.title: Twenty-three drafts nobody was committed to
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "After thirteen days and some twenty-three drafts, the United States had a text it was prepared to recommend. When President Carter did recommend it, Israel and Egypt accepted."
cards.why: The one-text procedure: one draft nobody owns, criticism instead of concessions, repeat. Each draft is easier to criticize than a position is to abandon, so positions soften without anyone losing face.
cards.uw: Two sides are locked into incompatible proposals and direct bargaining keeps failing.

cards.title: Then you won't mind a contingent agreement
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "'Then you won't mind a contingent agreement. Your client will agree to make child support payments. We'll provide that if, for some inexplicable reason which you estimate at zero percent probability, he misses two payments, my client will get the equity in the house… and your client will no longer be liable for child support.' It is not easy for the husband's lawyer to object."
cards.why: Don't argue about trust. Propose a bet on their own certainty: if they are as sure as they claim, the penalty costs them nothing, and refusing it exposes the bluff.
cards.uw: The other side insists something will never happen and you need a guarantee anyway.

cards.title: Yes, agreed, but one small problem
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "Each time the British thought they had an agreement, he would say, 'Yes, agreed, but there is still one small problem.' And the small problem would turn out to be a £10 million cash advance or guaranteed jobs for dockyard and base workers for the life of the contract."
cards.why: Malta's prime minister timed escalating demands for the moment Britain thought it was done. Name the tactic, take a break, and return insisting on principle. Never reward the nibble with an impulsive concession.
cards.uw: Every agreement you reach sprouts one more demand.

cards.title: Trade fuel and food for hostages, never the principle
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "But local authorities in Cyprus and Algeria negotiated incessantly over things like permission for the plane to land, requests for additional fuel, access to news media, and deliveries of food. For each transaction these authorities successfully obtained the release of more hostages."
cards.why: During the Kuwait Airways 422 hijacking, Kuwait never retreated on the core principle while every small practical matter was traded one at a time, each for more hostages. Hold the principle fixed; negotiate everything around it.
cards.uw: You must deal with someone whose core demand you can never meet.

cards.title: She wanted to manage, not sell
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "The negotiation consultant asked why the second owner was asking for such a high price. The businessman didn't know; he was assuming the seller would retire. 'Does the seller want to retire? What does she do now?'… the businessman offered to buy only that portion of the owner's interest he needed for tax reasons and to keep her on as manager."
cards.why: The "exorbitant" price was really a desire to keep running the radio station. Buying less and keeping her as manager met the real interest for almost a million dollars less. When a price looks irrational, stop bidding and investigate the seller's life.
cards.uw: Raising your offer keeps failing and you have no idea why.

cards.title: Set a trip wire, not a bottom line
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "It is useful to identify one far from perfect agreement that is better than your BATNA. Before accepting any agreement worse than this trip-wire package, you should take a break and reexamine the situation."
cards.why: A bottom line is rigid and invites brinkmanship. A trip wire is an early-warning package: anything worse triggers an automatic pause, so fatigue or pressure can't slide you below your real minimum.
cards.uw: You are sending an agent to negotiate, or you fear you will accept a bad deal in the heat of the moment.

cards.title: Let someone else carry the threat
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "TURNBULL: If you and I could reach agreement now, Paul and I would move out immediately. If we can't reach an agreement, the hearing examiner at the Rent Control Board suggested that we stay in the apartment and withhold rent and/or sue you for reimbursement, treble damages, and legal fees. Paul and I are extremely reluctant to take either of these courses."
cards.why: Turnbull pairs an easy yes (move out now) with his walk-away stated as someone else's suggestion, then distances himself with visible reluctance. The threat is real but he never owns it, so Mrs. Jones can keep talking to him.
cards.uw: You need your walk-away to be vivid without making it a personal threat.

cards.title: Your voice is being recorded
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "At a coal mine where one of the authors was recently mediating, a large number of false but costly bomb threats were being received. These dropped off dramatically when the company's receptionist began answering all phone calls with 'Your voice is being recorded. What number are you calling?'"
cards.why: A threat only works if it gets delivered. Make delivering it risky and the threats stop, with no counter-threat needed.
cards.uw: Someone keeps pressuring you through a channel you control.

cards.title: The foreman's praise that started a walkout
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "That was the fifth time in two weeks he sent me out of our group as a replacement. He's got it in for me, and I'm tired of it."
cards.why: The foreman said: "I pick Jones because he's the best. I know I can trust him." The foreman meant it as praise. Jones read it as being picked on, and called a walkout. Nobody had asked.
cards.uw: You are sure you know why someone keeps doing the thing that bothers you.

cards.title: Pressure needs a door
cards.book: Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
cards.steal: "The Council's resolutions clearly stated that Iraq must withdraw, but did not state that upon withdrawal sanctions would end. If Saddam Hussein believed that sanctions would continue after Iraq withdrew from Kuwait, then those sanctions, though unpleasant, provided no incentive for Iraq to leave."
cards.why: The authors' reading of 1990: if complying doesn't visibly end the pain, and nobody has said exactly what counts as complying, the pain gives no reason to comply. Pressure must promise an end on compliance.
cards.uw: You are applying pressure and haven't said what would make you stop.

cards.title: Rebuild the Spectator from your own hints
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "I took some of the papers, and, making short hints of the sentiment in each sentence, laid them by a few days, and then, without looking at the book, try'd to compleat the papers again… Then I compared my Spectator with the original, discovered some of my faults, and corrected them."
cards.why: He had no teacher, so the original essay served as the answer key. Rebuilding from hints and comparing showed him exactly where his version fell short. He also jumbled the hints to practice arrangement as a separate skill.
cards.uw: You want to learn a craft from a master's work and reading it again isn't teaching you anything.

cards.title: Win with questions, then stop doing it
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal:
"I was charm'd with it, adopted it, dropt my abrupt contradiction and positive argumentation, and put on the humble inquirer and doubter."

"at last he grew ridiculously cautious, and would hardly answer me the most common question, without asking first, 'What do you intend to infer from that?'"
cards.why: The Socratic method won him "victories that neither myself nor my cause always deserved." Keimer's caution shows the cost: once people see the trap, they stop answering. He kept the modest manner and dropped the trap.
cards.uw: Your questions keep winning arguments and people have started refusing to answer them.

cards.title: Drop 'certainly' and grant where he'd be right
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal:
"I made it a rule to forbear all direct contradiction to the sentiments of others, and all positive assertion of my own."

"in answering I began by observing that in certain cases or circumstances his opinion would be right, but in the present case there appear'd or seem'd to me some difference, etc."
cards.why: He replaced "certainly" and "undoubtedly" with "I conceive" and "it appears to me," and opened every correction by granting the case where the other man was right. He says he was a bad speaker and "yet I generally carried my points." That result is his account.
cards.uw: You are right on the substance and still losing the room.

cards.title: Haul the paper home on a wheelbarrow
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal:
"I took care not only to be in reality industrious and frugal, but to avoid all appearances to the contrary. I drest plainly; I was seen at no places of idle diversion."

"to show that I was not above my business, I sometimes brought home the paper I purchas'd at the stores thro' the streets on a wheelbarrow."
cards.why: A new printer with debts needed credit. He managed the visible signs of industry as carefully as the work itself. By his account the stationery merchants then "solicited my custom."
cards.uw: Your work is solid but the people who decide on credit or business never see it.

cards.title: A club where every member owes a question
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal:
"every member, in his turn, should produce one or more queries on any point of Morals, Politics, or Natural Philosophy, to be discuss'd by the company; and once in three months produce and read an essay of his own writing"

"all expressions of positiveness in opinions, or direct contradiction, were after some time made contraband, and prohibited under small pecuniary penalties."
cards.why: The Junto required output from everyone: a query each turn, an essay each quarter, queries read a week ahead. Heat was priced with small fines. The library, the fire company and the branch clubs all came out of it.
cards.uw: Your discussion group talks a lot, produces nothing, and keeps sliding into debate.

cards.title: Call it a scheme of a number of friends
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "I therefore put myself as much as I could out of sight, and stated it as a scheme of a number of friends, who had requested me to go about and propose it to such as they thought lovers of reading. In this way my affair went on more smoothly, and I ever after practis'd it on such occasions"
cards.why: Asking neighbors to fund his library raised the suspicion that he wanted to rise above them. Hiding his authorship removed the objection. He used the same cover for the academy pamphlet, published as the work of "publick-spirited gentlemen."
cards.uw: Your project needs other people's money or help and your name on it is causing resistance.

cards.title: A black spot for every fault
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "I rul'd each page with red ink, so as to have seven columns, one for each day of the week, marking each column with a letter for the day. I cross'd these columns with thirteen red lines, marking the beginning of each line with the first letter of one of the virtues, on which line, and in its proper column, I might mark, by a little black spot, every fault I found upon examination to have been committed respecting that virtue upon that day."
cards.why: The book reproduces the thirteen precepts and a sample page. He defined each virtue narrowly enough to check daily, and the page kept the count instead of his memory. "I was surpris'd to find myself so much fuller of faults than I had imagined" is his report of the results.
cards.uw: You keep resolving to change a habit and have no record of how often you slip.

cards.title: Weed one bed at a time
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "like him who, having a garden to weed, does not attempt to eradicate all the bad herbs at once, which would exceed his reach and his strength, but works on one of the beds at a time"
cards.why: He gave each virtue a week of strict attention and kept the earlier lines clear while adding the next. Thirteen virtues made "a course compleat in thirteen weeks, and four courses in a year."
cards.uw: You are trying to fix everything at once and none of it is sticking.

cards.title: 'I think I like a speckled ax best'
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "'No,' said the smith, 'turn on, turn on; we shall have it bright by-and-by; as yet, it is only speckled.' 'Yes,' says the man, 'but I think I like a speckled ax best.'"
cards.why: Order was the virtue he could not master. He tells the ax story against himself: the man tired of turning the wheel and called the half-done job his preference. Franklin says something "that pretended to be reason" made him the same offer.
cards.uw: You are about to lower a standard and call it a preference.

cards.title: Put the proverbs in the almanac's empty spaces
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal:
"I consider'd it as a proper vehicle for conveying instruction among the common people, who bought scarcely any other books; I therefore filled all the little spaces that occurr'd between the remarkable days in the calendar with proverbial sentences"

"The bringing all these scatter'd councils thus into a focus enabled them to make greater impression."
cards.why: He put his message in the one book people already bought, then gathered the proverbs into a single speech, The Way to Wealth (in the Appendix). The sales and reprint figures are his.
cards.uw: Your message has no audience of its own and there is a channel people already read.

cards.title: Borrow the rival's scarce book
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal:
"Having heard that he had in his library a certain very scarce and curious book, I wrote a note to him, expressing my desire of perusing that book, and requesting he would do me the favour of lending it to me for a few days."

"He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another, than he whom you yourself have obliged."
cards.why: A new Assembly member had spoken against him. Franklin asked a small favor instead of offering one, returned the book in a week with thanks, and says they "became great friends." The outcome is his account.
cards.uw: Someone with influence over you dislikes you and doing them favors hasn't helped.

cards.title: Fifty subscribers at forty shillings
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal:
"by thus clubbing our books to a common library, we should, while we lik'd to keep them together, have each of us the advantage of using the books of all the other members"

"fifty persons, mostly young tradesmen, willing to pay down for this purpose forty shillings each, and ten shillings per annum."
cards.why: The Junto first pooled its own books in one room. When that worked, he turned it into a subscription: small payments from many people, renewed each year. He calls it "the mother of all the North American subscription libraries"; that is his claim.
cards.uw: You need to fund something useful and no single patron will pay for it.

cards.title: Render accounts with great clearness
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "they should always render accounts, and make remittances, with great clearness and punctuality."
cards.why: His Charleston partner, honest but "ignorant in matters of account," never sent a clear statement. The partner's widow, schooled in accounts in Holland, reported every quarter and kept the business paying. Bradford lost the postmaster's commission over inexact accounts, and Franklin got it.
cards.uw: You handle other people's money or affairs and want more of their trust.

cards.title: The winner at chess sets the grammar
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "I at length refus'd to play any more, unless on this condition, that the victor in every game should have a right to impose a task, either in parts of the grammar to be got by heart, or in translations, etc., which tasks the vanquish'd was to perform upon honour, before our next meeting. As we play'd pretty equally, we thus beat one another into that language."
cards.why: Chess was eating the time he and a friend had set aside for Italian. He kept the game and made the loser pay in study.
cards.uw: A habit you enjoy is eating the time meant for something you need to learn.

cards.title: The regret is the same either way
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal:
"In 1736 I lost one of my sons, a fine boy of four years old, by the small-pox, taken in the common way. I long regretted bitterly, and still regret that I had not given it to him by inoculation."

"my example showing that the regret may be the same either way, and that, therefore, the safer should be chosen."
cards.why: Parents skipped inoculation because they feared regretting a death they had caused. He lost his son to the disease and regretted it all the same. When both choices carry regret, the regret cannot decide; the odds should.
cards.uw: You are avoiding the safer choice because you fear regretting it if it goes wrong.

cards.title: Branch clubs that don't know they are branches
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal:
"every member separately should endeavour to form a subordinate club, with the same rules respecting queries, etc., and without informing them of the connection with the Junto."

"the Junto member might propose what queries we should desire, and was to report to the Junto what pass'd in his separate club"
cards.why: Each Junto member started a club on the same rules. The branches fed back the town's opinion and spread proposals "as arising in each of them." Five or six were formed. Their effect on later measures is his account.
cards.uw: You need to know what a wider group thinks and to put ideas in front of it without a central sponsor.

cards.title: Fines for missed meetings buy the fire engines
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal:
"Our articles of agreement oblig'd every member to keep always in good order, and fit for use, a certain number of leather buckets, with strong bags and baskets (for packing and transporting of goods), which were to be brought to every fire"

"The small fines that have been paid by members for absence at the monthly meetings have been apply'd to the purchase of fire-engines, ladders, fire-hooks, and other useful implements for each company"
cards.why: The Union Fire Company wrote each member's duty into the articles and turned absence into equipment. The city's fire record he gives afterward is his claim.
cards.uw: You are starting a volunteer group and need both attendance and gear without a budget.

cards.title: Make the grant conditional so the clause works both ways
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal:
"it shall and may be lawful for the said speaker, and he is hereby required, to sign an order on the provincial treasurer for the payment of two thousand pounds"

"we urg'd the conditional promise of the law as an additional motive to give, since every man's donation would be doubled; thus the clause work'd both ways."
cards.why: The Assembly doubted the hospital could raise two thousand pounds privately. Franklin wrote the grant to pay only when it did, which cost the doubters nothing to pass. Donors then heard their money would be doubled. The clause is reproduced in the book; the outcome is his account.
cards.uw: The funder doubts you can raise the rest, and the donors want to know their money counts.

cards.title: Write the wagon terms from the owners' side
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal:
"three or four of such as cannot separately spare from the business of their plantations a waggon and four horses and a driver, may do it together, one furnishing the waggon, another one or two horses, and another the driver, and divide the pay proportionately between you"

"The owners, however, alleging they did not know General Braddock, or what dependence might be had on his promise, insisted on my bond for the performance, which I accordingly gave them."
cards.why: Braddock had found twenty-five wagons. Franklin's printed advertisement set pay in advance, appraisal of horses, shared teams, and the threat of soldiers seizing them otherwise. The advertisement is reproduced; the 150 wagons and his near-ruin over the claims are his account.
cards.uw: You are asked to get something from people who have no reason to trust the person asking.

cards.title: Let the papers shift for themselves
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "I concluded to let my papers shift for themselves, believing it was better to spend what time I could spare from public business in making new experiments, than in disputing about those already made."
cards.why: The Abbé Nollet attacked his electrical work in print. His experiments could be repeated by anyone, so an answer would add nothing. He kept working. That Nollet lived "to see himself the last of his sect" is his account.
cards.uw: A critic attacks work that others can check, and a reply would cost time you need for the next piece.

cards.title: A friend's list of instances adds Humility
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "a Quaker friend having kindly informed me that I was generally thought proud; that my pride show'd itself frequently in conversation; that I was not content with being in the right when discussing any point, but was overbearing, and rather insolent, of which he convinc'd me by mentioning several instances"
cards.why: His list had twelve virtues. The friend's examples, not a principle, added the thirteenth. Franklin admits he got the appearance of humility more than the reality.
cards.uw: Someone you trust names a fault of yours and backs it with specific instances.

cards.title: Proud of my humility
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "Disguise it, struggle with it, beat it down, stifle it, mortify it as much as one pleases, it is still alive, and will every now and then peep out and show itself; you will see it, perhaps, often in this history; for, even if I could conceive that I had compleatly overcome it, I should probably be proud of my humility."
cards.why: Claiming victory over pride is itself pride. He tells the reader to look for it in this memoir.
cards.uw: You are about to announce that you have beaten a flaw.

cards.title: Don't give too much for the whistle
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "This, however, was afterwards of use to me, the impression continuing on my mind; so that often, when I was tempted to buy some unnecessary thing, I said to myself, Don't give too much for the whistle; and I saved my money."
cards.why: At seven he gave all his coppers for a whistle and his family told him he had paid four times its worth. He kept the phrase as a price check, then applied it to courtiers, misers and men who chase popularity.
cards.uw: You are about to pay for something you wanted on sight.

cards.title: Emptying your pockets at home won't save you
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "As he proceeded I began to soften, and concluded to give the coppers. Another stroke of his oratory made me asham'd of that, and determin'd me to give the silver; and he finish'd so admirably, that I empty'd my pocket wholly into the collector's dish, gold and all."
cards.why: He had "silently resolved" Whitefield would get nothing. A friend at the same sermon had emptied his pockets before leaving home and still tried to borrow money to give. Neither man's advance decision survived the sermon.
cards.uw: You are walking into a strong pitch you have already decided to refuse.

cards.title: Write the means and manner, skip the exhortation
cards.book: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin — Benjamin Franklin
cards.steal: "I should have called my book The Art of Virtue, because it would have shown the means and manner of obtaining virtue, which would have distinguished it from the mere exhortation to be good, that does not instruct and indicate the means"
cards.why: He planned a book that taught method rather than urging goodness, and compared exhortation to telling the hungry to be fed. He never wrote it. The memoir's chapter on the virtue table is the closest he came.
cards.uw: You are about to tell someone what to be without telling them how.

cards.title: Hand the boss advice as something he forgot
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal: "They will allow a man to help them but not to surpass them, and will have any advice tendered them appear like a recollection of something they have forgotten rather than as a guide to something they cannot find."
cards.why: Gracián says superiors will concede you luck or temper but never better judgment. Framing a correction as a reminder lets the superior keep ownership of the good sense while still taking the advice.
cards.uw: You have to correct someone above you who is proud of their judgment.

cards.title: Find the idol, then say the one word
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"All men are idolaters, some of fame, others of self-interest, most of pleasure. Skill consists in knowing these idols in order to bring them into play."

"First guess a man's ruling passion, appeal to it by a word, set it in motion by temptation"
cards.why: The maxim is a three-step sequence: diagnose the dominant motive, name it briefly, then offer something that feeds it. He adds that the working motive is more often the lowest part of a person's nature than the highest.
cards.uw: Your good arguments keep failing on someone and you have not asked what they actually want.

cards.title: Hold the dissent, say it later to a few
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal: "To dissent from others' views is regarded as an insult, because it is their condemnation. Disgust is doubled on account of the thing blamed and of the person who praised it."
cards.why: Disagreeing in public offends twice: once for the thing blamed and once for the person who praised it. Gracián keeps the private judgment and voices it "before few and fit persons."
cards.uw: You think a popular plan is wrong and are tempted to say so in the all-hands.

cards.title: Time and I against any two
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"You must pass through the circumference of time before arriving at the centre of opportunity."

"Time's crutch effects more than the iron club of Hercules."
cards.why: Gracián quotes the saying "Time and I against any two." The side without a deadline can let the side with one make the concessions.
cards.uw: The other side needs the deal closed this quarter and you do not.

cards.title: Show one purpose, strike with the other
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"It lets a purpose appear in order to attract the opponent's attention, but then turns round and conquers by the unexpected."

"It lets the first impulse pass by and waits for the second, or even the third."
cards.why: The maxim covers both sides of a feint. The attacker shows a decoy aim. The defender treats the first move as probably false and waits for the second or third before reacting.
cards.uw: An opening demand looks too obvious, or you are about to react to the other side's first move.

cards.title: Don't let them learn your tastes
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"He that plays with cards exposed runs a risk of losing the stakes."

"Do not even let your tastes be known, lest others utilise them either by running counter to them or by flattering them."
cards.why: Gracián extends secrecy from plans to tastes. A known preference gives the other side two levers: block what you like, or flatter it to soften you.
cards.uw: You are about to tell a counterpart which option you love before the terms are set.

cards.title: When they grab the right side, take it anyway
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal: "Thus the only way to drive him from the better course is to take it yourself, for his folly will cause him to desert it"
cards.why: Gracián says arguing the worse side out of pride means "you begin the fight already beaten." Take the better course yourself, and an obstinate opponent will often desert it to keep disagreeing.
cards.uw: Your rival staked out the sensible position first and you feel pressure to oppose it.

cards.title: Lead with their business to get to yours
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"His affair seems to be in train when it is really only leading the way for another's."

"Likewise with persons who always say No at first, it is useful to ward off this blow"
cards.why: Opening on the other person's interest gets them moving before your request arrives. Gracián recommends it most for people whose reflex answer is no.
cards.uw: Your contact refuses any request that opens with what you need.

cards.title: Sell it as for connoisseurs, never as easy
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"it is generally an inducement to profess to supply only connoisseurs, for all think themselves such, and if not, the sense of want arouses the desire."

"Never call things easy or common: that makes them depreciated rather than made accessible."
cards.why: Gracián's levers on price are praise, a striking name, and a claim to serve connoisseurs. Calling a thing easy or common makes it "depreciated rather than made accessible."
cards.uw: You are writing a launch page and reaching for "simple" and "for everyone."

cards.title: Float it first so you can still withdraw
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"Throw Straws in the Air, to find how things will be received, especially those whose reception or success is doubtful."

"an opportunity is afforded for going on in earnest or withdrawing entirely."
cards.why: A trial balloon tells you how the proposal lands while you can still deny you meant it. He calls it the rule "in asking, in desiring, and in ruling."
cards.uw: You want to know if a big ask will fly before you make it on the record.

cards.title: Talk about today's mistake as if it were long past
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal: "A pleasant manner has here an opportunity for a display of skill: with the same truth it can flatter one and fell another to the ground. Matters of to-day should be treated as if they were long past."
cards.why: Gracián's technique for bitter truths is distance in time. Discussing a live error as old history lets the person agree without having to defend their present self.
cards.uw: You need to tell someone their current project is failing.

cards.title: Satisfy the want, keep the dependence
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"The wise man would rather see men needing him than thanking him. To keep them on the threshold of hope is diplomatic, to trust to their gratitude boorish ; hope has a good memory, gratitude a bad one."

"It is a subtle point to satisfy the desire and yet preserve the dependence."
cards.why: Gracián would rather see men needing him than thanking him. Deliver enough to keep them engaged and hold back the part that ends their need.
cards.uw: You are about to give the client everything up front and lose your leverage for phase two.

cards.title: Watch the man who comes second on purpose
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal: "they dissemble their desire so as to attain it. They put themselves second so as to come out first in the final spurt."
cards.why: A counterpart who seems indifferent may be hiding how badly they want the outcome. Gracián says such men put themselves second to come out first.
cards.uw: Someone is a little too relaxed about a deal they started.

cards.title: Doubt the secret out of them
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"Tepid incredulity acts as an emetic on secrets."

"A sly depreciation of another's mysterious word scents out the profoundest secrets"
cards.why: Gracián's move: meet a hinted secret with mild disbelief. To prove it, the speaker has to tell it.
cards.uw: Someone hints they have a better offer and won't say what it is.

cards.title: Ask after the meal, never after a refusal
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"Surprise them when in a pleasant mood, when a repast of body or soul has just left them refreshed"

"It is no use applying when another has been refused, since the objection to a No has just been overcome."
cards.why: Timing gets three rules: ask when the person is in a good mood, avoid asking just after they refused someone else, and avoid asking after a loss. Having just said no once, they find the next no easy.
cards.uw: You need a yes from someone and can pick the moment to ask.

cards.title: Pay the reward before it's earned
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"the same gift which would afterwards be merely a reward is beforehand an obligation."

"with men of lower stamp the honorarium paid beforehand acts rather as a bit than as a spur."
cards.why: The same favor changes meaning with timing. Given afterward it settles a debt; given in advance it creates one. Gracián limits it to people who feel obligation.
cards.uw: You plan to reward a partner after delivery and wonder whether to give it now instead.

cards.title: Call the break a cooling, never a fight
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"Every one may be of importance as an enemy if not as a friend. Few can do us good, almost any can do us harm."

"If, however, a breach is inevitable, let it be rather excused as a slackening of friendship than by an outburst of wrath"
cards.why: A loud rupture invites hidden enemies to use your declared one against you. Letting a relationship fade without a scene closes the door with fewer enemies made.
cards.uw: A partnership has to end and you want to say what you really think on the way out.

cards.title: Turn the attacker into a confidant
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"It is an uncommon piece of shrewdness to change a rival into a confidant"

"he leaves no time for injuries that fills it up with gratitude."
cards.why: Gracián prefers preventing an injury to avenging it. Bringing a rival inside, with favors and confidence, fills their time with obligations to you.
cards.uw: Someone has started to undermine you and retaliation is the first idea you have.

cards.title: Announce the decision after, never before
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal: "A resolution declared is never highly thought of; it only leaves room for criticism. And if it happens to fail, you are doubly unfortunate."
cards.why: Announcing a plan early gives critics a target and doubles the cost of failure, once for failing and once for having said you would succeed.
cards.uw: You want to tell everyone what you are about to try.

cards.title: Don't show the sore point
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"nor complain about it, for malice always aims where weakness can be injured."

"The wise never own to being hit, or disclose any evil, whether personal or hereditary."
cards.why: Gracián says a known sore spot becomes the place everything knocks against, and complaining about it marks the target. In a negotiation that means keeping quiet about the term you can least afford to lose.
cards.uw: You're tempted to tell the other side which concession would hurt you most.

cards.title: Show your teeth at the first encroachment
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal: "Give way to the first and you must yield to the second, and so on till the last, and to gain your point at last costs as much trouble as would have gained much more at first."
cards.why: Gracián prices concessions as a chain: each one you grant makes the next harder to refuse. Pushing back at the first costs less than recovering ground after several.
cards.uw: A counterpart has just asked for a small extra that wasn't in the deal.

cards.title: Give a gilded No
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"Some men's No is thought more of than the Yes of others : for a gilded No is more satisfactory than a dry Yes."

"Your refusal need not be point-blank : let the disappointment come by degrees. Nor let the refusal be final"
cards.why: Gracián's refusal has a method: let the disappointment arrive in stages, leave some hope in place, and cover the gap with courtesy. He warns that people who lead with No get no credit even when they later give way.
cards.uw: You have to turn down a request from someone you'll need again.

cards.title: Never fight someone with nothing to lose
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"The other enters without anxiety ; having lost everything, including shame, he has no further loss to fear."

"For even by victory he cannot gain what he has lost by exposing himself to the chances of loss."
cards.why: The contest is unequal because only one side has a reputation at stake. Gracián says even winning doesn't repay what you risked by stepping in.
cards.uw: Someone with no standing to protect is baiting you into a public dispute.

cards.title: Arrive underbilled
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal:
"Hope is a great falsifier of truth ; let skill guard against this by ensuring that fruition exceeds desire."

"A few creditable attempts at the beginning are sufficient to arouse curiosity without pledging one to the final object."
cards.why: Gracián says the real can never match the imagined, and disappointed people turn critical. His fix is to let early results build curiosity without promising the finished thing.
cards.uw: You're about to announce a launch, a hire or a product with big claims attached.

cards.title: Get it by seeming not to want it
cards.book: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Baltasar Gracián
cards.steal: "generally they are not to be had when sought for, but fall into one's hands when one is not looking for them."
cards.why: Gracián opens the maxim on getting things "by affecting to depreciate them." He says wanted things flee whoever chases them and follow whoever walks away.
cards.uw: You badly want the deal and the other side can tell.

cards.title: Pasture the horse beside the tracks
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"How would you cure a horse that is afraid of cars—graze him in a back-woods lot where he would never see steam-engines or automobiles, or drive or pasture him where he would frequently see the machines?"

"You must learn to speak by speaking."
cards.why: The opening chapter's cure for stage fright is repeated exposure. Books can coach you, but in their words "no one ever learns to swim" in a wetless bathing suit.
cards.uw: You've been reading about public speaking instead of booking a talk.

cards.title: Pour water in the glass to get the air out
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"One way to get air out of a glass is to pour in water."

"fill your mind with your speech-material and, like the infilling water in the glass, it will drive out your unsubstantial fears."
cards.why: A mind packed with the material has no room left for "How does my hair look?" The blacksmith's rope on the horse's nose is the same trick, distraction by something stronger.
cards.uw: You're backstage replaying everything that could go wrong.

cards.title: Script the first few sentences word for word
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal: "Have the first few sentences worked out completely so that you may not be troubled in the beginning to find words. Know your subject better than your hearers know it, and you have nothing to fear."
cards.why: The authors want the opening fixed so you are not hunting for words at the start. Knowing the subject better than your hearers is their other cure.
cards.uw: You're preparing a talk and plan to improvise the opening.

cards.title: Whisper the word that matters
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal: "To make a word emphatic, deliver it differently from the manner in which the words surrounding it are delivered. If you have been talking loudly, utter the emphatic word in a concentrated whisper—and you have intense emphasis."
cards.why: Emphasis comes from contrast. A Fifth Avenue bus turns heads in a farm town and an ox team turns heads on Fifth Avenue, so whatever you've been doing, change it on the key word.
cards.uw: You've been raising your voice to stress points and the room has tuned out.

cards.title: Stress the man who bit the dog
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"'But,' said Mr. Dana, 'if you see a man bite a dog, hurry back to the office and write the story.'"

"'New stars and suns' are hardly as emphatic as the word 'larger.' Why? Because we expect an astronomer to discover heavenly bodies rather than cooking recipes."
cards.why: Words the audience already expects don't need stress. Save emphasis for the new or surprising word, the part that is news. The authors treat the average sentence as "just one big word, with the important word as the accented syllable," the way nobody stresses every syllable of "Massachusetts."
cards.uw: You're marking up a script and stressing the obvious nouns.

cards.title: Stress one word and they hear its opposite
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"If you say, 'My horse is not black,' what color immediately comes into mind? White, naturally, for that is the opposite of black."

"Strongly emphasizing a single word has a tendency to suggest its antithesis."
cards.why: Heavy stress implies a contrast. Leaning on "chance" in "Destiny is not a matter of chance" sets up "choice" before you say it.
cards.uw: You want the audience to arrive at your point a beat before you state it.

cards.title: Pause on both sides of the big phrase
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal: "one of the most important means of developing power in public speaking is to pause either before or after, or both before and after, an important word or phrase."
cards.why: The authors separate this from stumbling with "uh" and "er." A deliberate pause makes the audience wait and makes the phrase land. They say it is hard to grasp until you notice good speakers doing it.
cards.uw: Your key line goes by before anyone registers it.

cards.title: Circle the pivot, box the anecdote
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"he may underscore a catch-word heavily, draw a red circle around a pivotal idea, enclose the key-word of an anecdote in a wavy-lined box"

"nothing so eludes the swift-glancing eye of the speaker as the sameness of typewriting"
cards.why: Uniform text is hard to find with a half-second glance. Visual marks act as handles, and the authors say even an accidental blot can help you recall a point.
cards.uw: You lose your place in your notes mid-talk.

cards.title: Memorize the joints, improvise the rest
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal: "Others again write and commit a few important parts of the address—the introduction, the conclusion, some vital argument, some pat illustration—and depend on the hour for the language of the rest."
cards.why: Write and memorize the introduction, the conclusion and the key argument, and speak the rest. Fully memorized lines, the authors warn, usually "sound like memorized words, and repel."
cards.uw: You're choosing between reading a script and winging it.

cards.title: Tell the joke that fits, skip the one that's funnier
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"An anecdote without bearing may be funny but one less funny that fits theme and occasion is far preferable."

"humor alone rarely scores so heavily as the two combined, while the utterly grave speech never does on such occasions."
cards.why: At banquets and occasions the authors want humor mixed with substance. A string of unrelated jokes joined by "And that reminds me" wastes the chance.
cards.uw: You've got a great joke for a toast and it has nothing to do with the occasion.

cards.title: Ask who else is speaking and whether there's a desk
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal: "Who else will speak? Do I speak first, last, or where, on the program? What are the other speakers going to talk about? What is the nature of the auditorium? Is there a desk?"
cards.why: The checklist covers the audience, their likely attitude, the program order, the room and the exact time. The authors put most speech misfits down to never asking.
cards.uw: You've been invited to speak and know only the topic.

cards.title: Ten minutes means neither nine nor eleven
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"Let ten minutes mean neither nine nor eleven—though better nine than eleven, at all events."

"Blessed is the man that maketh short speeches, for he shall be invited to speak again."
cards.why: Running over takes time from the next speaker and the audience. The fix is planning: give each point its share of time and decide in advance where the main section sits.
cards.uw: Your talks keep running long.

cards.title: Count the rolls yourself
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal: "Your words come with the weight of authority when you can say, 'I have examined the employment rolls of every mill in this district and find that thirty-two per cent of the children employed are under the legal age.' No citation of authorities can equal that."
cards.why: A first-hand fact can't be waved off as hearsay, and the authors add that seeing the facts yourself changes how you deliver them.
cards.uw: Your argument rests on numbers you've only read secondhand.

cards.title: Close while their last thought is yours
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"Most of us are captured by the latest strong attack, and if we can be induced to act while under the stress of that last insistent thought, we lose sight of counter influences."

"ninety per cent of the people who bought books by subscription never read them."
cards.why: The authors quote a publisher: subscription buyers acted while the salesman's picture filled their minds and every objection was crowded out.
cards.uw: You're about to sign something while the pitch is still ringing in your ears.

cards.title: Don't tell them not to put beans up their noses
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"To warn children that they should not put beans up their noses is the surest method of getting them to do it."

"Every thought called up in the mind of your audience will work either for or against you."
cards.why: Naming an action plants it, even inside a prohibition. The authors say a speaker should avoid calling up the very thoughts that work against the goal.
cards.uw: Your warning slide lists the exact mistakes you don't want people to make.

cards.title: Suggest their minds are already changing
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"Suggest to a man that it is impossible to change his mind and in most cases it becomes more difficult to do so"

"Suggest subtly and persistently that the opinions of those in the audience who are opposed to your views are changing"
cards.why: The authors say feelings, thoughts and wills "tend to follow the line of least resistance." Telling people they are dug in digs them in; suggesting that opinion is already shifting makes holding out the effort. They note the born contrarian needs the reverse.
cards.uw: You're addressing people who are against you and about to call them stubborn.

cards.title: Call the half-empty room a great gathering
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"A gloomy day, in a drab room, sparsely tenanted by listeners, invites platform disaster. Everyone feels it in the air."

"let the speaker walk squarely up to the issue and suggest by all his feeling, manner and words that this is going to be a great gathering in every vital sense"
cards.why: The setting suggests a flop unless something stronger suggests otherwise. Here the stronger signal is the speaker's own manner, set against the room.
cards.uw: Turnout is thin and you're tempted to apologize for it.

cards.title: Lead with the cities that already adopted it
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal: "The advocates of the commission-form of government of cities, the champions of votes for women, reserve as their strongest arguments the fact that a number of cities and states have already successfully accepted their plans."
cards.why: The authors note that reformers save as their strongest argument the places that have already adopted the plan. It answers "has it worked?" and "am I alone?" at once.
cards.uw: You're proposing a change to a cautious group.

cards.title: Imply it so nobody can dispute it
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"Figurative and indirect language has suggestive force, because it does not make statements that can be directly disputed."

"When immediate action or persuasion is desired, suggestion is more efficacious than argument—when both are judiciously mixed, the effect is irresistible."
cards.why: The authors say indirect language persuades because it "does not make statements that can be directly disputed." They still want a logical base under it.
cards.uw: Every direct statement you make draws a rebuttal.

cards.title: Start with their pains
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"Patent medicine advertisement usually begins by talking about your pains—they begin on your interests."

"Recently a book-salesman entered an attorney's office in New York and inquired: 'Do you want to buy a book?' Had the lawyer wanted a book he would probably have bought one without waiting for a book-salesman to call."
cards.why: Advertising that opened with the firm's size or the remedy's strength went unread. Opening with the reader's problem made them ask for the solution. The authors set it against a book salesman whose opening, "Do you want to buy a book?", talked only in terms of his own interest.
cards.uw: Your pitch opens with your company's history.

cards.title: Pack them into the front pews
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"It is as hard to kindle enthusiasm in a scattered audience as to build a fire with scattered sticks."

"Have your audience seated compactly."
cards.why: The authors say feeling catches across a packed crowd and dies across empty benches, and point out that St. Peter's moves ordinary services into side chapels.
cards.uw: Forty people are scattered across a room for three hundred.

cards.title: Repeat their claim while your facts take it apart
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"For Brutus is an honorable man, So are they all, all honorable men"

"He hath brought many captives home to Rome, Whose ransoms did the general coffers fill: Did this in Caesar seem ambitious?"
cards.why: The authors print Antony's oration as their model of turning listeners into a crowd. Antony never attacks Brutus's claim head-on. He repeats it after each fact (the ransoms, the refused crown, the tears for the poor) until the refrain itself sounds like an accusation.
cards.uw: You have to answer a respected opponent without attacking them by name.

cards.title: Show the prize, then refuse to read it
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"Let but the commons hear this testament-- Which, pardon me, I do not mean to read--"

"You will compel me then to read the will?"
cards.why: Antony holds up Caesar's will and declines to read it, so the crowd demands it. By the time he gives in, they are asking for the argument he came to make.
cards.uw: You have a strong document or number and want the room to ask for it.

cards.title: Start on the motive they have, end on the highest
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"Notice how at the last the pleader sweeps on to the highest ground he can take."

"This is a notable example of progressive appeal, beginning with a low motive and ending with a high one in such a way as to carry all the force of prejudice yet gain all the value of patriotic fervor."
cards.why: The authors use a Kipling war speech that opens on self-interest and ends on patriotism. They call the appeal to prejudice rarely justifiable and still show the sequence: meet people at the motive they already feel, then climb.
cards.uw: Your audience cares about their own costs and you need them to care about the larger cause.

cards.title: Carry your license
cards.book: The Art of Public Speaking — J. Berg Esenwein & Dale Carnegie
cards.steal:
"Ignorance and credulity will remain unchanged unless the suggestion of authority be followed promptly by facts."

"Don't claim authority unless you carry your license in your pocket. Let reason support the position that suggestion has assumed."
cards.why: Reputation gets a hearing, and the authors say facts have to follow fast. They cite Bryan, whose fame filled halls, and add that "back of it all, he is a great speaker."
cards.uw: Your title or credentials got you the invitation and you're tempted to coast on them.

cards.title: Workers slow down to keep the record secret
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal: "The greater part of the systematic soldiering, however, is done by the men with the deliberate object of keeping their employers ignorant of how fast work can be done."
cards.why: Taylor quotes his own earlier paper: the employer rarely forces a faster pace without "an actual record proving conclusively how fast the work can be done." So the crew's main interest is making sure no such record ever exists.
cards.uw: Your team's estimates never get shorter no matter how familiar the work becomes.

cards.title: Cut the rate twice and you've trained them to hold back
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal: "…after a workman has had the price per piece of the work he is doing lowered two or three times as a result of his having worked harder and increased his output, he is likely entirely to lose sight of his employer's side of the case…"
cards.why: Each rate cut punished the extra output that triggered it. Taylor says the result is a "grim determination to have no more cuts" and suspicion of any proposal, however reasonable.
cards.uw: You are tempted to raise a quota because someone beat it.

cards.title: The twelve-year-old caddy's pay lesson
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal: "…since they were paid by the hour, the faster they went the less money they got, and finally telling him that if he went too fast the other boys would give him a licking."
cards.why: A twelve-year-old had worked out the incentive and the enforcement on his own. Hourly pay rewarded slowness, and the group policed anyone who went faster.
cards.uw: You are setting up pay for work where you can't easily see the pace.

cards.title: Fifty ways to do a task, one is fastest
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"…there are many different ways in common use for doing the same thing, perhaps forty, fifty, or a hundred ways of doing each act in each trade…"

"…among the various methods and implements used in each element of each trade there is always one method and one implement which is quicker and better than any of the rest."
cards.why: Skills passed on by watching the person at the next bench produce dozens of local variants. Taylor's claim is that comparing them element by element turns up a best one that can be taught.
cards.uw: Every person on the team does the same recurring task differently.

cards.title: Stop hunting for the ready-made hire
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal: "What we are all looking for, however, is the readymade, competent man; the man whom some one else has trained."
cards.why: Taylor says demand for competent people always runs ahead of supply because everyone is shopping for the finished product. His alternative is to systematically train the competent hire yourself.
cards.uw: A role has been open for months because nobody fully qualified applies.

cards.title: Replace the one foreman with eight specialists
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"Under functional management, the old-fashioned single foreman is superseded by eight different men, each one of whom has his own special duties…"

"…they are able not only to tell the workman what he should do, but in case of necessity they do the work themselves in the presence of the workman, so as to show him not only the best but also the quickest methods."
cards.why: Taylor splits the foreman's job by function: one teacher for drawings and quality, others for speeds, motions and timing, each acting for the planning department. Each is picked for skill in one specialty and can demonstrate the work, which one generalist foreman can't do across every area.
cards.uw: One supervisor is expected to coach quality, speed, scheduling and discipline all at once.

cards.title: Put the planning on a desk, away from the machine
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"…it would be physically impossible for him to work at his machine and at a desk at the same time."

"…under scientific management fully one-half of the problem is 'up to the management.'"
cards.why: Under the old system the worker did the planning in his head while running the machine. Taylor moves it to a planning room and says the work splits better when "one type of man is needed to plan ahead and an entirely different type to execute the work."
cards.uw: Your best makers are also doing all the scheduling and tooling decisions in their heads.

cards.title: Hand out the task with the how and the time attached
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal: "This task specifies not only what is to be done but how it is to be done and the exact time allowed for doing it."
cards.why: Taylor's task card was planned a day ahead and came with written method and a time limit, plus a 30 to 100 per cent bonus for hitting it. He insists the pace must be one a suited worker can sustain for years.
cards.uw: Assignments go out as a goal with no method and no time estimate.

cards.title: Rest 57 per cent of the day and carry more
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal: "…when pig iron is being handled (each pig weighing 92 pounds), a first-class workman can only be under load 43 per cent of the day. He must be entirely free from load during 57 per cent of the day."
cards.why: Carl Barth plotted the data and found that how heavy the load was set how much of the day a man could be under it. Scheduled rest was what made the higher daily tonnage possible.
cards.uw: People are grinding without breaks on heavy work and output is falling.

cards.title: Size the shovel to the material, aim for 21 pounds
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"…it was found that a first-class man would do his biggest day's work with a shovel load of about 21 pounds."

"…he would frequently go from shoveling ore, with a load of about 30 pounds per shovel, to handling rice coal, with a load on the same shovel of less than 4 pounds."
cards.why: One shovel per man meant he was overloaded on ore and nearly idle on coal. Bethlehem stocked 8 to 10 shovel types so every material came out near the same optimal load.
cards.uw: Everyone uses the same tool for every job because that's the tool they own.

cards.title: White slip, yellow slip
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"…yellow paper showed the man that he had failed to do his full task the day before…"

"…whenever the men received white slips they knew that everything was all right, and whenever they received yellow slips they realized that they must do better…"
cards.why: Each morning every laborer got yesterday's result on a colored slip. Many couldn't read, and the color carried the message anyway. Daily, individual feedback replaced a foreman's general impression.
cards.uw: People find out how they're doing only at an annual review.

cards.title: Send a teacher before you fire
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
