cards.steal: "…if the workman fails to do his task, some competent teacher should be sent to show him exactly how his work can best be done, to guide, help, and encourage him, and, at the same time, to study his possibilities as a workman."
cards.why: The first response to a miss was instruction. If that failed the man was moved to work he was better suited to, "instead of brutally discharging the man or lowering his wages."
cards.uw: Someone misses targets in their first month and the reflex is to let them go.

cards.title: Gangs sink to the worst man in them
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"…when men work in gangs, their individual efficiency falls almost invariably down to or below the level of the worst man in the gang…"

"…not more than four men were to be allowed to work in a labor gang without a special permit, signed by the General Superintendent…"
cards.why: Bethlehem made big gangs a paperwork burden. The superintendent ran 5000 men and had little time to sign permits, so work got split into individual tasks with individual pay.
cards.uw: Output from a team effort is lower than its members manage alone.

cards.title: Wish them well at the higher rate and leave the door open
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"Just remember, however, that at any time in the future, when you get out of a job, you can always come right back to us."

"Now, Jimmy, you and I will throw a shovel full whenever this little devil throws one, and not another shovel full."
cards.why: Bethlehem urged its best shovelers to take a higher per-ton offer in Pittsburgh. Most came back within six weeks to the lower rate, because the Pittsburgh gang pace had cut their real earnings.
cards.uw: A competitor is offering your people a better headline rate.

cards.title: Bring the bricks up to the bricklayer
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"…each bricklayer lowering his body, weighing, say, 150 pounds, down two feet and raising it up again every time a brick (weighing about 5 pounds) is laid in the wall! And this each bricklayer did about one thousand times a day."

"…Mr. Gilbreth has reduced his movements from eighteen motions per brick to five…"
cards.why: Frank Gilbreth raised the scaffold, pre-sorted bricks into packs and tempered the mortar so bricks needed no tapping. Taylor reports 350 bricks per man per hour against a local average of 120.
cards.uw: A skilled job still has the same physical setup it had decades ago.

cards.title: The vote said no, the shorter day raised output
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"…when the vote was taken the girls were unanimous that 10 1/2 hours was good enough for them and they wanted no innovation of any kind."

"…with each shortening of the working day the output increased instead of diminishing."
cards.why: Individually the inspectors agreed ten hours would do. As a group they voted it down. Months later Taylor cut hours in steps to 8 1/2 at the same pay and output rose each time. He calls the vote a lapse into tact he regretted.
cards.uw: You plan to put a change to a group vote that people agreed to one by one.

cards.title: Lock quality before you pay for quantity
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal: "It is necessary in almost all cases, therefore, to take definite steps to insure against any falling off in quality before moving in any way towards an increase in quantity."
cards.why: At the bicycle ball plant, over-inspection came first: trusted inspectors re-checked anonymous lots from the day before. Only after that did output pay begin.
cards.uw: You're about to start paying or ranking people on volume.

cards.title: Salt the batch with known defects
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal: "Every two or three days a lot of balls was especially prepared by the foreman, who counted out a definite number of perfect balls, and added a recorded number of defective balls of each kind."
cards.why: Neither inspectors nor over-inspectors could tell the seeded lot from real ones, so each count could be scored against a known answer. Taylor says this removed "all temptation to slight their work or make false returns."
cards.uw: You rely on reviewers or QA and have no way to measure what they miss.

cards.title: Stop them at an hour and a quarter
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"…after about an hour and one-half of consecutive work they began to get nervous."

"It is wise to stop short of the point at which overstrain begins, so we arranged for them to have a ten minutes period for recreation at the end of each hour and one quarter."
cards.why: The breaks were scheduled just before observed fatigue set in, and the inspectors were required to get up and walk around. Taylor reports the same group earlier lost much of a long day to half-working.
cards.uw: Detail work like reviewing, proofreading or inspection drifts in quality late in the day.

cards.title: Select for the one trait the job turns on
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"Mr. Thompson soon recognized that the quality most needed for bicycle ball inspectors was a low personal coefficient."

"…this involved laying off many of the most intelligent, hardest working, and most trustworthy girls merely because they did not possess the quality of quick perception followed by quick action."
cards.why: Reaction time, measured as in a psychology lab, decided who stayed. Taylor admits the cost plainly: good workers lost the job over a trait unrelated to effort or honesty.
cards.uw: You are hiring on general merit for a job that depends on one measurable ability.

cards.title: A stranger with a slide rule beat the twelve-year veteran
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal: "…the gain in time made through running the machine according to scientific principles ranged from two and one-half times the speed in the slowest instance to nine times the speed in the highest."
cards.why: The lathe had been run for ten to twelve years by a first-class mechanic. A man who had never seen the jobs, using slide rules built from years of metal-cutting experiments, set speeds and feeds that beat him on every part.
cards.uw: You assume long experience on a machine means the settings are already optimal.

cards.title: Test the worker's idea and pay for it
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal: "…whenever the new method is found to be markedly superior to the old, it should be adopted as the standard for the whole establishment. The workman should be given the full credit for the improvement, and should be paid a cash premium as a reward for his ingenuity."
cards.why: Suggestions get a formal experiment against the current standard, and the winner becomes the new standard with credit and cash to its author.
cards.uw: You have standardized a process and need a way to keep improving it.

cards.title: Copying the tools without the philosophy breaks things
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal: "The mechanism of management must not be mistaken for its essence, or underlying philosophy. Precisely the same mechanism will in one case produce disastrous results and in another the most beneficent."
cards.why: Taylor lists his own tools, including time study, instruction cards, slide rules and the planning room, and warns they fail when used without real cooperation with the workers. He says rushed adoptions have ended in strikes.
cards.uw: You are adopting another company's process tools as a quick fix.

cards.title: Convert one worker, then wait for a quarter to tip
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"…only one workman at a time should be dealt with at the start. Until this single man has been thoroughly convinced that a great gain has come to him from the new method, no further change should be made."

"…very rapid progress can be made, because at about this time there is, generally, a complete revolution in the public opinion of the whole establishment…"
cards.why: Taylor put a full changeover at two to three years and sometimes four to five. It starts with one convinced worker, and once a quarter to a third of the workforce has switched, opinion turns and the rest ask to join.
cards.uw: You are rolling out a new way of working and want to announce it to everyone on day one.

cards.title: Are you a high-priced man?
cards.book: The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor
cards.steal:
"Schmidt, are you a high-priced man?"

"He worked when he was told to work, and rested when he was told to rest, and at half-past five in the afternoon had his 47 and a half tons loaded on the car."
cards.why: Taylor tied the job to a wage the man wanted ($1.85 against $1.15) and to doing exactly what a man with a stopwatch said, including when to rest. He says the pitch kept Schmidt's attention "on the high wages which he wants." This is Taylor's account; it has not been checked against outside sources.
cards.uw: You are offering more pay in exchange for following a prescribed method exactly.

cards.title: Don't plan on supplies you haven't counted
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal: "you are prepared to rely on what you do not know? Do you forget that the needs of the morrow must be high, not to speak of the outlay for the day?"
cards.why: Cyrus is counting on an ally to feed his whole army and has never asked how much the ally can give. Three questions from his father expose the gap: the amount, the cost of tomorrow, and what happens if the ally can't or won't deliver.
cards.uw: Your plan depends on a partner's resources you have never actually seen.

cards.title: Raise the money while you're flush
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal: "never put off the collecting of supplies until the day of need, make the season of your abundance provide against the time of dearth. You will gain better terms from those on whom you must depend if you are not thought to be in straits"
cards.why: Cambyses ties reserves to bargaining power and authority. A leader who isn't visibly short gets better terms from suppliers and more willing followers.
cards.uw: You plan to start fundraising when the runway gets short.

cards.title: Pay above the promise and it lands as a gift
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal: "They are well aware of the terms Cyaxares has offered for their help: but whatever they get over and above the covenanted amount they will look upon as a free gift, and for that they will, in all likelihood, feel most gratitude to the giver."
cards.why: Cyrus reasons that promised pay is owed, so the thanks go to whoever promised it. Only what comes above the agreed amount reads as a gift from him.
cards.uw: You're deciding whether a bonus should be built into the contract or given on top.

cards.title: The general's teacher only taught tactics
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"'He taught me tactics.'"

"'And pray what will be the use of tactics to an army without supplies, without health, without discipline, without knowledge of those arts and inventions that are of use in war?'"
cards.why: Cambyses quizzes Cyrus on whether his paid instructor covered economy, health, morale or obedience. The answer each time is no. Cambyses runs through supplies, health, discipline and morale, and the teacher covered none of them.
cards.uw: You're hiring or training a manager on technical skill alone.

cards.title: Doctors patch, leaders prevent
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal: "these excellent men are, after all, much the same as the tailors who patch torn garments. When folk are ill, your doctors can patch them up, but your own care for their health ought to go far deeper than that: your prime object should be to save your men from falling ill at all."
cards.why: Cyrus is proud of the medical staff he hired. His father says that is repair and puts prevention on the leader: a healthy camp site, controlled diet, steady exercise.
cards.uw: You're proud of your support function and it's mostly cleaning up avoidable problems.

cards.title: An idle army eats itself
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal: "A single man is hard enough to support in idleness, a household is harder still, an army hardest of all. There are more mouths to be filled, less wealth to start with, and greater waste; and therefore an army should never be unemployed."
cards.why: Cambyses reasons from cost: a large group consumes more and wastes more, so it must always be either gaining ground or improving itself.
cards.uw: Your team is between projects and you're letting the gap drift.

cards.title: Set competitions with prizes
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal: "Let him propose competitions of every kind and offer prizes; the standard of skill will rise, and he will soon have a body of troops ready to his hand for any service he requires."
cards.why: Cyrus's own idea, and his father approves. Contests make practice voluntary and visible, and later chapters show Cyrus running them across every skill.
cards.uw: Training feels like a chore and nobody practises unless forced.

cards.title: Don't cry the view-halloo too often
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"Let a man rouse false expectations often enough, and in the end, even when hope is at the door, he may cry the good news in vain."

"his agents may step in and do it in his place; but he should reserve his own appeal for the supreme crises of supreme danger, and not dissipate his credit."
cards.why: Hounds stop answering a huntsman who has called false sightings. Cambyses' fix is to let subordinates do the routine encouragement and save the leader's own promise for the moment it must be believed.
cards.uw: You're about to tell the team, again, that this quarter will turn things around.

cards.title: Be greedy for your share of the cold
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"I hold that the ruler should be marked out from other men, not by taking life easily, but by his forethought and his wisdom and his eagerness for work."

"if the campaign is in summer the general must show himself greedy for his share of the sun and the heat, and in winter for the cold and the frost, and in all labours for toil and fatigue."
cards.why: Cyrus wants the ruler set apart by forethought and work. Cambyses says a leader can't always do people good, but can always share their hardship and look ahead for them. He also notes the leader's pain is lighter because he works in public view.
cards.uw: Your team is pulling a hard stretch and you're working from somewhere comfortable.

cards.title: The surer you feel, the more you guard
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal: "the more I felt persuaded of my own superiority and the power of my troops, the more I should be inclined to stand on my guard, just as we put our greatest treasures in the safest place we have."
cards.why: Cyrus asks whether a well-prepared army should attack at once. His father says only if it gains something, and treats a strong force like a treasure: the thing you keep safest.
cards.uw: Your position is strong and you feel the urge to press it just because you can.

cards.title: Both sides have to eat and sleep
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"both of you must take your meals sometime; both of you must sleep; your men must scatter in the morning to satisfy the needs of nature"

"wherever you are weaker, there you must be most on your guard, and wherever your foe is most assailable, there you must press the attack."
cards.why: Cambyses points to the routines neither side can skip: meals, sleep, the morning scatter. Guard your side where you are weakest at those moments and press theirs.
cards.uw: You're planning a competitive move and looking only at the other side's strengths.

cards.title: If it's night, plan the day
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"if you wish your men to follow you, remember that they expect you to plan for them."

"if it be night, you must consider what your troops shall do when it is day; if day, how the night had best be spent."
cards.why: Cambyses names the deal followers expect: they give obedience and you give a plan for the next stretch. He says a leader can never afford a careless mood.
cards.uw: Your team keeps arriving in the morning to find nobody has decided the day's priorities.

cards.title: Put merit pay to a vote you expect to win
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"I cannot help seeing that within our ranks are men of every kind, some better and some worse, and yet if anything is won every man will claim an equal share."

"it would seem too base to deny that he who works the hardest and does most for the common good deserves the highest recompense."
cards.why: Cyrus could have decreed it. He puts it to the army because the spoils feel like common property, and he expects few will say aloud that the hardest worker deserves less. The commoner Pheraulas then carried the vote.
cards.uw: You're switching from equal splits to performance-based rewards.

cards.title: Clubs against clods
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"half were equipped with stout staves of fennel, and half were ordered to snatch up clods of earth and do what they could with these."

"on the next day the whole plain was studded with combats of this type, and whenever the army had nothing more serious in hand, this sport was their delight."
cards.why: A brigadier ran a rough mock battle showing that close fighting beats missiles. Cyrus asked about the bandages at dinner, the story spread, and the whole army copied the drill unasked.
cards.uw: You want a lesson to spread through a team without issuing a directive.

cards.title: Tens, hundreds, thousands, and one order
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"He remembered how the captains of ten supervised the squads of ten, and were supervised themselves by the company-captains, and they by the captains of the thousands, and these by the captains of ten thousand, and thus even with hundreds of thousands not a man was left without supervision"

"by conferring with a few officers he could keep the whole system under his control, and actually have more leisure for himself than the manager of a single household or the master of a single ship."
cards.why: Cyrus took the army's span of control and applied it to the finances and departments of an empire. The structure handed him back his time, and he spent it training his deputies.
cards.uw: You're the bottleneck for every decision in a growing organization.

cards.title: Have a friend claim the truant's estate
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal: "He would go to one of his most intimate friends and bid him lay hands on the property of the offender, asserting that it was his own. Then of course the truants would appear at once crying out that they had been robbed."
cards.why: Nobles who skipped court came running once their property was at stake. Cyrus then delayed hearing them for days, gave the best tasks to people who turned up on time, and in the end handed a persistent truant's holdings to someone who came when called.
cards.uw: Key people keep skipping the meetings where decisions get made.

cards.title: My friends are my treasury
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"There, Croesus, that is treasure number one; and now run through the rest, and count what sums I have in hand, in case I need them."

"But I hold to it that if I make my friends rich they will be my treasures themselves"
cards.why: Croesus warned that Cyrus's gifts would ruin him. Cyrus sent a request round his friends, and the pledges came to more than a hoard would have held, with no envy and no hired guards attached.
cards.uw: You're weighing whether to keep the surplus or spread it among your key people.

cards.title: Many king's eyes, never one
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"It is little that one man can see or one man hear, and to hand over the office to one single person would be to bid all others go to sleep."

"Cyrus' munificence toward all who told him what it was well for him to know set countless people listening with all their ears and watching with all their eyes"
cards.why: Rewarding anyone who brought useful news gave Cyrus an information network with no single informant to dodge. Xenophon adds that one known "eye" would make everyone guarded around that person.
cards.uw: You rely on a single trusted source to tell you what's really happening.

cards.title: Don't quarrel with all your people at once
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal: "it seems to me a grievous error in a ruler to quarrel with all his subjects at once. Widespread terror must needs be followed by widespread hate: anger with all creates unity among all."
cards.why: Cyaxares was furious that his Medes had followed Cyrus. Cyrus's answer is that collective punishment unites the punished against the one doing the punishing.
cards.uw: A whole team let you down and you're about to come down on all of them together.

cards.title: Make the new standard a point of honor
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal: "suppose we make it a rule that every one who receives a horse from me shall be considered to disgrace himself if he is seen trudging afoot, be his journey long or short?"
cards.why: Cyrus was building a Persian cavalry from foot soldiers. Tying status to the new skill made riding a matter of pride, and Xenophon says Persian gentlemen still avoided being seen on foot in his day.
cards.uw: You're introducing a new tool or skill and people keep slipping back to the old way.

cards.title: Feed the camp servants like soldiers
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal: "he always insisted that the army servants should share and share alike with the soldiers in everything, for he held that those who did such service for the army were as much to be honoured as heralds or ambassadors."
cards.why: Cyrus expected support staff to be loyal, quick and calm and to treat any order as within their dignity, so he gave them the soldiers' share.
cards.uw: Your support staff are held to high standards and rewarded like an afterthought.

cards.title: Pray only for what you've trained for
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal: "a man had no right to pray he might win a cavalry charge if he had never learnt how to ride, or triumph over master-bowmen if he could not draw a bow, or bring a ship safe home to harbour if he did not know how to steer"
cards.why: Cyrus recalls his father's rule that some outcomes are earned through learning and training, and that asking for luck without that work is asking for something forbidden.
cards.uw: Your plan for a hard outcome leans on luck in places where training would do.

cards.title: Seat people by merit and let the seating move
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"where the world believes merit will win no crown and receive no proclamation, there the spirit of emulation dies, but if all see that the best man gains most, then the rivalry grows keen."

"he made it a law that by good deeds a man might rise into a higher seat or through sloth descend into a lower"
cards.why: Cyrus made rank visible at his table and kept it moving: good work raised a guest's seat, slack work lowered it. He also made sure the most honored guest was seen to get the most favors, so the seating meant something.
cards.uw: Your team can't tell who is doing well or what doing well earns.

cards.title: Send the dish to the absent friend
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"all that was set before him, after he and his guests had dined, he would send out to his absent friends, in token of affection and remembrance."

"He would include those who had won his approval by their work on guard, or in attendance on himself, or in any other service, letting them see that no desire to please him could ever escape his eyes."
cards.why: Cyrus turned his own table into a running record of who had done good work, including guards and servants who were never at dinner. Xenophon adds that people then courted whoever received the king's dishes, so a gift also told everyone else who was in favor.
cards.uw: Good work happens out of your sight and you want people to know you noticed.

cards.title: Have them rule on the case before you name the defendant
cards.book: Cyropaedia — Xenophon
cards.steal:
"If you have an officer and he does wrong, do you suffer him to remain in office, or do you set up another in his stead?"

"Son of Armenia, we have heard your own judgment in this case, and now tell us, what ought we to do?"
cards.why: Cyrus puts the rebel Armenian king through questions about how he treats his own disloyal officers, one point at a time, then hands the answers back to him. Xenophon has Cyrus use the same method on his grandfather as a boy, asking what he'd do to a runaway slave before announcing his own plan to run off hunting.
cards.uw: You need someone to accept a consequence they will resist once they see it applies to them.

cards.title: Break three dozen pots into test tiles
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal: "He began by breaking three dozen new earthen pots, the pieces of which he covered with different materials which he had compounded, and then took them to a neighbouring glass-furnace to be baked."
cards.why: Palissy could not afford to fire whole pieces for every guess at the white enamel. Shards let him test many compounds in one firing, and the hotter glass furnace gave him "a glimmer of hope."
cards.uw: Each full test of an idea is expensive and you are testing one variable at a time.

cards.title: Notice what turns white in the fire
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal: "he noticed that a certain earth containing silica, which was black before calcination, became white after exposure to the heat of a furnace."
cards.why: Wedgwood studied chemistry in his spare hours and caught one small change in color. Mixing silica into the local red clay gave him the white body behind English earthenware.
cards.uw: You keep seeing a small anomaly in your materials and haven't asked what it would let you make.

cards.title: Drop the product before you cheapen it
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal: "He aimed throughout at the highest excellence, declaring his determination 'to give over manufacturing any article, whatsoever it might be, rather than to degrade it.'"
cards.why: Wedgwood made the line explicit: when quality couldn't be held, the article stopped. Smiles credits the standard with lifting the whole Staffordshire district.
cards.uw: Margins are squeezed and the easy fix is a cheaper version under the same name.

cards.title: Learn the hand craft before you build the machine
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal: "He first studied the art of making the Buckingham or pillow-lace by hand, with the object of effecting the same motions by mechanical means."
cards.why: Heathcoat mastered the motions himself before trying to mechanize them. His master called him "undaunted by failures and mistakes," and the result was the bobbin-net machine.
cards.uw: You are automating a process you have never done by hand.

cards.title: Watch your daughters comb their hair
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal:
"he found himself almost unconsciously watching his daughters coming their long hair and drawing it out at full length between their fingers."

"if he could successfully imitate in a machine the process of combing out the longest hair and forcing back the short by reversing the action of the comb, it might serve to extricate him from his difficulty."
cards.why: Heilmann had a professionally built model and still couldn't make it work. The answer came from an ordinary motion at home, which he copied into the combing machine. ("coming" is the Gutenberg text's misprint for "combing".)
cards.uw: You've been stuck on a mechanism for months and have only looked at other machines.

cards.title: The spider's net, the lobster shell, the shipworm
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal:
"he saw a tiny spider's net suspended across his path. The idea immediately occurred to him, that a bridge of iron ropes or chains might be constructed in like manner"

"Sir Isambert Brunel took his first lessons in forming the Thames Tunnel from the tiny shipworm"
cards.why: Three engineers, three borrowed designs: Brown's suspension bridge from a web, Watt's jointed river pipe from a lobster shell, Brunel's tunneling shield from a boring worm. Each was already studying the problem when he saw the model.
cards.uw: You are designing a structure and haven't asked what in nature already solves it.

cards.title: Trifles make perfection
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal: "'I have retouched this part—polished that—softened this feature—brought out that muscle—given some expression to this lip, and more energy to that limb.' 'But these are trifles,' remarked the visitor. 'It may be so,' replied the sculptor, 'but recollect that trifles make perfection, and perfection is no trifle.'"
cards.why: The visitor saw no change; Michelangelo listed six. Smiles pairs it with Poussin's answer on his reputation: "Because I have neglected nothing."
cards.uw: Someone asks why the last 5 per cent is taking so long.

cards.title: Keep the subject before you until it dawns
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal: "'I keep the subject continually before me, and wait till the first dawnings open slowly by little and little into a full and clear light.'"
cards.why: Asked how he made his discoveries, Newton said "By always thinking unto them." His rest was switching subjects, which kept the main problem in view without forcing it.
cards.uw: A hard problem needs sustained attention and you keep starting fresh on it each week.

cards.title: Make him repeat the sermon at lunch
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal: "his father was accustomed to set him up at table to practise speaking extempore; and he early accustomed him to repeat as much of the Sunday's sermon as he could remember."
cards.why: Smiles calls Peel's natural powers "mediocre." The weekly drill built the recall he later used to answer opponents point by point in Parliament.
cards.uw: You want to build a skill like recall or quick replies and are waiting for talent to show up.

cards.title: Rats ate the drawings, so draw better ones
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal:
"a pair of Norway rats had taken possession of the whole, and reared a young family among the gnawed bits of paper"

"I felt pleased that I might now make better drawings than before; and, ere a period not exceeding three years had elapsed, my portfolio was again filled."

"He had no draft, and was compelled to rake up from his memory facts, ideas, and expressions, which had been long since dismissed."
cards.why: Audubon lost two hundred original drawings. In his own account he was flattened for days, then treated the redo as a chance to improve, and refilled the portfolio in under three years. Smiles pairs it with Carlyle, whose lent manuscript of the first French Revolution volume was burned as waste paper and rewritten from memory.
cards.uw: Months of work are gone and you can't face starting again.

cards.title: Pay someone a crown to drag you out of bed
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal:
"He then called his servant, Joseph, to his help, and promised him the reward of a crown every time that he succeeded in getting him up before six."

"he was accustomed to say that he owed to Joseph three or four volumes of his Natural History."
cards.why: Willpower alone failed. Buffon paid for each success, and Joseph earned his pay by ignoring protests and threats, once with a basin of ice water. The precommitment worked where resolutions hadn't.
cards.uw: You keep breaking a resolution you've made to yourself many times.

cards.title: Pack the box, one thing at once
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal:
"'Method,' said the Reverend Richard Cecil, 'is like packing things in a box; a good packer will get in half as much again as a bad one.'"

"'The shortest way to do many things is to do only one thing at once;'"
cards.why: Cecil never left a task half done to return to later. De Witt's version was "One thing at a time": think of nothing else until the current dispatch is finished.
cards.uw: You have ten things open and none of them is getting done.

cards.title: When the front stalls, the rear piles up
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal: "Do instantly whatever is to be done, and take the hours of recreation after business, never before it. When a regiment is under march, the rear is often thrown into confusion because the front do not move steadily and without interruption."
cards.why: Walter Scott's advice to a young clerk names the problem as dawdling and the cost as a backlog where "affairs begin to press all at once." Clearing the first item keeps everything behind it moving.
cards.uw: Small tasks are stacking up behind one you keep putting off.

cards.title: Too much fame too early
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal: "West might have been a greater painter, had he not been injured by too early success: his fame, though great, was not purchased by study, trials, and difficulties, and it has not been enduring."
cards.why: This is Smiles's verdict on Benjamin West, a child prodigy. He makes the same point about Rossini through Beethoven: facility that comes too easily can stop the hard practice.
cards.uw: Early praise is arriving faster than your skill is growing.

cards.title: Ask for a book of blots
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal:
"John Hunter used to remark that the art of surgery would not advance until professional men had the courage to publish their failures as well as their successes."

"Watt the engineer said, of all things most wanted in mechanical engineering was a history of failures: 'We want,' he said, 'a book of blots.'"

"I thank God I was not made a dexterous manipulator, for the most important of my discoveries have been suggested to me by failures."
cards.why: John Hunter wanted surgeons to publish failures as well as successes, and Watt asked for "a book of blots." Davy said his most important discoveries came from failures.
cards.uw: Your team writes up wins and quietly forgets what didn't work.

cards.title: Four years dinning the project into ears
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal:
"At first he was laughed at; but his ceaseless importunity at length prevailed, and after four years' dinning of his project into the ears of the great and influential—during which time he lived in poverty—he at length succeeded."

"a diver came up with a solid bar of silver in his arms."
cards.why: After a failed first voyage the Admiralty refused Phipps another ship. He raised the money privately through a twenty-share company and found the Spanish wreck when a sailor sent a diver after a sea plant.
cards.uw: Your first attempt failed in public and the original backer won't fund a second.

cards.title: Brushes from the cat's tail
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal:
"Benjamin West made his first brushes out of the cat's tail."

"Watt made his first model of the condensing steam-engine out of an old anatomist's syringe"
cards.why: Smiles lists a run of first instruments: Wilkie's burnt stick, Ferguson's bead-and-thread star map, Franklin's silk kite, Rittenhouse's plough handle. None waited for proper tools.
cards.uw: You're holding off on starting until you have the right equipment.

cards.title: The ifs and the buts are out of season
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal:
"'The ifs and the buts,' said he, 'are at present out of season, and above all it must be done with speed.'"

"To Massena he writes, 'Let me know if your biscuit and bread arrangements are yet completed.'"
cards.why: From a small chateau in Poland, Napoleon chased muskets, shirts, sabres and biscuit by letter. Smiles says he chose agents well and still checked the details where results depended on them.
cards.uw: A big operation depends on supplies you've delegated and never verified.

cards.title: Pay your own bills
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal: "'I make a point,' said he to Mr. Gleig, 'of paying my own bills, and I advise every one to do the same; formerly I used to trust a confidential servant to pay them, but I was cured of that folly by receiving one morning, to my great surprise, duns of a year or two's standing."
cards.why: Wellington's servant had speculated with the money and left the bills unpaid. Keeping "an accurate detailed account of all the moneys received and expended" was the fix.
cards.uw: Someone else handles your money and you haven't looked at the accounts in months.

cards.title: Set down sudden thoughts for use
cards.book: Self-Help — Samuel Smiles
cards.steal:
"Lord Bacon left behind him many manuscripts entitled 'Sudden thoughts set down for use.'"

"These note-books afterwards proved, like Richter's 'quarries,' the great storehouse from which he drew his illustrations."
cards.why: Bacon, Eldon, Pye Smith and John Hunter all kept running notes, and the habit gave them stock to draw on later. Pye Smith's biographer called him "always at work, always in advance, always accumulating."
cards.uw: Good ideas show up when you aren't working and are gone by the time you are.

cards.title: Silent trade: lay it out, step back, wait
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"they [Carthaginians] come here and unload their cargo; then, having laid it out along the beach, they go back aboard their ships and light a smoking fire."

"if it seems to them a fair price for their cargo, they take it and go away; but if not, they go back aboard and wait, and the people come back and add more gold until the sailors are satisfied."
cards.why: Herodotus describes Carthaginian traders dealing with a people whose language they didn't share. Each side set down its offer and withdrew. Nobody touched the other side's goods until one side accepted, so the turns did the negotiating.
cards.uw: You have to strike a deal with no common language and no trust.

cards.title: Cut the oxhide into strips
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"‘as much land as could be covered by a single hide of an ox’"

"Then, she secretly has the oxhide cut into the thinnest possible strips."
cards.why: In Justin's telling, Dido asked a local king for one oxhide of land, then cut the hide into a thread long enough to circle the hill that became the Byrsa citadel. The price was agreed. She changed the unit. MacDonald notes the story fed the Roman picture of the tricky Carthaginian.
cards.uw: Someone asks you for 'just one' of something and nobody has said how it is measured.

cards.title: Pack the god and the brides
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"Elissa and her group of rebels fled the city by night, taking sacred artefacts that belonged to the god Melqart with them."

"The rebels’ first stop was the island of Cyprus, where they collected young women to join their party as brides."
cards.why: The founders took the sacred objects of Tyre's patron god and stopped on Cyprus to collect young women as brides. MacDonald reads the legend as a planned colony. They carried the two things a new city can't make for itself: its god and its families.
cards.uw: You are founding something far from home and it has to outlast the founders.

cards.title: Send families, not just crews
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal: "He set sail with sixty fifty-oared ships, about thirty thousand men and women, food and other equipment."
cards.why: Carthage ordered Hanno to sail past the Pillars of Herakles and found cities on the Atlantic coast of Africa. MacDonald calls the numbers exaggerated. The roster still shows the intent: women as well as men, and supplies for settlers who would stay.
cards.uw: You are opening a new location and need it to put down roots.

cards.title: Sail around the middlemen
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal: "Their expedition may well have been an attempt to cut out the desert middlemen by establishing direct links themselves, travelling by sea and setting up a network of contacts and colonies to facilitate this trade."
cards.why: Carthage bought West African gold through traders at the Saharan oases. MacDonald reads Hanno's voyage as a try for the same gold by sea, with the margin kept at home. She also calls it the oldest move colonisers have.
cards.uw: A middleman controls the only route to your supply.

cards.title: Nail the logbook to the temple wall
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"The original document, we believe, was written down and fixed to a temple wall in Carthage not long after the voyage took place."

"The skins were hung in the temple of Ba‘al Hammon on the return of the voyagers."
cards.why: Hanno's account of the voyage went up on a temple wall, and the skins of the two 'gorillas' his crew killed went up in the temple of Ba'al Hammon. Sailors copied the posted log as a guide for centuries, and it survives in Greek manuscripts.
cards.uw: A team has come back from new ground and the route should outlive the crew.

cards.title: Carry half the token
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"Inscribed on a wild boar-shaped ivory card were the words ‘I am Puinel from Carthage’, in the Etruscan language."

"A merchant in Carthage or an Etruscan city would send one half of the card with an associate who travelled to different ports and negotiated deals."
cards.why: The token was found in a tomb at Carthage, written in the trading partner's language. MacDonald reconstructs how such guest cards worked: the agent carried one half, and the matching half travelled with the goods as the guarantee. Its owner was buried with it.
cards.uw: You need a stranger in another port to trust your agent or your shipment.

cards.title: Write the report under the wax
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"informing it of Alexander’s plans using hidden texts, written on wooden tablets and then covered with wax."

"he was executed for treason ‘on the grounds that he had tried to sell Carthage to the [Macedonian] king’."
cards.why: Carthage's envoy Hamilcar the Rhodian got into Alexander's circle by claiming to defect, and sent reports home hidden under the wax of writing tablets. When he came back after Alexander died, Carthage executed him. His cover had convinced his own city too.
cards.uw: You are placing someone inside a rival's camp and your own side needs to know the defection is staged.

cards.title: Pay off the army in stages, in sight
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"Polybius records that Gisgo wanted to demobilise the Sicilian army in stages with each group being paid as they arrived in Carthage and then disbanded."

"Removing the soldiers to Sicca was not a strategically sound decision."
cards.why: Gisgo planned to bring the Sicilian army home in groups, paying each group off on arrival. The government let the men pile up unpaid in the city instead, then sent them to wait at Sicca, a region taxed and conscripted for 23 years. The soldiers asked where the generals who had made them promises were. The Mercenary War followed.
cards.uw: You owe a large group money you can't pay all at once.

cards.title: Full authority in the field, full liability at home
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"The Carthaginian commander in the field oversaw negotiating treaties, making decisions on settlements, judicial matters in camp and minting coinage."

"The appointment to general was a whole project at which the commander either succeeded or failed."
cards.why: A Carthaginian general made treaties, settled land, judged cases and struck coins without referring home, for as long as his war lasted. Then he answered for the result in person before a council of 104. Failure meant exile or crucifixion. Malchus, the first general on record, was prosecuted for treason.
cards.uw: You are handing someone a large project far from oversight.

cards.title: Choose for merit and for means
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"‘for the Carthaginians choose their magistrates, and particularly the highest of them – their kings [sufetes] and generals – with an eye both to merit and to wealth.’"

"Even more interesting is Herodotus’ description of Hamilcar as Carthaginian on his father’s side and Syracusan on his mother’s side, and that he had become leader at Carthage on ‘merit’."
cards.why: Aristotle, who rated Carthage's government 'excellent', says it chose sufetes and generals on two tests at once: ability and wealth. Herodotus's Hamilcar, the commander at Himera, had a Syracusan mother and rose on merit.
cards.uw: You are filling a role where talent matters and so does having something to lose.

cards.title: Marry into the neighbours
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"Success for the population at Carthage was largely dependent on the goodwill of the city’s neighbours for the first few centuries of its existence."

"Hamilcar gave his daughter in marriage to Naravas, sealing the bond between the two men."
cards.why: For centuries Carthage ate mostly locally grown food and depended on the Libyans whose land it had settled. MacDonald credits intermarriage: the mixed rural families, the Libyphoenicians, farmed and fought for the city. The habit reached the top when Hamilcar married his daughter to the Numidian prince Naravas, who arrived with 2,000 cavalry.
cards.uw: You have moved into someone else's territory and depend on them for the basics.

cards.title: Build the new base instead of patching the old
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"Founded as a modern Mediterranean city, Lilybaeum grew easily and quickly into a thriving port with up-to-date facilities and easy access to Carthage south across the sea."

"By far the longest-lasting imprint of the Carthaginians in the Iberian Peninsula took place under the command of Hasdrubal when he founded a new city on the southeastern coast."
cards.why: After Motya fell, Carthage built Lilybaeum on the Sicilian mainland nearby, and trade left the old island town. In Iberia, Hasdrubal founded New Carthage on the coast. New Carthage took the mother city's own name, Qart Hadasht, which means New City.
cards.uw: Restoring a damaged site would cost more than building a better one nearby.

cards.title: Post the price list
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"‘for each sacrifice which a person poor in cattle or in birds sacrifices the priests shall not receive [a thing]’"

"‘any priest who takes a fee against what is set in this tablet shall be fined.’"
cards.why: A tariff from the Temple of Ba'al Saphon, set by thirty men in charge of fees and dated by the sitting sufet, priced every offering from an ox down to flour and oil, in silver shekels. Clans, guilds and drinking clubs paid by the same list. The poor paid the priests nothing, and a priest who charged off the list was fined.
cards.uw: You run something where insiders set the price and outsiders can't check it.

cards.title: Atone in their rite
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"They [the magistrates of Carthage] unanimously decided to appease the offended gods by all possible means."

"they selected their most esteemed citizens as priests for these goddesses and with great solemnity, they consecrated statues of Kore and Demeter and performed rituals in accordance with Greek customs."
cards.why: A Carthaginian army sacked a temple of Demeter and Kore outside Syracuse. Diodorus says the magistrates brought the two goddesses' cult into Carthage, made leading citizens their priests, held the rites by Greek custom and appointed distinguished Greek residents to serve.
cards.uw: Your side has wronged another community and an apology won't cover it.

cards.title: Back the visiting trader's debts
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"the Romans may come for trading purposes, and the Carthaginian state engages to secure payment of their just debts."

"‘[the] Romans may not make either marauding expeditions, or trade, or found cities’"
cards.why: In Carthage's first treaty with Rome, as Polybius copied it, the Carthaginian state undertook that Roman traders would be paid what they were owed in its ports. The same text listed what Romans could not do in Carthaginian territory, and one headland, the Fair Promontory, marked where they could not sail.
cards.uw: You want outside traders in your market and need them to trust it.

cards.title: Hop port to port with land in sight
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"The way it worked is that a ship would move from port to port, region to region, dropping off and picking up goods along the way, never straying far from land."

"This shows a circular, counterclockwise navigation of the sea that accommodated winds and currents"
cards.why: The Phoenician traders Carthage came from didn't cross open water in one run. They worked the coast in a loop that went with the winds and currents, selling and buying at every stop. Each leg was short, and each port was a market.
cards.uw: You are planning a long push into new ground and want every step to pay for itself.

cards.title: Two kings, one year
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"‘in the twentieth year of the rule of the sufetes in Carthage’"

"These magistrates held the power of a king, but for a limited time."
cards.why: Carthage replaced its kings with two sufetes, elected each year from the aristocratic council, and an inscription dates itself by the new system. The office kept a king's power, split it between two people and put it on a clock.
cards.uw: You are designing the top job for a group that doesn't want a strongman.

cards.title: No wine at the helm or on the bench
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal: "At Carthage, drinking alcohol was banned if you were working on pilot boats in the ports, if you were sitting as a judge and if you were trying to conceive a child"
cards.why: The city imported Rhodian wine by the amphora and banned drinking in three places: on the harbour pilot boats, on the judge's bench and when a couple was trying for a child. The ancient source for the rule is Plato's Laws, Book II, which gives it as Carthaginian law.
cards.uw: You need a sobriety rule people will actually keep.

cards.title: A harbour that shows visitors nothing
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"‘for a double wall enclosed them, and there were gates by which merchant ships could pass from the first port to the city without traversing the dockyards’"

"It was built up to a height that allowed the admiral to observe what was going on out at sea, but anyone approaching by water did not have a clear view of the inside of the port."
cards.why: Appian describes two harbours sharing one entrance closed with iron chains. Merchant ships used the rectangular port and passed into the city through gates. Warships sat in the circular port behind a double wall, 220 berths round an island, and the admiral's house on the island watched the sea while arriving ships saw nothing of the docks.
cards.uw: One site has to host visitors and keep sensitive work private.

cards.title: Build up when you can't build out
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"The African style of building was a very stable construction method and was innovative as it allowed for walls that could bear a substantial load, and for the buildings to be built higher."

"Carthage’s growth was constrained by geographical factors: the sea lay to the east, cemeteries to the north and southwest, and to the south, the Tophet."
cards.why: Hemmed in on every side, Carthage went up. Its builders set upright stone blocks at intervals and filled between them with rubble or mud brick, which carried several storeys. The Romans admired the method and called it 'African style'.
cards.uw: Your footprint is fixed and demand keeps growing.

cards.title: Keep paying the mother temple
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"The fact that Carthage would continue to pay tribute to the temple of the god Melqart at Tyre throughout its 600-year existence makes it clear that this was a move with colonial intentions; an annual tithe points to a close and very specific relationship with the mother city."

"The young man had been on a mission to Tyre where he had taken the tribute to the great temple of Melqart from the wars in Sicily."
cards.why: Carthage sent an annual tithe to Melqart's temple at Tyre for six centuries, long after it outgrew Tyre. Malchus's son carried Sicilian war tribute there and finished the mission while his father was besieging Carthage.
cards.uw: An offshoot has outgrown its parent and wants to keep the tie on its own terms.

cards.title: Same goddess, two languages
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"Worshipped at this temple was a goddess presented in the inscription as both the Phoenician Astarte and the Etruscan Uni."

"The Etruscan texts are longer and the Phoenician translation is not literal but seems to convey the same meaning."
cards.why: Gold sheets nailed up at Pyrgi, the port of the Etruscan city of Caere, dedicate one temple to one goddess, called Astarte in Phoenician and Uni in Etruscan. The translation follows the meaning. Carthaginian merchants had a shrine of their own in an allied port.
cards.uw: You are building a partnership across languages and customs.

cards.title: Check the enemy's story against the ground
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"we know this act of mass sacrifice never appears in any of the physical evidence discovered to date – the infant cremations there are individual burials, not mass graves."

"This kind of mass sacrifice would also have caused a massive rupture in natural population growth that would have ultimately destroyed the city."
cards.why: Diodorus has 200 noble children thrown into a fire in a single day of panic. MacDonald runs two tests. The excavated Tophet holds individual burials only, and a city that did that would have wrecked its own birth rate.
cards.uw: The only account of a group comes from its enemies.

cards.title: Pick the general for war, the magistrate for office
cards.book: Carthage: A New History — Eve MacDonald
cards.steal:
"Here we can see that military duties were separated from the civic magistracies, which is unlike Rome where military leadership was predicated on holding a civil magistracy."

"A military commander could go into the civic magistracies but did not necessarily evolve out of them."
cards.why: In Rome you had to hold civil office before you could command an army. Carthage split the two tracks over time. Its general, the rab mahanet or head of the camp, was chosen for the war in front of him and held the job for that war, whatever his political career looked like.
cards.uw: Everyone assumes the person who runs the place should also lead the hard project.

cards.title: Number the notes, not the topics
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "The trick is that he did not organise his notes by topic, but in the rather abstract way of giving them fixed numbers. The numbers bore no meaning and were only there to identify each note permanently."
cards.why: Luhmann filed each new note directly behind the note it answered, so 22 became 22a and then 22a1. A topic folder forces you to decide in advance what an idea belongs to. A fixed number lets an idea grow wherever it connects.
cards.uw: Your files or notes are sorted into categories that no longer match how you actually think about the work.

cards.title: One idea per note, one screen per note
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal:
"By restricting ourselves to one format, we also restrict ourselves to just one idea per note and force ourselves to be as precise and brief as possible."

"A good rule of thumb for working digitally is: Each note should fit onto the screen and there should be no need of scrolling."
cards.why: Luhmann used A6 slips. The size limit made every note a single unit that could be moved and recombined with others later. A note holding three ideas can only ever sit in one place.
cards.uw: You're building a library of ideas, research or reusable material and want the pieces to combine later.

cards.title: Write every note for a stranger
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "Write exactly one note for each idea and write as if you were writing for someone else: Use full sentences, disclose your sources, make references and try to be as precise, clear and brief as possible."
cards.why: The stranger is your future self, who will have forgotten the context within weeks. Notes written in full sentences can be dropped straight into a draft. Keyword scraps have to be rethought from scratch.
cards.uw: You're capturing anything you expect to use in writing, a pitch or a decision months from now.

cards.title: Everything lands in one inbox, cleared within a day
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "If you use other tools, make sure everything ends up in one place, a central inbox or something like that, where you can process it soon, ideally within a day."
cards.why: Ahrens treats quick jottings as reminders of a thought, too thin to hold the thought itself. They go stale fast. One collection point and a one-day deadline turn them into proper notes or into trash before you forget what they meant.
cards.uw: Your ideas are scattered across apps, notebooks and voice memos and you can't find any of them.

cards.title: Pick the topic from what has already piled up
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "Do not brainstorm for a topic. Look into the slip-box instead to see where chains of notes have developed and ideas have been built up to clusters."
cards.why: A topic chosen by brainstorming starts with nothing behind it. A cluster of notes shows where your interest and material already are, so the project starts half-researched.
cards.uw: You need to choose your next project, essay or product idea and are staring at a blank page.

cards.title: Brainstorming is a memory test in disguise
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "Remember the lesson: ‘An idea or a fact is not worth more merely because it is easily available to you.’"
cards.why: Ahrens opens his case against brainstorming with Munger's line. What comes to mind in a session is what is most recent or vivid, which is a poor proxy for what is most promising. An external store of notes widens the pool.
cards.uw: A team is about to pick a direction from whatever ideas surface in a single meeting.

cards.title: Index by when you'll want it back
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "The archivist asks: Which keyword is the most fitting? A writer asks: In which circumstances will I want to stumble upon this note, even if I forget about it?"
cards.why: Ahrens's example is a Tversky and Kahneman finding. An archivist tags it "psychology." An economist tags it "capital allocation problems," which ties it to questions already on the table and gets it found again.
cards.uw: You're tagging files, research or bookmarks and the tags describe the item instead of the use.

cards.title: Hunt for the two ideas you believe that can't both be true
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "When we realise that we used to accept two contradicting ideas as equally true, we know that we have a problem – and problems are good because we now have something to solve."
cards.why: Laying notes next to each other surfaces contradictions that stay hidden when each idea lives in its own context. Ahrens cites Albert Rothenberg's finding that building oppositions is a reliable way to produce new ideas.
cards.uw: Your thinking on a subject feels settled and you want to find where it is weak.

cards.title: Darwin's golden rule: write down the objection at once
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "…whenever a published fact, a new observation or thought came across me, which was opposed to my general results, to make a memorandum of it without fail and at once; for I had found by experience that such facts and thoughts were far more apt to escape from the memory than favorable ones."
cards.why: Memory filters out what contradicts us. Darwin countered it by recording disconfirming facts immediately, and wrote that as a result very few objections were raised against his views that he hadn't already noticed and tried to answer.
cards.uw: You're building a case for a plan or a thesis and want the objections in hand before anyone else raises them.

cards.title: Tie yourself to the mast with the workflow
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "With a good system, the mere necessities of the workflow will force us to act more virtuously without actually having to become more virtuous."
cards.why: Odysseus didn't rely on willpower against the Sirens. Ahrens applies the same move to confirmation bias: if the system has you collect every relevant note regardless of which side it supports, good habits come from the process.
cards.uw: You keep resolving to be more disciplined and want to design the process so discipline isn't required.

cards.title: Write it down and the brain lets go
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal:
"Open tasks tend to occupy our short-term memory – until they are done."

"All we have to do is to write them down in a way that convinces us that it will be taken care of."
cards.why: Bluma Zeigarnik saw a waiter recall unpaid orders perfectly and forget them once paid. Her follow-up research showed that writing a task down in a trusted place frees the mind about as well as finishing it.
cards.uw: Unfinished tasks keep pulling at your attention while you try to focus on one thing.

cards.title: Separate writing from proofreading
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal:
"We tend to call extremely slow writers, who always try to write as if for print, perfectionists."

"A real professional would wait until it was time for proofreading, so he or she can focus on one thing at a time."
cards.why: Finding words needs loose, floating attention. Correcting them needs narrow, focused attention. Trying to do both in the same pass stalls the work, which is what gets mislabeled as perfectionism.
cards.uw: You or someone on your team edits every sentence while drafting and the draft barely moves.

cards.title: Handwriting forces you to translate
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "Handwriting makes pure copying impossible, but instead facilitates the translation of what is said (or written) into one’s own words."
cards.why: In Mueller and Oppenheimer's study, students who took notes on laptops wrote more but understood less. Slower handwriting forced them to choose and rephrase, and that processing is where the understanding happened.
cards.uw: You take long notes in meetings or lectures and remember little of what was said.

cards.title: Rereading feels like learning
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "Rereading is especially dangerous because of the mere-exposure effect: The moment we become familiar with something, we start believing we also understand it."
cards.why: Familiarity produces the sensation of knowing without the substance. Ahrens recommends testing yourself and writing the idea out in your own words, both harder and both more accurate signals of what you've learned.
cards.uw: You're preparing for a test, a pitch or a board meeting by going over the same material again.

cards.title: The introductory lecture test
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "Physicist and Nobel Prize winner Richard Feynman once said that he could only determine whether he understood something if he could give an introductory lecture on it."
cards.why: Ahrens calls reading with a pen in hand the small-scale version of that lecture. A note written for someone who lacks your context exposes the gaps that rereading hides.
cards.uw: You think you understand a subject well enough to explain it, sell it or decide on it.

cards.title: Rephrase the quote before you file it
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "Be extra selective with quotes – don’t copy them to skip the step of really understanding what they mean."
cards.why: Copying a passage feels productive and defers the thinking. Restating it in your own words forces the understanding at the moment you have the source open.
cards.uw: Your research files are full of highlighted passages you couldn't explain without rereading them.

cards.title: Compound interest versus a piggy bank
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "But the main reason is the slip-box, which compares to Trollope’s technique as investing with compounded interest compares to a piggy-bank."
cards.why: Trollope wrote 250 words every 15 minutes before work, and the pages added up linearly. Luhmann's notes linked to each other, so each new note made the old ones more useful. He published 58 books and hundreds of articles.
cards.uw: You're choosing between a daily output quota and a system where past work feeds future work.

cards.title: The slip-box got him a professorship in a year
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "He turned to his slip-box, and with its help he obtained all requirements in less than a year."
cards.why: Luhmann was a civil servant without a doctorate when Helmut Schelsky urged him toward a professorship, which normally meant years of degrees. Because his notes were already a body of work, he could write the dissertation and habilitation quickly.
cards.uw: A big opportunity opens and you need to show finished work fast.

cards.title: Do only what is easy
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "I only do what is easy. I only write when I immediately know how to do it. If I falter for a moment, I put the matter aside and do something else."
cards.why: Luhmann's statement sounds lazy until you see the system behind it. With dozens of open threads in the slip-box, there was always another task he knew how to do, so getting stuck on one never stopped the work.
cards.uw: You're grinding on one blocked task and could be moving another forward.

cards.title: Simple boxes beat optimal packing
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "Most ship owners had in fact considered the idea of putting different kinds of products into the same sized boxes as fairly abstruse."
cards.why: Experienced stevedores could pack a hold better than any standard container. Malcom McLean's container won anyway, because standardizing the unit made every step around it faster and cheaper. Ahrens argues standard notes work the same way.
cards.uw: Experts defend a custom process that performs well at one step and slows down the whole chain.

cards.title: Pretend it's just notes for yourself
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "…he wouldn’t be able to write a single sentence if he didn’t start by convincing himself he was only writing down some ideas for himself, and that maybe he could turn it into something publishable later."
cards.why: Slavoj Žižek said this in an interview about how he starts. Lowering the stakes in your own head gets the words moving. By the time he stopped, the only thing left was revising the draft he already had.
cards.uw: The importance of a piece of writing is keeping you from starting it.

cards.title: Cut to a second file you'll never open
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "For every document I write, I have another called “xy-rest.doc,” and every single time I cut something, I copy it into the other document, convincing myself that I will later look through it and add it back where it might fit. Of course, it never happens – but it still works."
cards.why: Deleting a good passage feels like a loss, so people keep material that has no job in the argument. Moving it to a holding file removes the loss and the passage disappears from the draft. Ahrens notes Richard Thaler does the same.
cards.uw: A draft, deck or product is bloated with pieces you can't bring yourself to cut.

cards.title: Keep the outline movable until the end
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "The structure of an argument is part of it and therefore will change during the process of developing it – it is not a vessel to be filled with content."
cards.why: Ahrens keeps a separate outline for each project and expects it to change until late. Once it stops changing much, he calls it a table of contents, and chapters can still move at the very end.
cards.uw: You've locked a plan or outline early and the material keeps fighting it.

cards.title: External rewards don't build a loop
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "Any attempts to trick ourselves into work with external rewards (like doing something nice after finishing a chapter) are only short-term solutions with no prospect of establishing a positive feedback loop."
cards.why: Ahrens argues motivation only sustains itself when the work produces its own visible progress. A slip-box gives that feedback every day, as notes pile up and connect.
cards.uw: You're relying on treats or bonuses to keep yourself or a team going on long work.

cards.title: The brain jumps to conclusions, paper doesn't
cards.book: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens
cards.steal: "Luhmann states as clearly as possible: it is not possible to think systematically without writing (Luhmann 1992, 53)."
cards.why: Ahrens pairs this with Kahneman's description of the brain as "a machine for jumping to conclusions." Writing an argument out makes its gaps visible in a way that thinking it through in your head does not.
cards.uw: You're about to make a decision you've only reasoned through in your head.

cards.title: Persuade the people closest to you first
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "Here’s the operating principle: All other things being equal, you’ll be most persuasive to the people with whom you have the closest connection."
cards.why: Wikler ranks outreach by how close the relationship is. Talking to undecided friends and family sits at the top. Shouting at strangers online sits at the bottom. Campaigns call the first one "relational organizing" and treat it as cutting-edge, though it is old.
cards.uw: You want to change minds and are about to start with the widest, least personal channel available.

cards.title: Lincoln's 1840 playbook
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "Keep a CONSTANT WATCH on the DOUBTFUL VOTERS, and from time to time have them TALKED TO by those IN WHOM THEY HAVE THE MOST CONFIDENCE."
cards.why: Lincoln wrote this to a Whig campaign committee. Wikler's point is that today's relational-organizing apps add data on who might be doubtful and who has talked to whom. The underlying method is unchanged.
cards.uw: You need to win over a wavering group and are deciding who should deliver the message.

cards.title: Every cheap new channel burns out
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "Whenever a new way to reach someone unsolicitedly and cheaply pops into existence—mail, texts, Facebook messages—it has a brief twinkling moment of effectiveness as a form of direct voter contact. And then it gets so totally overused that voters largely tune it out."
cards.why: Low cost invites everyone in, and saturation kills the effect. Wikler ranks channels: face-to-face beats calls, calls beat postcards, and texts to strangers mostly annoy. Human connection is the one channel that doesn't fade.
cards.uw: Your team is excited about a new cheap outreach channel because early numbers look great.

cards.title: One vote per thirty-three doors
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "The most recent review of the available evidence found that a conversation with someone at their doorstep in a “high-salience” election like a presidential race results in a 3 percent boost in that person’s likelihood to vote. So, talk to thirty-three people and (on average) you’ll generate one vote."
cards.why: Wikler tells canvassers to set expectations low. About one door in five opens, and most conversations change nothing. Knowing the base rate keeps people going through dull hours, and shows that the effect is real.
cards.uw: You're asking people to do slow, low-yield outreach and need them to understand what success looks like.

cards.title: Treat the surprising answer as a gift
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "When someone on the fence says something that surprises you, don’t sputter. Don’t judge. Instead, remind yourself that you’ve just received a gift: a chance to talk to someone who, just maybe, could vote your way because you took the time to visit."
cards.why: Wikler starts every doorstep conversation by reminding himself he has no idea what is happening in the other person's life. The undecided person is the whole point of the visit. Reacting with judgment ends the one conversation that could have moved something.
cards.uw: You're talking to someone on the fence and they say something that makes you want to argue.

cards.title: Ask voters leaving the polls to text three friends
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "When you see someone, flash them your winningest smile, and ask them if they can text three of their friends, right then, and remind them to vote early."
cards.why: Polling Place Vote Tripling, tested by the group Vote Rev, catches people at peak pride, just after voting. It turns strangers into relational organizers whose texts friends will actually read, and it reaches far more people per hour than knocking on doors.
cards.uw: You have a stream of people who just did the thing you want and could ask their friends to do it too.

cards.title: Don't lecture people a thousand miles away
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "Perhaps the most notorious example of this phenomenon came in 2004, when the UK’s Guardian newspaper launched “Operation Clark County,” urging its global readership to send personal letters to voters in Clark County, Ohio, “citizen to citizen, explaining why this election matters to you.”"
cards.why: The letters produced an avalanche of rage from Ohio voters. Outsiders telling people how to vote reads as condescension. Wikler's rule: the more the contact rests on a real relationship, the bigger the impact.
cards.uw: You're planning outreach to a community you don't belong to.

cards.title: Small groups are the secret sauce
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "Every one of the tactics listed above, and the many others you’ll discover in this volume, will be more effective when organized by a team rather than just done by you yourself. Small groups are the secret sauce of politics."
cards.why: Individual effort is fragile and hard to sustain. A team spreads the work, keeps people coming back and builds the power needed to take on bigger opponents. Wikler's advice: join a group, or start one.
cards.uw: You're trying to sustain a long effort on willpower alone.

cards.title: The lower the profile, the bigger your impact
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "The lower-profile the election, the bigger the impact of your work. If potential voters aren’t tuned in, volunteering makes a bigger difference."
cards.why: Swing voters in presidential years are buried in ads, mail and door hangers, so one more contact barely registers. In a city council race on a random Tuesday, one knock can decide a voter. Wikler calls this being an "elections hipster."
cards.uw: You're choosing where to spend limited effort and the high-profile contest is already saturated.

cards.title: Do something, regularly, for a long time
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal:
"I’m not asking you to do everything. I’m asking you to do something —regularly, for a long time."

"Movements, to flourish, need to give people time to fall back and recharge after their stints on the front lines."
cards.why: Wikler pairs this with Rabbi Tarfon's line that you are not obliged to finish the work but not free to neglect it. Rotation and modest, steady commitments keep volunteers around for years. Demanding everything burns them out in months.
cards.uw: You're asking people to commit to a long cause and they look overwhelmed.

cards.title: If you care about the big issue, talk about roads
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "That helped inspire my own mantra in the 2022 election cycle: If you care about democracy, talk about roads."
cards.why: A De Pere city council candidate ran against an opponent tied to a national scandal. She campaigned on eviction help and a highway connector project, and won. Voters trust candidates who talk about their lives, and the abstract stakes come through by contrast.
cards.uw: You care most about a big principle and your audience cares about their daily problems.

cards.title: Politics is over there, life is over here
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "For many people, all of politics—left, right, and center—is over there, whereas their real life is over here."
cards.why: In the survey Wikler cites, the biggest group of swing voters described their views in kitchen-table terms like "affordable" and "cost of living." They let the news come to them rather than seeking it out. A left-right pitch misses them entirely.
cards.uw: You're pitching to people who don't follow your field and you're about to use your field's categories.

cards.title: Meet them, bond, then ask
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "You meet people where they are. You build relationships. And then you offer an opportunity for action based on a value that you hold in common."
cards.why: Wikler presents it as the organizer's three-step sequence. Skipping to the ask turns a stranger into a target. The shared value gives the request a reason that belongs to both people.
cards.uw: You need someone to take an action for a cause and you've just met them.

cards.title: Build leaders before you knock on doors
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal:
