"She’s building relationships, looking not just for volunteers but for leaders."

"The door knocking and voter contacting begins only after the team is launched."
cards.why: In the "snowflake" model behind the Obama campaigns, the paid organizer spends weeks in one-on-one coffees recruiting a core team, and each team recruits more volunteers. Wisconsin volunteers knocked on twice as many doors in 2018 as in 2016 at roughly half the cost.
cards.uw: You're launching an effort and are tempted to start the work before you have people to lead it.

cards.title: The field margin
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "But the final percentage point or two in a campaign can come down to which side is better organized in the field—that is, which campaign has more successfully harnessed volunteer energy and turned it toward the kinds of voter contact that make the biggest difference."
cards.why: Conditions and the electorate set most of the outcome, and candidates and ads decide most of the rest. Organization only moves the last point or two. In an era of razor-thin races, that is what decides who wins.
cards.uw: The market or matchup is close and you're deciding whether execution details are worth the investment.

cards.title: Build the campaign before you know the candidate
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "…I said that we were building a “nominee-neutral presidential campaign” in Wisconsin. She laughed and responded that her goal was to build a campaign that was nominee- proof."
cards.why: Wisconsin and Michigan kept organizing teams running before the nominee was chosen. They were the only two states where the Biden campaign kept the existing infrastructure for the general election rather than building something new in the final stretch.
cards.uw: A big decision is still pending and you could start building the capability any outcome will need.

cards.title: The four years decide the last week
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "What you do in the four years between elections helps determine how many people are, by the time you reach those critical final days, already in the “decided” column."
cards.why: By the endgame of a campaign most people have chosen a side. The small group still undecided only matters if the race is close. That depends on work done long before anyone was paying attention.
cards.uw: You're saving effort for the final push of a sale, a vote or a launch.

cards.title: Move people one rung at a time
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "The idea is that, if someone’s at one rung of the ladder, your goal is to move them up to the next one."
cards.why: Organizers call it the ladder of engagement. Asking a first-time voter to staff a hotline fails. Asking them for the next small step works, and each step makes the one after it easier.
cards.uw: You want deep commitment from someone who has barely engaged yet.

cards.title: Action breeds interest
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal:
"Voting is habit-forming. It’s identity-forming."

"Once someone has taken action in politics (as in any endeavor), they become more interested in what happens next."
cards.why: A first vote in an off-year mayor's race makes a person more likely to vote for the rest of their life. Interest follows action. Getting someone to act once often matters more than convincing them first.
cards.uw: You're trying to build interest through argument and could instead get people to take one small action.

cards.title: After a loss: look at the data, keep the core
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "Take a step back. Look at the data. Listen to everyone. Use your common sense. Decide to win. Get better at it."
cards.why: Wikler warns against reading one loss as a permanent realignment. 2024 was a bad year for incumbent parties worldwide. His advice is to question tactics, message and spending hard while keeping the fundamental commitments.
cards.uw: You've just lost a big contest and people are calling for a complete reinvention.

cards.title: Strike first, on truth's side
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal:
"Our vote model isn’t the kind of thing that you can share with a media outlet. They’d assume that our analysis is just spin."

"Via my own Twitter account. Fight fire with fire; fight tweets with tweets. Strike first, on truth’s side."
cards.why: On the morning after the 2020 election, Wikler expected Trump to declare victory early. He called Wisconsin for Biden first, on his own name, based on the party's model. Twitter flagged the post as disputed. The call turned out to be correct.
cards.uw: You know something true before the official source confirms it and a false claim is about to fill the gap.

cards.title: Midterms go to the side whose turnout drops less
cards.book: This Is the Plan — Ben Wikler
cards.steal: "The party whose turnout drops by less from the presidential election is the one that wins the midterms."
cards.why: Turnout always falls in midterms. The winner is decided by which side's voters are more alarmed and mobilized. That is why the president's party nearly always loses seats.
cards.uw: You're forecasting a contest where both sides will lose participation and the question is who loses less.

cards.title: Negotiation, in one sentence
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal: "…‘negotiation is getting something by giving something, and it is the search for solutions when there are conflicts of interest between countries that meet the foreign policy goals of one country while giving enough to another to motivate it to keep its promises’."
cards.why: The definition builds in a test most deal-makers skip. A deal has to leave the other side enough to keep honoring it once the signing is over. Winning terms the counterpart will walk away from is a loss postponed.
cards.uw: You're pushing for the best possible terms and haven't asked whether the other side will still want to comply next year.

cards.title: Every public statement has two audiences
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"Public bluff and bluster intended to induce caution often induced risk-taking."

"Khrushchev had no way of knowing whether this statement was intended for a domestic audience or for him."
cards.why: David Welch finds that broadcast diplomacy before the Cuban missile crisis largely failed. Kennedy's September warning could be read as campaign talk for the midterms, which made Khrushchev's secret deployment look survivable. A message meant for one audience gets decoded by another.
cards.uw: You're sending a warning through a public channel and assuming the target will read it the way you meant it.

cards.title: Frame the threat as a shared problem
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"He was careful not to describe this as an ultimatum, but as a simple fact."

"In framing the problem thus, Robert Kennedy was, in effect, eliciting Dobrynin’s help as an ally against a common problem: namely, hawks in the US government and military."
cards.why: On 27 October Robert Kennedy told the Soviet ambassador that military action might come within days because of pressure on the president. He then offered the Turkish missiles as a carrot. Welch calls this the single most effective private channel of the crisis.
cards.uw: You need to convey a deadline without triggering the defiance an ultimatum invites.

cards.title: Let a neutral party propose your concession
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal: "Kennedy evidently felt that the idea would be more palatable to the American public and to NATO allies if Kennedy were seen to be responding to a proposal from the United Nations rather than responding to a Soviet offer, or—worse—offering a trade himself."
cards.why: Kennedy prepared a back channel so U Thant could propose the Turkey-for-Cuba missile trade if needed. The same concession costs less when it looks like accepting a third party's idea, compared with giving in to the opponent.
cards.uw: You're willing to concede something but can't be seen offering it.

cards.title: Time to cool down saved the world
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"As the audiotapes of deliberations on the first day of the private week make clear, Kennedy’s initial inclination was to respond at a minimum with air strikes against Soviet missile sites."

"The world is fortunate that Kennedy had a full week and Khrushchev nearly two full days in which to calm down and reflect."
cards.why: Both leaders' first reactions were rage. Delays from secrecy and from getting OAS approval for the quarantine gave them time to move past it. Welch worries that today's instant information would deny leaders that week.
cards.uw: You've just been provoked and the pressure is on to answer today.

cards.title: Empathy is a working tool
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"It is difficult to solve a tangible conflict of interest without understanding one’s protagonist’s wants, needs, fears, and general understanding of the world."

"The handmaiden of empathy is trust."
cards.why: Kennedy and Khrushchev stumbled into the crisis by misreading each other. Once the shock hit, they understood each other within days through limited, clumsy exchanges. Welch draws the lesson that empathy finds the settlement and trust lets you implement it.
cards.uw: You're trying to resolve a dispute without a real model of what the other side fears.

cards.title: Don't spend your trusted channel on a lie
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal: "In short, Khrushchev squandered on deception the one channel of communication President Kennedy trusted, complicating trust-building during the crisis itself."
cards.why: Khrushchev used the Robert Kennedy and Bolshakov back channel to promise he wouldn't rock the boat before the midterms, while missiles were on their way. When the crisis came, the one line Kennedy believed in had already been burned.
cards.uw: You're tempted to use a relationship built on candor to deliver a convenient falsehood.

cards.title: Ignored allies send the bill later
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"Khrushchev, as I have already mentioned, treated Castro paternalistically and at no time seriously solicited his views."

"Castro made clear that the price of his continued loyalty in the face of Khrushchev’s gross mistreatment would be billions of dollars’ worth of economic and military support year after year."
cards.why: Castro learned of the withdrawal after it was agreed and blocked UN inspections out of anger. The Soviet Union then paid for years. Leaving a junior partner out of a deal made over their head has costs that arrive after the crisis.
cards.uw: You're settling something that affects a partner who isn't in the room.

cards.title: Agree on what the words mean
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal: "But when American and Soviet negotiators met at the United Nations in New York to finalize the terms of the resolution, the Soviets were shocked to discover that the United States considered a long list of things ‘offensive’, including cruise missiles, obsolete Il-28 jet light bombers, air-to-surface rockets, guided missiles, motor torpedo boats, associated bombs or warheads, and a variety of communications and support equipment."
cards.why: Khrushchev agreed to remove the weapons Kennedy considered "offensive" and believed that meant strategic missiles. The undefined word set off a month-long "November crisis." A settlement's key terms need definitions before anyone celebrates.
cards.uw: You've reached agreement in principle and the central term hasn't been spelled out.

cards.title: Build a workaround when the formal check fails
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal: "It is a mark of the trust that Kennedy and Khrushchev had been able to build during the public week of the crisis and the early part of November that they managed a work-around whereby the Soviets permitted American reconnaissance planes to photograph departing weapons on the decks of homebound ships."
cards.why: Castro refused UN inspection, which was the agreed verification. Instead of letting the deal collapse, the two sides found another way to see the missiles leave. Verification can be redesigned when both parties want the deal to hold.
cards.uw: The agreed method of checking compliance has been blocked by someone outside the deal.

cards.title: Be an honest broker, not a neutral one
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"I much prefer the term ‘honest broker’. For me it is important that the negotiating parties know who I am, what I stand for, and where I draw the red lines."

"The more mediators hide their influence, the more they actually increase their chance of being seen as manipulative."
cards.why: Martti Ahtisaari, who mediated in Namibia, Aceh and Kosovo, separates impartiality toward the parties from neutrality on the issues. Norway's Sri Lanka mediators pressed on children's rights while staying balanced between the sides. Declared positions earn more trust than a pose of having none.
cards.uw: You're mediating between two people or teams and feel you have to hide your own views.

cards.title: Only the parties can make the peace
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"It is the negotiators who matter, not the mediators—but in some cases mediators can help."

"Mediation cannot succeed unless the right people are at the negotiating table."
cards.why: Ahtisaari warns that focusing on the mediator disempowers the parties and suggests peace comes from outside. The people at the table must be able to deliver their side. If a group has no legitimate leader, he says there is no point mediating until one emerges.
cards.uw: You're brokering a deal and one side has sent someone who can't commit.

cards.title: Test motives instead of pleading
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal: "Mediation may not be the right answer when the parties do not demonstrate serious intent to explore a political solution. In such circumstances, the mediator needs to test parties’ motives and avoid pleading for the engagement."
cards.why: A mediator who begs the parties to talk has lost leverage and may legitimize a dominant side's conduct. Ahtisaari would rather do pre-negotiation work, such as unofficial dialogue and capacity-building, until the situation is ripe.
cards.uw: You're chasing a reluctant party to the table and wondering why each round goes nowhere.

cards.title: Spoilers don't get a seat, but they get heard
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"The greatest source of risk often comes from spoilers—leaders and parties who believe that peace emerging from negotiations threatens their power, world view, and interests, and use violence to try and undermine the process."

"Spoilers do not automatically get a seat at the negotiation table, but they must be listened to."
cards.why: People who lose from a deal will try to wreck it. Ahtisaari's answer is multi-track outreach that lets issues be reframed until more people see a stake in the outcome. He doesn't hand spoilers a veto.
cards.uw: Someone who loses from a pending agreement is quietly working against it.

cards.title: Constituents need to know why
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal: "Constituents are less likely to accept an agreement reached if they have not been involved in the process enough to understand why the agreement was designed as it was and why it is the best alternative available."
cards.why: A deal that surprises the people who must live with it gets rejected even if its terms are good. In Namibia, Ahtisaari's UN staff spread across forty-two offices to build local ownership of the transition.
cards.uw: You're closing a deal at the top that the wider team will have to carry out.

cards.title: Signing is the beginning
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal: "A peace agreement is not the end, it is the beginning. The implementation of the treaty and resulting democratic changes within the society are the true test of the agreement and will take several years."
cards.why: Ahtisaari notes that many peace agreements revert to violence within a few years. Quick support for implementation reassures uncertain parties and shows early results. Treating the signature as the finish line leaves the hardest part unfunded.
cards.uw: A hard-won agreement has just been signed and attention is moving elsewhere.

cards.title: Name the stall when you see it
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"Waiting for Godot—interminably delaying for the arrival of some mythical moment when the time is perfectly ripe."

"Quicksand—bogging an initiative down in questions, objections, or demands for definitions or an inquiry."

"Ping-Pong—shunting an issue back and forth between different committees, institutions, or negotiating forums."
cards.why: Rebecca Johnson's catalogue of arms-control tactics gives names to blocking moves that rarely say no outright. Once you can name the stall, you can respond to the tactic instead of answering every new question.
cards.uw: A proposal is going nowhere through endless questions, studies and referrals.

cards.title: Fronting and slipstreaming
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"Slipstreaming—concealing preferences behind the positions of another state or delegation."

"Fronting—a form of collaborative slipstreaming, in which one delegation adopts a position that is stronger than its own interests would require, enabling others to benefit by coasting in its wake."
cards.why: In multiparty talks the loudest hardliner isn't always the only one who wants the hard line. Others may let a front-runner carry the cost of the position they quietly share. Reading who's coasting tells you where the real opposition sits.
cards.uw: One party is carrying a tough position alone in a group negotiation and the others are quiet.

cards.title: Moving the goalposts, best versus good
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"Moving the goalposts—whatever is achievable becomes by definition inadequate so that the reachable is perpetually ditched for a more inaccessible position."

"Best versus good—rejecting adequate or useful agreements on the grounds that they do not match up with some grander but less practical or accessible ideal."
cards.why: Both are defection tactics that let a party block a deal while appearing more ambitious than everyone else. They also catch sincere idealists, who walk away from a usable agreement while waiting for a perfect one.
cards.uw: Each time a deal gets close, someone declares it not good enough.

cards.title: Unpack and reframe
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"Reframing—recasting hurdles, problems, or solution options in less adversarial terms, offering integrative solutions with mutual gains."

"Unpacking—in which a problem is disaggregated or separated into its constituent parts to facilitate incremental agreement or progress."
cards.why: Johnson lists these among the constructive tactics behind positive-sum deals. Breaking a deadlocked issue into parts lets the parties bank agreement where they can. Reframing makes the remaining gap feel shared instead of adversarial.
cards.uw: A negotiation is stuck on one big all-or-nothing issue.

cards.title: Lead from a circle, not a mountain
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"Leaders need to think of themselves as being in a circle rather than atop a mountain. That means that two-way communications are more effective than commands."

"Soft power may appear less risky than economic or military power, but it is often hard to use, easy to lose, and costly to re-establish."
cards.why: Joseph Nye argues that attraction works through credibility. Credibility collapses when the audience senses manipulation. Two-way exchange persuades better than broadcasting, but results are slow and governments don't control all the tools.
cards.uw: You're trying to win people over by announcing things at them.

cards.title: Whose story wins
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal: "Politics has become a contest of competitive credibility. The world of traditional power politics is typically about whose military or economy wins."
cards.why: Nye says governments now compete for credibility with media, companies, NGOs and scientific networks. Politics in an information age may come down to whose story wins. Reputation turns into a contested asset that can be built or destroyed.
cards.uw: You're relying on authority or size to win an argument that is really about who is believed.

cards.title: Listen and then think
cards.book: The Oxford Handbook of Modern Diplomacy — Andrew F. Cooper, Jorge Heine & Ramesh Thakur
cards.steal:
"What is his advice? Above all, ‘listen and then think’ before speaking."

"On one level, this may appear elementary, but the dynamics of contemporary society militate against listening, reflection, and learning, not least as social media and electronic communication (through blogging and otherwise) have unleashed a torrent of self-expression not always matched by eagerness to learn."
cards.why: The advice comes from Jean-David Levitte, foreign policy adviser to two French presidents, as reported by David Malone. It sounds basic, but the incentives run against it: politicians score points for speaking to their own side first.
cards.uw: You're preparing what to say in a meeting where you haven't yet heard the other side.

cards.title: Choose the face the judges will choose
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal:
"Keynes asks us to imagine a newspaper which holds a contest where readers are rewarded for choosing which contestant will be chosen by the most other readers."

"The task is not to choose the most beautiful woman, but instead to choose the woman others will think is most beautiful."
cards.why: Donnelly uses Keynes' contest to explain why buying the cheapest stock on a spreadsheet can lose. Prices move on what other participants will believe next, and that is a different question from what's true.
cards.uw: You're right on the merits and need to predict how a crowd, market or committee will actually decide.

cards.title: The Smarties test for adults
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal:
"Younger children, or those without a fully developed Theory of Mind, will say that James will say: “pencils,” because they are unable to separate their own knowledge from someone else’s perspective."

"Adults in financial markets often operate like the children in the Smarties Test. They think that everyone sees the world the way they do."
cards.why: A child who has just seen pencils in the Smarties tube assumes a friend will know too. Donnelly sees the same error in traders who can't model what others believe. They keep insisting on their own view while the market moves on everyone else's.
cards.uw: You're sure the other side must see what you see.

cards.title: Early is the same as wrong, and so is late
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal:
"There is a market aphorism that says: Early is the same thing as wrong."

"You underperform as you wait for your dream trade to come true and eventually get fired three weeks before it finally works. Then again, it’s important to remember that late is the same thing as wrong."
cards.why: Being right too soon burns money, attention and credibility while you wait. Donnelly says "it's come too far, too fast" is a poor reason to bet against a move. You need a specific reason the trend will turn now.
cards.uw: You're about to bet against a trend just because it has gone a long way.

cards.title: The calmest mind wins, not the biggest brain
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal: "The money is made by those who can get outside themselves to combine second-order thinking with ultrarational behavior to forecast and exploit the emotional, irrational, and sometimes predictable behavior of the market hivemind."
cards.why: Markets keep swinging between fear and greed, and Donnelly no longer believes first-order fundamentals make money. His Principle 10 is that the most rational trader wins. Intelligence and hard work don't protect anyone from the emotions they share with the crowd.
cards.uw: You're relying on being smarter than the competition in a field driven by crowd emotion.

cards.title: Worry about what you're doing
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal: "“Brady, I want you to stop worrying about what all the other players on our team are doing. All you do is worry about what the starter is doing, what the second guy is doing, what everyone else is doing. You don’t worry about what you’re doing.”"
cards.why: Tom Brady wanted to leave Michigan because he barely got practice reps. His coach pointed his attention back to the one thing he controlled. Donnelly uses the story for his Serenity Prayer principle: separate what you can change from what you can't.
cards.uw: You're frustrated by others getting the opportunities and have stopped working on your own game.

cards.title: Forecasters herd to protect their careers
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal:
"If you put a forecast way above everyone else and the number comes in low, you look stupid. If you submit a forecast just a bit higher than everyone else, then no matter how strong the number is, you look smart!"

"Herding around the mean is rational if you want to avoid looking stupid or getting fired, but as a market professional you need to be aware that the data is not clustered the way the forecasts imply."
cards.why: Economists shade their forecasts toward the consensus, so the range of published estimates is narrower than the range of real outcomes. Actual surprises are bigger and more frequent than the clustered forecasts suggest.
cards.uw: You're treating a tight consensus of expert forecasts as a measure of real uncertainty.

cards.title: Am I doing this for fun or for money?
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal:
"Ask yourself regularly: Am I trading for fun, or to make money?"

"If you find yourself putting on the “correct” position size and then 15 minutes later doubling it because you’re bored… You’re trading for excitement, not to make money."
cards.why: Donnelly says position size should come from a calculation. Doubling it out of boredom signals that excitement is driving the decision. Being honest about the motive is the first step to separating the two.
cards.uw: You notice yourself raising the stakes on a decision because the safe version feels dull.

cards.title: Avoid ruin first, maximize returns second
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal: "Principle 14: Avoid risk of ruin first. Maximize returns second. If you blow up, there will be no returns."
cards.why: Getting stopped out on a trade that later works is a cost of staying in the game. Donnelly treats it as luck that evens out. A loss that ends the game never evens out, so survival constraints come before upside.
cards.uw: A high-return plan carries a small chance of wiping you out.

cards.title: Watch for the market eating an Oreo
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal:
"One of the best tells in markets is a market that fails to react to good or bad news."

"More often than not, a market that doesn’t respond to clearly good or bad news is going to trend in the opposite direction for the next 24 to 48 hours."
cards.why: In Rounders, Teddy KGB eats the Oreo only when his hand is strong. Donnelly's top market tell is a price that ignores the news. It suggests stronger hands are using the headline as cover to exit.
cards.uw: Something that should have moved the other side didn't, and you're inclined to ignore it.

cards.title: Find the player on tilt
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal: "In poker, the dream scenario is you run into a player on tilt. They are easy to read, they play loose, and they repeatedly put their chips in with the second or third-best hand."
cards.why: Emotional players make predictable, oversized mistakes, and that is when the calm player extracts the most. Donnelly asks the same of whole markets: can you tell when the crowd itself is on tilt?
cards.uw: The other side is visibly emotional and you're tempted to match their energy.

cards.title: Falling volatility says the move is tired
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal: "When a market enters a tight trading range after a significant move and volatility begins to contract sharply, it tells you that the order imbalance in the market has been rectified, and a more stable short- term equilibrium has been found."
cards.why: Even if prices keep inching up, shrinking swings signal that the forced buying or selling behind the move is done. Donnelly reads it as a clue that the trend is nearly exhausted.
cards.uw: A trend is still going but the swings around it have gone quiet.

cards.title: The group average isn't your average
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal:
"The simple definition of an ergodic system is one where the expected value of an activity performed by a group is the same for an individual carrying out the same activity over time."

"Nobody would choose to play this game 100 times in a row because the expected outcome is almost certain death."
cards.why: If 100 people play Russian roulette once for $10 million, the group's average is attractive. One person playing 100 times dies. Donnelly applies this to all-in betting: a positive average can still ruin the individual who repeats the bet.
cards.uw: A bet looks good on average and you'll be making it over and over with the same bankroll.

cards.title: Starting points decide the reaction
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal: "We saw opposite market reactions to identical policy announcements because the market viewed the U.S. and U.K. starting points as fragile, and Germany’s initial conditions as robust."
cards.why: In 2025 the US and UK raised spending and were punished, while Germany did the same and rallied. Debt was 130%, 100% and about 60% of GDP. The same news means different things depending on where you start.
cards.uw: You're predicting the effect of a move by copying what happened when someone else made it.

cards.title: Narrative contagion
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal:
"Narrative contagion is the process whereby a story shared by one person or organization prompts others to share their own stories, spreading narrative themes organically through a community."

"Markets are social systems, not machines that take in fundamental information and spit out logical prices."
cards.why: Stories start near a truth and then morph into caricatures as more people tell their own versions. Donnelly's example is GameStop, which began with a few Reddit posts. The spread drives sentiment and price. His advice is to watch dispassionately while the crowd goes mad.
cards.uw: A story about your industry or company is spreading faster than the facts behind it.

cards.title: Weight their view by how wide they quote
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal: "All other things equal, you should think that Jo only has 40% (0.20/0.50) of the confidence in her fair value as you do in yours."
cards.why: Donnelly quotes Agustin Lebron's example from The Laws of Trading. Your rival's price is 0.50 wide and yours is 0.20, so blend the two fair values weighted by confidence. You end up with a better estimate than blindly trusting either one.
cards.uw: The other side's number differs from yours and you have to decide how much to move.

cards.title: Don't let adverse selection paralyze you
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal:
"If adverse selection dominated, nobody would ever trade because everyone would be afraid that everyone else has better information than they do."

"If you know what you are doing, you will be adversely selecting others much more often than you are adversely selected yourself."
cards.why: Most trades in liquid markets are hedges and routine flows with no hidden information. The danger is real in thin markets, where the counterparty likely knows more and exiting is expensive. Donnelly says to fear it where it applies and nowhere else.
cards.uw: You're worried that anyone willing to deal with you must know something you don't.

cards.title: The too-hard pile
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal: "I don’t shy away from hard topics, but if the answer to the following three questions is yes, I put the topic in the too hard pile. 1. Not particularly interesting. 2. Not critical to developing an edge in my business. 3. Complex and time consuming to learn."
cards.why: Donnelly learned just enough short-term interest rate trading to read central bank expectations and skipped the rest. Years spent mastering it would barely have moved his career. A deliberate skip list frees time for what builds an edge.
cards.uw: You feel you should master everything adjacent to your work.

cards.title: Match the analysis to the time horizon
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal:
"I would write a big piece about Australian Terms of Trade and the employment situation in Australia and so on... And then go long AUDUSD with a stop loss 1% away."

"When trading (and investing), your time horizon must match your analysis."
cards.why: Donnelly's early write-ups paired analysis suited to a month or a year with trades that could be stopped out in about a day. Slow fundamentals can't protect a fast position, so the timeframe of the plan and of the evidence must line up.
cards.uw: Your argument is about the long run and your commitment can be shaken out next week.

cards.title: Count the mental capital a bet consumes
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal:
"Mental capital is an important, underappreciated and finite resource."

"This sort of trade could be mathematically positive EV but be so mentally taxing that even when it works, it has cost you more than you earned."
cards.why: Long, stressful, attention-hungry positions drain focus from everything else. People tend to bail out of them early just to relieve the anxiety. Donnelly counts that drain as a real cost of the position.
cards.uw: A project looks good on paper and would occupy your head every day for months.

cards.title: Stack new edges before the old one dies
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal: "The more profitable my strategy, the more likely someone else will discover it. Keep stacking new ideas on top of old ones. When the old ones stop working, the new ones will pay the bills."
cards.why: Donnelly's fast lead/lag correlation trades in FX were steady money in the 2000s. Then algorithms and other traders caught on and the trade disappeared. Profitable methods attract competition and get arbitraged away, so the next one has to be built while the current one still pays.
cards.uw: Your current advantage is working well and you've stopped developing a replacement.

cards.title: Your reputation is a teacup
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal:
"“Your reputation is like a teacup. Once it’s broken, it’s almost impossible to put back together.”"

"All your actions accumulate in the long run. Be nice to the person who sweeps the floors in your office."
cards.why: Donnelly opens with Ben Hunt's line and notes how old connections keep resurfacing. He says people remember how you treated them decades later. His rules: treat PAs and brokers the way you treat managing directors, and volunteer for the holiday shift. Small acts compound into a reputation.
cards.uw: Cutting a corner or snubbing someone junior looks free in the short run.

cards.title: Growth is slow and linear
cards.book: Trade Outside the Box — Brent Donnelly
cards.steal: "There is a meme that says: If you improve by 1% per day, you will be 37.78 times better after one year. It’s a nice thought, but it’s wrong."
cards.why: Bank interest compounds. Push-ups don't: a 1% daily increase would mean 770 million push-ups in five years. Expecting exponential personal gains sets people up to quit when progress turns out slow and lumpy.
cards.uw: You're discouraged that skills or results aren't compounding the way the self-help math promised.

cards.title: Ask them for the car, not the chassis
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal:
"“We’ve learned to bite off smaller pieces with our integrations, get them working well, and then expand."

"When they ask for a car, they want to see a car. They don’t want to see a chassis and then hear you say ‘once that’s right, we’ll put on the hood, the engine, and everything else.’"
cards.why: The American Cancer Society's CIO, Ricky Koch, builds small, complete integrations with a little data first. Mistakes surface early, and business teams see something that works. A half-built big system shows them nothing they can use.
cards.uw: You're building something large for non-technical stakeholders who need to see progress.

cards.title: Ship a limited scope, then iterate
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal:
"“Previously, we were built for large-scale project implementations. We’d take three to five years and roll them out only when they were as close to perfect as we could get them."

"We’ll take a limited scope, implement, and iterate. We move a lot faster.”"
cards.why: The Credit Union of Colorado switched from multi-year launches to small releases. It built integrations nearly five times faster, and its new digital member experience contributed to a 5% leap in NPS scores. Aiming for perfect at launch had mostly made launches late.
cards.uw: Your team holds releases until they're nearly perfect and projects take years.

cards.title: Efficiency isn't always the right measure
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal:
"They want to pick up the phone because that might be their weekly conversation with somebody."

"Efficiency isn’t always the right measure for success. Asking, ‘What is the value that we’re adding?’ is a better approach."
cards.why: Kalyra, an aged-care provider, nearly bought software to cut client phone calls. A regional manager pointed out that many clients live alone. For them the call was part of the service, and cutting it would have saved staff time at the cost of what clients valued.
cards.uw: You're automating away a customer touchpoint and measuring only time saved.

cards.title: Ask whose life gets easier
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal:
"Instead, ask yourself, “How will this initiative make life easier for the actual people who have to use it?”"

"It actually creates failure – expensive failure."
cards.why: Larry Quinlan, Deloitte's former global CIO, says the implementations that succeeded were the ones tightly tied to the people using them. Digital for its own sake gets redone, delayed and abandoned, and careers stall with it.
cards.uw: You're approving a technology project justified by the system rather than the user.

cards.title: My systems would work well if you stopped using them
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "They were set up to take care of technology, not people. People were an unnecessary distraction. The old IT joke was, “My systems would work well if you stopped using them.”"
cards.why: Quinlan uses the joke to describe how IT departments used to measure themselves. Today almost everything a CIO wants to do depends on other business units, so a team built to protect its systems from users fails at its job.
cards.uw: A support function is optimizing for its own metrics at the expense of the people it serves.

cards.title: The three Ps, and the biggest P
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "I would advise always thinking about the three “Ps” – people, process, and platforms. By far, the biggest “P” of all is people."
cards.why: Quinlan's test for a transformation: what will people get from it, how can you prove they're getting it, and did you ask whether they liked it. Without those answers, he says, projects flounder.
cards.uw: You're planning a rollout and the plan is mostly about the platform.

cards.title: Data is the new sand
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal:
"In my opinion, “data is the new oil” was always a simplistic and flawed concept."

"There’s no gold star for the business with the most data."
cards.why: Oil is scarce and data isn't. Lucas argues most stored data is sand: disconnected, unused and a storage cost on the ledger. Value comes from precise, accurate slices put to work, which calls for planning around demand instead of hoarding supply.
cards.uw: Your organization is collecting everything in the hope it becomes useful later.

cards.title: Bad data is worse than none
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "We’ve learned firsthand that you can have years and years of data, but if it’s not in a usable state and accurate, then it’s no good."
cards.why: Nature Fresh Farms' IT head, Keith Bradley, records every metric on its greenhouse plants. He warns that inaccurate historical data is even more of a hindrance than none, because models trained on it go wrong with confidence.
cards.uw: You're about to train or analyze on a large historical dataset nobody has audited.

cards.title: Ask the CIO: what's the status of our data?
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "It would be a very clarifying question for a CEO to ask their CIO: “What’s the status of our data?”"
cards.why: Former Ford CEO Mark Fields applies "garbage in, garbage out" to AI. Many companies announce AI plans without knowing what data they have or where it lives. One question exposes that gap before money is spent.
cards.uw: Leadership is excited about an AI initiative and nobody has checked the inputs.

cards.title: Let manufacturing see the design early
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal:
"When we started on digital transformation at Ford, I created a single data and analytics group."

"So, if the engineers had this great new idea for an engine, transmission, or HVAC system, the manufacturing folks could say, “Hold on, if you design it that way, it will cost more, and servicing it will be harder.”"
cards.why: Fields found pockets of Ford each analyzing only their own data. Pooling it let downstream teams flag costs before designs were locked. Catching the problem late had meant redone work, extra cost and slipped timelines.
cards.uw: Teams downstream discover problems only after the upstream team has committed.

cards.title: The tier-two supplier is what shuts you down
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "In my time, I never had a tier-one supplier ever shut us down. It was always the tier-two and tier-three suppliers that shut us down because we didn’t have good visibility down there and never saw it coming."
cards.why: Ford bought $90 billion a year in parts from suppliers. Risk hid where it couldn't see: its suppliers' suppliers. Fields would point a monitoring agent at their financial health and news.
cards.uw: You're assessing supply or vendor risk and only looking one level down.

cards.title: Look for the damaged plant, not the bug
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "“The moment this robot makes noise coming through, it just flies away. So, we decided not to look for bugs hurting the plant and look for plants impacted by bugs. That’s always a sure-tell sign where they are.”"
cards.why: Nature Fresh Farms' camera robots couldn't find pests, which hid under leaves and fled the noise. Switching the target from the elusive cause to its visible effect made detection work.
cards.uw: You keep failing to detect a cause directly and its effects are easy to see.

cards.title: Be willing to destroy the path
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "The biggest stigma with AI is thinking that when you’re going down a path, you have to stick to it. We’ve learned that sometimes you have to destroy that path, go back to the data, and start rebuilding it in a new way."
cards.why: Bradley says the farm has failed many times on AI projects. Treating each approach as disposable kept failures cheap, and the farm's yield runs eight to ten times traditional farming per square meter.
cards.uw: A project is failing and the team feels committed to the approach it started with.

cards.title: Change management starts at go-live
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "Lastly, change management doesn’t end with the change itself. In some regards, that’s when the change management starts. Prepare for the first six months similarly to the previous six months before a go-live."
cards.why: Tropicana had about 18 months to build a full IT operation when PepsiCo sold it. Its CIO, Jeff Lischett, budgets the same effort after launch as before it, because adoption problems only show up once people use the new system.
cards.uw: You're planning a big rollout and the plan ends on launch day.

cards.title: Moving out of mom and dad's house
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "“We described it as ‘moving out of mom and dad’s house.’ It pulled the team together and unified a clear intention in building our own capabilities – built by us, for us.”"
cards.why: A simple, shared metaphor turned a technical carve-out into a story everyone understood. Lischett paired it with two fixed principles, simplicity and speed, and the team met its timeline.
cards.uw: You're leading a team through a complex separation or launch and need everyone pointed the same way.

cards.title: Know what you're building before you pick up the hammer
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "Everyone thinks, ‘My data is my data, and that’s exactly the way I want it.’ My advice is to get your arms around your data and decide what you want and can do before you get started."
cards.why: Cornell's integration architect, John Parker, found the hard part was matching data to satisfy parties who each wanted it their own way. Agreeing on scope first avoids building something no side accepts.
cards.uw: You're starting a project that merges information owned by several teams.

cards.title: Every system thinks it's the smartest in the room
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "“Every system, probably just like every person, probably thinks that they are the smartest one in any conversation. But you need integration, sitting between them, smiling, and making their interactions work."
cards.why: Abhinav Gaur, who speaks four languages, manages integrations at Tony's Chocolonely. He compares systems to people who each believe their own grammar is correct. The fix is a go-between that lets each side keep its own terms.
cards.uw: You're mediating between teams, partners or systems that each insist on their own way of working.

cards.title: How many more beakers for five dollars?
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "“My whole goal is to reduce IT as a cost center and ensure more money is put into the mission,” he said. “I think about it in simple terms. How many more beakers can you buy with an additional $5? How many more nights can we provide in a lodge stay if I save $100?”"
cards.why: Koch translates back-office savings into the mission's own units, research beakers and lodge nights for patients. It makes cost-cutting concrete for everyone and ties a support team's work to the goal.
cards.uw: You need a team to care about costs that seem far removed from the real work.

cards.title: Disruptive and overhyped at the same time
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal:
"It’s both incredibly disruptive and overhyped. It’s possible to believe both things simultaneously."

"The hallucination problem will not just go away. It’s fundamental to the nature of the technology."
cards.why: Vishal Sikka, SAP's former CTO, holds both views. AI can't do certain things people assume it can, and it is still enormously powerful. Holding both keeps you from overbuying and from dismissing it.
cards.uw: A debate about AI has split into hype versus skepticism and you need a working position.

cards.title: We always underestimate the rollout
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "Three to five years. We always underestimate how long it will take to get these technologies into the real world and consume them."
cards.why: Former Red Hat CEO Paul Cormier compares AI to Linux, when there weren't enough engineers for every company to hire its own. Skills, not the technology, set the pace. He still says to invest and experiment now.
cards.uw: You're setting expectations for when a new technology will pay off.

cards.title: Ninety percent of your apps nobody approved
cards.book: Digital Impact — Steve Lucas
cards.steal: "One notable example of digital chaos was that 89% of the 200-plus applications at Australian Red Cross consisted of “shadow IT” – deployed without the technical team’s knowledge or oversight."
cards.why: The result was siloed data, poor visibility and security risk. The overhaul started with finding out what was actually running, then replaced the tangle with seven core systems and one connectivity layer, and cut about 10% of its applications.
cards.uw: You're planning a technology overhaul and assuming your inventory of tools is complete.

cards.title: The fire-in-the-belly test
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“Can you live with yourself if you pass on it?” he’ll ask. “Or will you always look back and say, ‘What if?’"
cards.why: Todd Young ran for Congress as a virtual unknown with newborn twins, after thoughtful people told him it probably wasn't achievable. He now asks this question of anyone seeking his advice about running. It tests desire, which the odds can't measure.
cards.uw: You're weighing a long-shot venture and the analysis says no.

cards.title: Fill the reservoir of trust before you need it
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal:
"But Todd had made a point of building relationships across the aisle, what he calls “a reservoir of trust and goodwill.”"

"“We also discovered a mutual animus toward the Chinese Communist Party,” Todd says."
cards.why: Young and Chuck Schumer met on stationary bikes in the Senate gym while leading opposing campaign committees. Months of small talk surfaced a shared enemy. That became the CHIPS Act, a bill to bring semiconductor manufacturing back to the United States.
cards.uw: You'll eventually need a deal with a rival and have no reason yet to talk to them.

cards.title: Talk only about the substance
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“Obviously I work for the president and he’s in the opposing party, but I never felt that made a difference. We always just talked about the substance.”"
cards.why: Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo, from the other party, said this about working with Young on CHIPS. Keeping talks on the policy itself kept party identity from becoming the subject of the negotiation.
cards.uw: You're negotiating with someone from a camp your side distrusts.

cards.title: It's always easier to vote no
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“It’s always easier to vote no,” says John Connell, Todd’s chief of staff for fifteen years. “But we had to compromise on stuff. He always took those votes—acknowledged their shortcomings—but approached it with kind of a realistic perspective. And he never hid the ball from his constituents.”"
cards.why: During the 2011 debt-ceiling standoff, many Republicans privately backed the compromise and voted against it in public. Young voted yes and explained the flaws openly. Owning an imperfect deal out loud builds more credibility than a safe no.
cards.uw: You support a compromise that has obvious flaws and opposing it would be easier.

cards.title: Be ready to be misunderstood by your own side
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "This is not hard if you feel like you don’t share the values of a particular group of constituents. But it becomes very challenging—and requires what I would call moral courage—to stand your ground with people whose values you share."
cards.why: Young says the right vote is usually clear. The hard part is holding it when people he loves and respects disagree. He sees himself as their trustee, with no duty to follow a daily opinion poll.
cards.uw: People you respect are pressing you to reverse a decision you still believe is right.

cards.title: Pick the one that's easier to explain
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“Pick the one that’s easier for you to explain,” Manchin advised Mark."
cards.why: Joe Manchin gave this to Mark Kelly when he was a freshman senator. Kelly had spent a career on carriers and launch pads, where what counted was making good decisions and articulating them clearly. If you can't explain a choice to the people affected, that tells you something about the choice.
cards.uw: Two options look close and you'll have to defend whichever you pick.

cards.title: Stop counting the political cost
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“If you do this job and you’re always worried about the political consequences, it’s just not fun,” he says. “If I lose an election because of something I voted for, or something I said that I know to be true, so what?"
cards.why: Kelly backed a border bill that a dozen Arizona immigrant groups called a betrayal. Accepting the worst case ahead of time removed the pressure that had made the decision hard.
cards.uw: Fear of backlash is shaping every decision you make.

cards.title: Lead, follow, or get out of the way
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“She likes to say the Navy taught her that you lead, follow, or get the hell out of the way,” Jason says. “And Mikie’s not someone who just stands there.”"
cards.why: After the disastrous 2024 debate, Mikie Sherrill's leader asked members to wait. She called on the president to step aside anyway, thinking she might have ended her career. She was elected governor of New Jersey the following year.
cards.uw: Your group is stalled waiting for someone else to move first.

cards.title: Run the race your way
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“Mikie ran the race her way,” says her onetime campaign manager turned adviser Mollie Binotto. “Based on her values, her strengths, to show people who she was and what kind of leader she would be.”"
cards.why: Sherrill's governor's campaign was built around her own record and style, and she won. A campaign shaped around the candidate's strengths is easier to sustain and harder to copy than one built from consultants' templates.
cards.uw: You're launching something and advisers want you to look like everyone else in the field.

cards.title: Make them try to be like you
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“I just have one piece of advice,” the Speaker said. “Do not spend a second trying to be like them. Make them try to be like you. If you do that, you might actually have a shot at winning this thing.”"
cards.why: Wes Moore showed up to a ninety-five-degree forum in shorts while the career politicians baked in suits, and was mocked as a vanity candidate. Speaker Adrienne Jones told him to keep his difference. He went on to win the governorship.
cards.uw: You're the outsider in a field and feel pressure to imitate the incumbents.

cards.title: Ten bills, ten signatures
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "In his initial twelve months, Wes proposed ten priority bills and signed all ten into law, each with bipartisan support."
cards.why: Moore kept a countdown clock of his term on his desk. A short, fixed list let him put full weight behind each item and finish all of them, which a long agenda wouldn't have allowed.
cards.uw: You're setting first-year priorities and the list keeps growing.

cards.title: Deliver an ironclad bloc
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal:
"Brian assured him he had thirteen Republican votes, “ironclad.”"

"All thirteen Republicans in Brian’s bloc held firm and provided the winning margin."
cards.why: Brian Fitzpatrick sent the White House a daily whip count on the infrastructure bill. A small, disciplined bloc that keeps its word becomes the deciding vote. That made a handful of minority-party members essential to the president's signature bill.
cards.uw: You lead a small group in a close contest and could trade its unity for influence.

cards.title: State your price, then stop talking
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "Republican leaders had stopped calling Brian. In his view, they knew where he stood. He had told them what he needed changed to get his vote. They knew how to reach him if they made his changes."
cards.why: During a seven-hour floor vote, the longest in House history, the Speaker pleaded with every holdout. Fitzpatrick's specific, stated conditions left nothing to haggle over. The next move belonged to the other side.
cards.uw: You're being pressured to fold and have already told the other side what it would take.

cards.title: Go home to your bosses
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "He often remembers his older brother’s advice: “Once votes are done, get on the train and get the hell out of D.C. Get back home to be with your bosses.”"
cards.why: Party leaders kept telling Fitzpatrick to "put the jersey on." Time in the district reminded him who he actually answers to, which made the pressure in Washington easier to resist.
cards.uw: You spend most of your time with peers and insiders and want to stay anchored to the people you serve.

cards.title: Do something, or be something?
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal:
"He opened with a question: “Are you here to do something, or to be something?”"

"If they wanted to do something, to legislate and shape outcomes, Dan said they would need to build relationships across party lines, keep their word, and resist the urge to speak out on every cultural flashpoint."
cards.why: Dan Crenshaw asked newly elected members of Congress this at Harvard. Being something rewards attention and outrage. Doing something requires the quieter discipline of relationships and kept promises.
cards.uw: You're starting a new role and deciding what kind of reputation to build.

cards.title: Try harder not to be offended
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "Good rule in life: I try hard not to offend; I try harder not to be offended."
cards.why: Saturday Night Live mocked Crenshaw's eye patch, which covers a wound from Afghanistan. He answered on Twitter with this line before his complaint, and the show invited him on to accept an on-air apology. Grace under attack won him a larger audience than anger would have.
cards.uw: Someone takes a public shot at you and you want to come out ahead.

cards.title: Marine Corps Leadership 101 for a campaign
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“I applied Marine Corps Leadership 101 to the campaign,” Phaneuf recalls. “Look out for your people, give them a clear plan, and hold them accountable. We listened to advice from our general consultant and pollster, asked tough questions, made decisions, and ruthlessly executed.”"
cards.why: Seth Moulton's campaign manager had never run a phone bank. Local Democratic leaders told Moulton to run for school board instead. They beat a senior incumbent no Democrat had challenged in fourteen years, with a coalition that bypassed the party establishment.
cards.uw: You're running a first-time team on an underdog project.

cards.title: Leaders asking for help gives others permission
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "Seth recalls, “A vet came up to me in Nevada and said, ‘I decided that if a Marine serving in Congress can find the courage to ask for help, then I can, too.’”"
cards.why: Moulton spoke publicly about his own post-traumatic stress, a lesson he says his young Marines taught him. The veteran told him it was the first time since Vietnam he had dealt with his own. When someone senior goes first, it lowers the cost for everyone below.
cards.uw: You want people on your team to raise problems they've been hiding.

cards.title: Mission first, people always
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "That night in Baghdad, John came to understand an Army saying that he would carry for the rest of his life: “Mission first, people always.”"
cards.why: The saying holds two priorities John James learned as an Apache pilot: the job comes first in sequence, and the people doing it are never expendable.
cards.uw: A deadline is pulling you toward burning out the people who meet it.

cards.title: Get advice, make your own call
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“They taught us to be objective by listening to both sides,” Lorron recalls. “They taught us to seek advice from people we respected—but to make our own decisions in the end.”"
cards.why: James's brother describes how their parents raised them. Hearing both sides and asking trusted people widens what you see. Keeping the final decision with you keeps you accountable for it.
cards.uw: You're gathering opinions on a big decision and risk handing it to the loudest adviser.

cards.title: Know the boss's priorities and get them done
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“Always have a smile,” he says, describing his approach to service as a junior officer. “Always be energized. Work hard. Know what the priorities are for the boss. Get’em done.”"
cards.why: Don Bacon graduated with the most demerits in his class and the title Most Improved, then rose to brigadier general. His formula for a junior officer is to bring energy, find out what matters to the person above you, and finish it.
cards.uw: You're new in a role and want to become indispensable quickly.

cards.title: Make them earn your vote
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“I will never let anyone bring me to my knees like that,” he says. “If you’re going to get my vote, you’re going to earn it."
cards.why: When White House aides hinted that destroyer funding for Maine depended on his vote, Jared Golden called it an illegal quid pro quo. The funding stayed. Refusing a threat on the spot made the next one less likely.
cards.uw: The other side links an unrelated favor to your agreement.

cards.title: Follow the sources, find who paid
cards.book: Courage Can Save Us — Rye Barcott
cards.steal: "“Dig into it,” he says. “If you read a book, follow the sources. Find out who paid for the book.”"
cards.why: Golden picked up this habit at Bates instead of taking cues from party leaders or advocacy groups. When his staff pressed him to declare a position on impeachment before the hearings ended, he refused and studied the record first.
cards.uw: You're forming a view on a contested issue from secondhand summaries.

cards.title: Know your weekly nut
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "At this point the business model was pretty simple: if I could sell $3,400 worth of ads in the newspaper, I would break even."
cards.why: Portnoy moved home, cut every other expense and reduced the business to one number. Every week was a fight to hit it. A single break-even target tells you exactly how much selling the week requires.
cards.uw: You're running a new venture on thin cash and the finances feel vague.

cards.title: Sell the ads before the paper exists
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "How do you sell ads for a newspaper that doesn’t exist? On promises."
cards.why: Portnoy pitched Hooters and gambling companies on one thing: his paper would reach men aged twenty-five to thirty-five, their exact customers. A tight audience promise was enough to bring in revenue before the first issue printed.
cards.uw: You need paying customers before you have a finished product.

cards.title: Call every advertiser your competitors have
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "I’d sift through all my competitors’ publications in Boston and call every single one of their advertisers every single week to poach them to Barstool."
cards.why: Competitors' pages are a free, pre-qualified list of businesses that already pay for exactly what you sell. Portnoy worked the list weekly instead of hunting for new categories of buyer.
cards.uw: You're looking for your first customers and your competitors publish who theirs are.

cards.title: The job ad that filters for love of the game
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "Barstool is looking to hire writers. We don’t pay at all, but we make up for it by offering zero benefits."
cards.why: Only a few people answered. Three of them became the original "Core 4" with Portnoy, and one still writes for Barstool two decades later. A blunt ad screens out everyone except the people who would do the work anyway.
cards.uw: You can't pay yet and need contributors who care about the work itself.

cards.title: Hire for a track record of output
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "I needed to see that prospective hires were consistent over time; that they had been updating and adding to their own blog at a pace and frequency that were within the realm of how we did things at Barstool."
cards.why: Big Cat was a caller to Portnoy's radio show who already ran his own Chicago blog. Portnoy knew within seconds that he was the hire. An existing body of work at your pace beats any interview.
cards.uw: You're hiring for a role where sustained output matters and candidates can show what they've already made.

cards.title: Let talented people run wild
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal:
"For months, I had tried to guide, nudge, and suggest what Jenna should do for content. The work that came from those efforts was okay… nothing great or memorable."

"…the lesson here was simple: hire great, talented people and let them run wild."
cards.why: Jenna Marbles' breakout video, made on her own, became the most viral thing a Barstool employee had ever released. Portnoy's direction had produced nothing comparable. Talent does its best work on ideas the boss couldn't have come up with.
cards.uw: You've hired someone strong and catch yourself steering their ideas.

cards.title: Rising nobodies beat established stars
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal:
"In twenty years of doing this shit, I’ve learned that it is far easier to work with nobodies or people who are on their way up than established stars."

"But the more you pay people, the more they feel that they’re doing you some kind of favor."
cards.why: Portnoy paid an unknown $20,000 for an entire spring tour and had a great time. On the next tour he paid established acts over $100,000 a show, and they arrived late and didn't care. The money bought less commitment.
cards.uw: You're deciding between a proven big name and a hungry up-and-comer.

cards.title: Find out what's actually selling the tickets
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "The other (and more important) thing I learned was that Barstool was driving the ticket sales; not the artists."
cards.why: Paying for far bigger acts sold exactly the same number of tickets as the cheap tour, and fans wanted photos with Portnoy. He swore off paying for outside talent. The next tour used in-house people and cleared about $200,000 a night.
cards.uw: You're paying a premium for an outside draw and haven't tested whether your own brand is the real pull.

cards.title: Keep it skeleton until demand proves itself
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "It was a skeleton structure that we would add only a few minor bells and whistles to as the tour picked up steam."
cards.why: The Blackout Tour started as a sponsor's free frat parties with blacklights from Spencer's Gifts and a house DJ. Portnoy rented equipment at first and only bought lasers and cannons once ticket sales kept rolling in.
cards.uw: You're launching an experiment and want to spend on production before you know anyone will come.

cards.title: Give each crowd its own night to win
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal:
"Well, each show was assigned to a different college. So Monday was Barstool Blackout BC, Tuesday was Barstool Blackout BU, Wednesday was Suffolk, Thursday was Northeastern, etc."

"Pretty clever marketing on our part because each school wanted to brag that they had the best party."
cards.why: One generic Boston show would have competed with itself. Branding each night to a rival school turned school pride into demand, and the House of Blues sold out five straight nights.
cards.uw: You're selling the same event or product to several groups that compete with each other.

cards.title: Match the expectation the video set
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "But one thing was very clear to me: we needed to have the same special effects that the Iowa video did. That’s what these kids were expecting."
cards.why: The Iowa recap video made the party look bigger than it was, and frats across the country emailed asking to book it. Portnoy saw that the video had become the product promise, so every stop had to deliver CO2 cannons.
cards.uw: Your marketing has set an expectation and the actual product hasn't caught up.

cards.title: Don't beg for investment
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "If you ever have to beg for an investment, if you feel like a used car salesman during the process, if you aren’t 100 percent comfortable saying yes to a deal, then don’t do it. Investment should never be a last resort or come out of desperation."
cards.why: Portnoy wasn't looking for money when the Chernin Group approached. He gave them access to his analytics and nothing else. Being able to walk away is what let the price rise.
cards.uw: You're raising money and the process feels like pleading.

cards.title: Show them the engine, skip the pitch
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "So the only thing I really did was give them access to our Google Analytics numbers so they could see what was under the hood."
cards.why: The data showed most readers typed in the URL directly and stayed, refreshing all day like it was a fantasy sports site. That stickiness made the case better than a deck could have.
cards.uw: You have a metric that proves your value better than any presentation.

cards.title: Direct visitors are worth more than clicks
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "They were direct, intentional visitors who knew where they were going and what they wanted to find."
cards.why: Portnoy turned down a link-sharing program that would have padded traffic. Drive-by clicks didn't buy T-shirts. People who came on purpose bought merch, commented and stayed, and that was what investors paid for.
cards.uw: You're tempted to inflate traffic or user numbers with visitors who don't care about you.

cards.title: Take the deal when the timing and the partner are right
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal:
"The opening bid from Peter Chernin and Mike Kerns was $7.5 million for 51 percent of the company, and I would retain all creative control over the content. It wasn’t just low; it was embarrassingly low."

"The timing was right and the number seemed right. It wasn’t even close to what the company was actually worth, but it all worked out in the end."
cards.why: Portnoy expected the talks to end at $7.5 million. Chernin came back at $12.5 million. He took it for $5 million of personal security, an end to his personal liability, equity his partners could cash in and an investor he trusted. Five years later the company sold at a $650 million valuation.
cards.uw: An offer undervalues you but solves your real constraints and comes from a partner you trust.

cards.title: Name the one term you'll walk over
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "What Chernin didn’t get at first is that this wasn’t a negotiation. It was take it or leave it. You either give Dan the $7 million signing bonus or I walk from the deal."
cards.why: During the Penn sale, Portnoy demanded a $7 million bonus for a partner whose equity hadn't paid out. Chernin first refused, then tried to split the cost with him. With the whole deal at stake, they paid.
cards.uw: You have one term you're truly willing to walk away over and the other side treats it as negotiable.

cards.title: Your investors are business partners
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "The Chernin guys did what they said. They gave us money. They gave us credibility. They stayed out of our way. But they will run you over if they think it’s in their best interests."
cards.why: This is the reference Portnoy gives founders. Chernin turned a $12 million stake into about $250 million and never offered him a raise or held a celebration. Expecting loyalty would have turned a good deal into a grievance.
cards.uw: You're taking money from investors and want to know what to expect from them.

cards.title: Pay before they ask
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal:
"If I think an employee of mine deserves a raise, I give it to them often before they ask for it."

"The way I do things is if you’re killing it, I renegotiate and pay you more."
cards.why: Portnoy saw the other side of this with Chernin, who never offered him more. He was ready to walk away from his own company. Unprompted raises keep strong performers from shopping themselves around.
cards.uw: Someone on your team is clearly outperforming their deal and hasn't brought it up.

cards.title: The SNL model: launch stars and expect them to leave
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "We want to create superstars, and if they leave for more money or better opportunities, that just proves our business model works and helps us find the next star."
cards.why: Pat McAfee, Alex Cooper and others built their brands on Barstool and left. Portnoy treats departures as proof of the system. Treating them as betrayals would push the company to hoard talent it can't hold.
cards.uw: Your best people keep getting poached and you're deciding whether to fight it or build around it.

cards.title: When the partnership splits, ask for the IP
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal:
"“I don’t want Sofia, even if she decides to take the deal. Can I get the entire IP for myself if I honor the deal?”"

"“Sure,” I said. Sofia had dragged her feet. You snooze, you lose. Better to have one than none."
cards.why: Call Her Daddy's two hosts held out on their contract together. When Alex Cooper asked to take Portnoy's offer alone, he agreed and kept the show. Splitting a joint holdout gave him a deal with the party who wanted one.
cards.uw: You're negotiating with a group that is holding out and one member wants to settle.

cards.title: Keep the name in-house
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "Why would I give the IP to somebody else? If I was going to make a frozen pizza, I wanted to own the pizza and the name and not let somebody else get rich off my IP."
cards.why: His sales team had agreed to lease the One Bite name to a pizza maker for ad dollars. Portnoy stopped the deal and restructured it so Barstool owned the product. He then had to admit on camera that the first version tasted bad.
cards.uw: A partner offers easy money to put your brand on their product.

cards.title: Buy it back for a dollar
cards.book: Cancel Me If You Can — Dave Portnoy
cards.steal: "At the time, Barstool was losing close to $12 million a year. I would buy the entire company back for one dollar, taking us off Penn’s books and inheriting all the expenses."
cards.why: Penn needed a money-losing asset gone to pursue its ESPN deal. Portnoy offered to take on the losses in exchange for ownership, plus a ten-year promise not to disparage ESPN Bet. A buyer's need to unload can be worth more than the price.
cards.uw: The owner of something you want is under pressure to get rid of it.

cards.title: Find the need: time and respect
cards.book: Matriarch — Tina Knowles
cards.steal: "Every woman I’d talked to hated that they’d sit in a salon for five hours—eating lunch under a dryer, listening to gossip—when they had a job or kids to get back to. I had found my niche, the consumer need that is vital to a new business: time and respect."
cards.why: Headliners priced high and aimed at professional women because Knowles respected that their time wasn't cheap. Her business plan came from hours she and her friend Cheryl had wasted in salons. The niche was a complaint every potential customer already had.
cards.uw: You're looking for a business idea and keep thinking about products instead of what annoys your customers.

cards.title: A cheap first visit, if you trust the product
cards.book: Matriarch — Tina Knowles
cards.steal:
"The flyer offered a $9.95 shampoo-and-blow-dry and reconstructive treatment for a first-time visit only—Mathew’s idea for a can’t-resist deal that would get people in the door."

"I could do that because I was confident in the service we would provide—and the power of deep conditioning."
cards.why: The stylists disliked giving away a thirty-dollar service. Knowles bet that one visit would convert women at the light, gas and water companies into regulars. At the grand opening she was booking days ahead. A loss-leader only works when the product sells itself on the second visit.
cards.uw: You're launching and debating whether to discount the first experience.

cards.title: Belonging is the secret of branding
cards.book: Matriarch — Tina Knowles
